#6113. Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core

I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania. Through the window, slightly fogged from the chilly morning air at 5,700 feet, I see the culprits: five chestnut-colored cows munching on grass just feet from my bedside, their bells and tails swinging away.

The Albanian Alps are one of our Best Places to Go in 2027.

I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass. Yesterday’s 10-mile trek from Çerem to Dobërdol is still fresh in my mind: dusty dirt trails edged with wild blueberries I couldn’t resist picking and patches of willow gentian, their petals so intensely purple they matched the berry stains on my fingers. The forests of pine, beech, and spruce in these parts are thick enough that the daylight dims inside of them; the valleys dizzyingly deep as they fold in on themselves.

The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro.

Local-owned guesthouses welcome trekkers with included meals, like fresh vegetables, homemade dairy, and cured sausages and meats.

It’s mid-September, and only 7 a.m., but breakfast is already in full swing, not an empty seat left at the tables squeezed into the cozy timber-framed room. The Kurmekaj brothers, our hosts, are frantically grabbing four plates apiece from the kitchen, loaded with fried eggs, sausage, fresh sheep cheese, and cucumber-and-tomato salad, a fixture on the Balkan plate. I do my best to duck out of their way as the door behind me swings open and more trekkers pile in.

This is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask. Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail offers both busy sections and quiet side trails where your only companions may be a single hiker or group of grazing cattle.

By those measures, it has been remarkably successful. A late 2025 study published in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism estimated that roughly 43,000 hikers now walk the trail each year—up from regional estimates of roughly 20,000 in the pre-pandemic era—injecting more than €25 million ($27.7 million USD) annually into mountain regions where family homes, shepherd settlements, and seasonal villages have increasingly become guesthouses for trekkers. But that success is also beginning to crowd some of the places that the trail was created to support, as a growing number of travelers takes interest.

Ricardo Fahrig of the Albania-based adventure travel company Zbulo, which has been running Peaks trips since the trail’s early years, helped me piece together my own self-guided route on these trails. He says the contrast between busy Dobërdol and the quieter terrain I’m soon to enter after breakfast gets to the heart of the issue. “It’s not the number of travelers on the Peaks of the Balkans trail,” he tells me, “but rather the distribution. Some sections remain sparsely visited, while others, like Dobërdol, struggle with volume during a relatively short season”, a period from roughly June through September, with some hikers continuing into early October.

After breakfast, just a few steps down the trail from the guesthouse in Dobërdol, the clatter and congestion of the morning fade immediately. So do the other trekkers, flowing like a stream up the steep green lip of the expansive bowl-shaped valley we all woke up in, then onward to Milishevc, Montenegro, the usual stop after Dobërdol.

Stepping off the primary Peak of the Balkans trail—which the writer did with a self-guided itinerary from Zbulo—allows for quieter moments and a greater sense of solitude.

All except two. Stef Van Dam, a seasoned Dutch thru-hiker I’d met on my second day on the trail, falls into step beside me on the cattle-worn traces of the route we've chosen to take instead. He, too, is detouring off the official trail. Whereas I’m headed for the heart-shaped lake below Gjeravica, Kosovo’s highest peak, he will peel off later to summit it—“the peak of the Peaks of the Balkans,” he calls the mountain.

At the empty pass marking the Albania-Kosovo border, 1,600 feet of ascent later, we collapse onto the same rock—for all we know, Van Dam is munching his apple in Albania while I air my blisters in Kosovo just next to him. From up here, this border is steeped in irony—a line so invisible we have to guess at where exactly it’s drawn, yet a matter that has been fought over, fortified, closed, and redrawn for more than a century.

Ahead, a narrow dirt track just below the Kosovo side of the pass continues along the contour line, snaking through the treeless and boulder-strewn landscape. To our left and many mountain miles away, we spot the village of Junik where we’re both planning to sleep that night, me in a gueshouse and Van Dam in his tent somewhere nearby. As if marking the spot, a golden eagle circles in the unblemished autumn sky above it.

“This is exactly what I came to this trail to find,” Van Dam says, the first to interrupt the silence. “I wanted something quiet, more remote than other trails in Europe. I’ve found it here.”

Having myself walked a few of the more notably crowded European trails, including the Camino de Santiago, I know what he means. Besides the two of us and the eagle riding the thermals overhead, there isn’t another soul in sight.

Along the route, small guesthouses warmly welcome trekkers, who have created a reason to stay—or return—to communities once disrupted by conflict and emagration.

By late afternoon, after Van Dam and I part ways below Gjeravica. What appeared as a scattering of rooftops no bigger than a thumbnail now reveals itself in the distinct forms of summer homes and traditional katuns, seasonal shepherd settlements composed of simple huts and stone-walled livestock pens.

The family has only recently begun welcoming trekkers into their home, and they radiate the kind of excitement that comes from still being delighted by every single arrival. Renaja leads me to my room for the night, tucked on the third floor beneath the A-frame eaves. Downstairs, pizza bakes in an old wood-burning stove while Renaja's mother and grandmother set a long table for the dozen or so guests still dribbling in.

The old highland idea of besa—that a house belongs not only to its owner, but to God and to the guest—is coming to life before my eyes. Or, as Fahrig, who first came to these mountains in 2012, later puts it: bukë, kripë, zemër, an Albanian expression meaning “bread, salt, and heart.” “The material offering may be simple,” he says. “The welcome is what makes it memorable.”

The following morning, I continue deeper into Kosovo, eventually rejoining the main Peaks of the Balkans route. Now, it’s Montenegro on the other side of the invisible line I keep crossing. Over the coming days, the trail shifts between empty mountain passes and occasional stretches of asphalt—the latter one being a reason, Fahrig says, that many trekkers truncate this section entirely. He estimates that places such as the Rugova Gorge—a river-carved passage whose 2-3,000-foot-deep limestone walls bear stone-blasted tunnels, a frothy emerald river, and viewpoints at every turn—currently receive around 30 percent or less of the traffic funneled through Dobërdol.

The Peaks of the Balkans stitches together sections that include dirt paths, country roads, and sometimes asphalt—but even the less photogenic portions lead to impactful destinations.

In Drelaj, where this dramatic gorge opens into a wider pastoral valley, skipping Kosovo begins to feel like missing the point. This quiet highland hamlet is embraced on all sides by forested mountains. Across its green curves and garden plots are chalet-like summer homes built out of wood and stone, each boasting a balcony or porch turned toward the mountains and the mosque whose slender minaret rises at the center of it all.

After a day of sharing the trail with more cows than people, passing by deserted villages, and hugging a gully’s edge on a heavily eroded and unpaved fire road, I eventually spill out of the forest onto asphalt that ends in Drelaj. My guesthouse, Konaku i Malsorit, is tucked just to the right of the minaret. An Albanian flag (this part of Kosovo is majority ethnic Albanian) whips in the breeze above the two-story home and its garden, ripe with peppers, tomatoes, onions, and maize.

Minarets dot the skyline in even small villages in Kosovo and Albania.

My host Blendi Lajqi tells me his family fled Drelaj during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War after their home was burned by Yugoslav and Serbian forces. He was six years old. After the war, the family moved to Peja, the nearest major city, and for around two decades, he says, the house and the land they left behind here were “dead, no longer a home.” The creation of the trail gave his family—and others in the village—a reason to return and reinvest in what they left behind. Looking around at it now, “dead” is hard to imagine.

The room I’m sleeping in, now completely redone into what could easily be a fully functioning apartment, once served as a makeshift hospital for the Kosovo Liberation Army (UÇK), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla force that fought the Yugoslav and Serbian forces during the war. Here, he tells me, Lajqi’s mother and aunt cared for the wounded.

Many hikers arrive knowing almost nothing about what happened here, he says. But for those who make a point to learn about it, the history of this region gives different weight to this trail—and the intention behind it. The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Lajqi tells me. “When we opened the guesthouse, our home became a place where people from all over the world could come, stay, eat, talk with us, and experience our way of life. For me, there’s something special about that.”

Trails in this region include a great deal of altitude change—and the views that come with that.

The writer gathers around the dinner table with fellow trekkers at a local guesthouse.

Few people, however, have watched tourism reshape these mountains as long as Skender Selimaj of Hotel Rezidenca Quku i Valbones in Valbona, Albania. When he and his brother Alfred returned from the United Kingdom in the early 2000s, after leaving Albania during the period of communism, the high-walled valley hemmed in by jagged limestone peaks still revolved largely around subsistence farming. In 2004, they opened Restaurant Rilindja—meaning “rebirth” in Albanian—without knowing whether enough travelers would come to sustain it. Then, in 2009, Selimaj helped clear the passes toward Theth and Çerem and carried some of the first wooden trail signs into the mountains himself.

As in many locations along the Peaks of the Balkans route, the influx of tourism has since reshaped the Valbona Valley. The single-day hike over Valbona Pass to Theth has become one of Albania’s most popular mountain routes, which is also why my self-guided Zbulo itinerary intentionally bypassed it. Even with the trade-offs, Valbona has benefited. Farmers can now sell cheese, meat, eggs, and milk locally at better prices. Families have new income, while local children, Selimaj says, sometimes grow up speaking English simply from meeting travelers from around the world.

Selimaj, who spent years working as a mountain guide and in mountain rescue, still spends his free time exploring the terrain he grew up in, though he’s faced the fact that solitude is increasingly difficult to find. Where he once expected wild goats and empty mountains, “everywhere you go, you see somebody,” he says. He doesn’t wish tourism away; he has seen too clearly what it has done for local livelihoods. What he does want is a Valbona that remains clean, green, and recognizably local, where old stone houses and family-run businesses aren’t crowded out by large-scale outside development.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail passes through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask.

For Fahrig of Zbulo, the answer to the newfound business isn’t necessarily fewer trekkers. What he hopes to preserve on this trail are “living communities rather than places shaped entirely around visitors.” Doing that, he argues, means spreading trekkers more evenly: encouraging hikers to continue through Kosovo, directing some traffic toward quieter alternatives just beyond the busiest passes, and steering repeat or more adventurous trekkers toward newer alternative long-distance routes like the 225-mile High Scardus Trail that traverses the remote and mountainous borderlands of North Macedonia, Kosovo, and Albania.

In Kosovo, some of that work is already underway. Lajqi is part of a volunteer effort with other guesthouse owners and tourism businesses to create more natural alternatives around paved sections of the original route without cutting the villages themselves out of the trail—the other risk of making changes. “The best solution is not to completely change the original trail,” Lajqi says, “but to offer more choices, preserving the connection between the villages while also giving hikers the kind of mountain experience they came for.”

Over the days that follow, I keep moving west, circling back towards Theth. Each day brings with it another 3,000-foot pass to scale, another cucumber-and-tomato sandwich to enjoy once I get there, along with a steady mix of surprise, (some) stress, and plenty of solitude. Occasionally, I get lost when my GPS stops working or the orange dots and red-and-white striped trail markers disappear, and yet I always find my way. I walk, at times, with no one, and in other moments with dozens of travelers. Sometimes, it's just me and cowbell-clanging bovine. I keep going like this, collecting these little moments and memories, until, on the 10th day, I pass a bunker, the crumbling Cold War-era concrete mushrooms built by communist dictator Enver Hoxha, and realize I must be back in Albania.

By the time I approach Theth—the end of my route—I feel like I’ve walked through both versions of the Peaks: the one overwhelmed by its own success and the quieter version still there available alongside it.

The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Blendi Lajqi of Konaku i Malsorit says.

For my final night on the trails, I hike into Bujtina Kometa, a guesthouse in the quiet hamlet of Okol situated roughly a mile-and-a-half from central Theth. A mezze spread of marinated chicken, seasoned potatoes, olives, tomatoes, soft cheese, and tzatziki for dipping lands on the table, all prepared by our host Ermira and her family. The thing about these trails is that even if you go your own way by day, you'll find yourself breaking bread with familiar faces by night. Every person around the table, I realize, is someone I've met somewhere along the trail—people I’ve shared miles with over the last 10 days as our paths kept crossing.

Ermira’s father tops up our water and hints at honey-soaked fruit for dessert; woodsmoke from a neighbor distilling homemade raki drifts through the low-lit dining room. Van Dam, seated across the table from me now, reaches for another forkful of potato dripping with tzatziki. The busy center of Theth, with its tour buses and day-trippers, still feels worlds away.

For one more night, these Accursed Mountains and all they carry—the besa, the borders, the beauty, and the stories etched into them—envelop us, proving that wide-open spaces and quiet still have their place in these mountains.

Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full Peaks of the Balkans route.

The complete Peaks of the Balkans circuit covers roughly 119 miles (192 km) across Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro. Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full route, though shorter itineraries of 5 to 8 days often cut or bypass certain stages. Most routes involve 5 to 8 hours of hiking per day, typically covering 8 to 17 miles with significant elevation gain and loss.

Getting there: Fly into Podgorica in Montenegro or Tirana in Albania, transferring via shuttle or 4x4 to trailheads in Theth, Valbona, or Plav.

When to go: The core trekking season runs from June through September, but is increasingly stretching into October. Late June through August generally offers more reliable pass conditions, though the trail can get busy. Early June can still mean snow lingering on the highest passes, while September is the sweet spot for favorable hiking weather (peak traffic proves that everyone knows this). Early-to-mid October can be beautiful for experienced hikers willing to gamble on shorter days, colder nights, and the occasional burst of snow; later in the month, high-altitude guesthouses begin winding down, and do not reopen again until early May or June.

Who to go with: Albania-based Zbulo offers guided and self-guided trips (with logistics arranged, but no guide) ranging from 8 to 12 days. These include cross-border permits, guesthouse reservations, meals, luggage transfers, and route planning. If you're traveling independently, be sure to secure your date-locked cross-border permits at least two weeks before hiking, or have an agency like Zbulo secure them for you.

Where to stay: Accommodation ranges from family-run guesthouses and homestays to simple mountain huts, cabins, and small hotels. In remote sections, expect basic rooms—sometimes shared—along with hearty home-cooked dinners, breakfasts, and often a packed lunch for the following day. Budget roughly $25-55 USD per person per night depending on the room and whether meals are included. Book ahead in high season, and carry plenty of cash in Albanian lek or Euros in small denominations; card payments and ATMs are scarce in the mountains. In May and other shoulder-season periods, it is possible to arrange rooms on the fly, but from June through September—especially in bottlenecks like Dobërdol and popular stops such as Theth and Valbona—it’s smarter to book several weeks ahead. Camping is also possible on parts of the route, including at some guesthouses that allow trekkers to pitch a tent for a small fee and use facilities or buy meals. You can arrange your accommodations directly with hosts over WhatsApp using contacts found through Google Maps, social media, or the official Peaks of the Balkans App; many are now available on platforms like Booking.com as well.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6112. Blue wave meets ballot box surprises as voters split on abortion, voter ID and billionaire taxes

Americans from across the country shared their midterm voting decisions with Fox News Digital, driven by everything from President Donald Trump to abortion, immigration enforcement and gun rights. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

While Democrats’ midterm sweep dominated election night, voters in several states delivered consequential — and sometimes crosscutting — verdicts on voter ID, abortion access, taxes and English-language laws.

But the down-ballot decisions largely unfolded beneath the shadow of the GOP’s crushing losses, offering a separate look at the policy priorities voters chose to elevate in their states.

Read on to learn more about some of the most significant ballot measure results that will be shaping the lives of thousands of Americans.

More than a dozen states held ballot measures on Election Day that were related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

DEMOCRATS ‘DIVORCED FROM VOTERS’ AS 5 STATES BACK CITIZEN-ONLY VOTING, BOLSTERING GOP PUSH

Voters in Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio all voted to pass voter ID requirements, even as talks among federal lawmakers have stalled on the issue, showcasing that the issue remains a point of public interest.

In North Carolina, the state has required photo ID for in-person voting since 2018. But with the adoption of a constitutional amendment in a 59.6% to 40.3% vote, the Tar Heel State expanded the requirement to all forms of voting.

Similarly, in Ohio, voters passed Issue 3 by a 65.3% to 34.6% vote. Although Ohio already had preexisting in-person voter ID laws, Issue 3 codified the requirement in the state’s constitution, making it harder to overturn later.

Finally, in Nevada, Question 7 passed by a 62.1% to 37.8% vote, establishing a constitutional amendment to enact the state’s first voter ID requirement. It compels voters to show ID when voting in person and, for mail and absentee ballots, asks voters to provide the last four digits of their driver's license or Social Security number.

The Idaho Capitol building in Boise, Idaho. (Getty Images)

EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING

In Idaho, voters approved HJR6 in a 63.1% to 36.8% outcome, a measure that makes English the official language of the state, codifying it for use in public proceedings with a constitutional amendment.

English had already been made Idaho’s official language through statute since 2007.

State Rep. Dale Hawkins, one of the champions behind HJR6, called it reflective of efforts by the Trump administration to make English the official language of the United States through executive order.

"Our current administration signed an executive order doing this for the entire United States, so we are just in line with what’s going on," Hawkins said in public remarks.

In an interview with local media, Hawkins also cited a concern that many newcomers to the U.S. had, in his view, overlooked the country’s linguistic identity.

"One of the things that unites us all as a culture, as a country, as a state, is language. And what used to be the desired effect, which was assimilation — learn the language, learn the culture, learn the history — those things have slipped away. And we don’t see assimilation anymore. And I believe that if we have a common language, then our culture will survive," Hawkins told the Idaho Capital Sun.

Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of the Susan B. Anthony List, speaks as she introduces former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence at the National Press Club Nov. 30, 2021, in Washington, D.C. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)

DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

Alongside their English language constitutional amendment, voters in Idaho rejected Proposition 1, which would have created a right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability, except in cases of medical emergency.

Proposition 1 failed with a 55.9% to 44.0% outcome.

Had it been successful, the measure would have greatly reduced the state’s current limits on abortion except to save the life of a pregnant woman or in cases of rape or incest.

To onlookers like Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, the outcome demonstrates that protecting life in the womb remains a priority and an ongoing contest at the state level.

"We are incredibly grateful for Stop Prop 1 and all who stood up to defend the unborn. This is a hard-fought win and an example to pro-life voters, candidates and elected officials across the country. … Voters were not fooled because pro-life leaders spoke up boldly to expose this initiative," Dannenfelser said in a statement.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a group of DSA supporters. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images; Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

In California, voters rejected the implementation of a 5% billionaire tax that carried the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The measure, Proposition 40, failed by a vote of 52.4% to 47.5%.

The proposition would have applied a 5% tax on assets like businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property while excluding select pensions, real estate and retirement accounts.

To prevent billionaires from simply leaving the state, Proposition 40 was designed to retroactively apply to billionaires who were residents of California on Jan. 1, 2026.

The DSA framed the measure as a way to distribute wealth and as a kind of scaled-up version of a progressive tax, a tax that scales relative to income.

"We have the money in California to pay for the quality schools and healthcare that we need. It just needs to be transferred from the wrong pockets to the right ones. We can do that by taxing the rich," according to a slide presentation.

Notably, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Proposition 40, arguing it would lessen California’s competitiveness relative to other states.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks while campaigning for Senate candidate Chris Pappas at Exeter Town Hall on Oct. 17, 2026, in Exeter, N.H. (John Tully/Getty Images)

Voters in California also rejected Proposition 39, a proposed constitutional amendment that would have required ID for in-person voting and checks for the state’s voter registration lists.

Like Nevada's Question 7, it also would have asked absentee voters to provide the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number before securing a mail-in ballot.

The measure failed in a 60.5% to 39.4% vote.

Ahead of Election Day, Gov. Newsom characterized Proposition 39 as an extension of efforts to restrict access to voting rights.

"Trump and his MAGA allies tried to rig our elections once, and California voters shut them down with Prop 50. Prop 39 is just their latest attempt to silence us, because they know they can’t win in California in a fair fight. It’s voter suppression, full stop, and Californians will vote it down in November," Newsom said in a statement.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

#6110. The Hidden Math Behind Delta Air Lines Being The Only US Carrier Flying Mainline Jets With Under 110 Seats

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

Delta Air Lines operates some of the smallest mainline aircraft in the United States (US), including the 109-seat Airbus A220-100 and 110-seat Boeing 717. While most major carriers rely on larger narrowbodies, Delta has maintained a niche for smaller jets within its extensive domestic network, allowing the company to reach markets with more modest passenger demand.

Pilot agreements, buying aircraft at affordable rates, and operational flexibility have helped ensure that these planes are viable. However, the 717's gradual retirement raises questions about how Delta will continue reaching out to these destinations and whether its small-aircraft strategy will evolve as the airline adjusts its fleet and domestic operations in the years ahead.

Delta Air Lines has an unusual selection of narrowbody aircraft as compared to other major US air carriers. Its mainline fleet includes two jets with approximately 110 seats: the 109-seat Airbus A220-100 and the 110-seat Boeing 717. Delta is the only major US airline to operate mainline aircraft within a particularly small seating arrangement, according to Simple Flying. While other carriers generally rely on larger narrowbodies for their mainline flying, Delta has retained a place for smaller jets, allowing it to serve routes where a larger plane may offer more capacity than needed.

Highlighting the difference between mainline and regional operations is important when looking at Delta's fleet. Mainline aircraft are operated directly by the airline, utilizing its own pilots and cabin crew. Regional flights, however, are typically outsourced to partner carriers operating under the Delta Connection brand.

These operators generally fly smaller planes, including the Embraer E175 and Bombardier CRJ900. However, the pricing and labor arrangements vary when an airline operates a smaller jet itself rather than relying on a regional partner. As Simple Flying explains in its overview of scope clauses, pilot agreements can significantly influence how airlines divide their flying between mainline and regional operations.

Delta's decision to keep jets such as the 717 and A220-100 in its mainline fleet is therefore about more than passenger demand. Its pilot agreement limits the number of aircraft regional partners can operate, while also incentivizing the retention of certain smaller jets in the mainline fleet. This helps to explain why Delta's fleet composition differs from those of its competitors. A comparison by AeroHaber also illustrates how Delta uses the A220 alongside other US operators.

Discover the secrets behind Delta's A220-100 cabin configuration.

One of the main reasons Delta operates smaller mainline aircraft comes down to an agreement with its pilots known as a scope clause. These provisions are included in collective bargaining agreements and determine how much regional flying an airline can allocate to regional partners. These agreements became increasingly important during the 1990s, when regional flights and routes grew in popularity. As a result, mainline pilots raised serious concerns about airlines shifting more routes to lower-cost regional operators. Aircraft Commerce explains that these restrictions put in place by scope clauses were intended to "protect the pilots of the major airlines."

Under the scope clauses used by many major US airlines, Simple Flying reports that regional partners are generally limited to planes with up to 76 seats and a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 86,000 lb (39,009 kg). Delta's agreement, on the other hand, includes an additional provision that gives the airline more room to expand its regional fleet.

Cranky Flier states that Delta can operate up to 153 regional planes with 71 to 76 seats. It can add another 70 aircraft in that category if it operates an eligible small narrowbody in its mainline fleet. Delta met that requirement by introducing the reliable Boeing 717, and later the Airbus A220-100. Further, Cranky Flier explains, the agreement gives Delta a larger regional aircraft allowance than it would otherwise not have.

United Airlines has a similar provision in its pilot agreement, but it has not introduced an eligible small narrowbody into its mainline fleet, which would allow it to gain an expanded regional fleet allowance. American Airlines negotiated a different arrangement, allowing a larger number of regional planes with up to 65 seats, alongside separate restrictions for larger regional jets. The agreements are not identical, but Delta's provision gives it a particular reason to retain smaller aircraft in its mainline fleet.

Have you ever wondered who was flying the plane?

Operating smaller planes with mainline crews can be expensive, but Delta found ways to make its Boeing 717 and Airbus A220-100 fleets work. The terms under which it purchased the aircraft were an important part of that equation. In 2012, Delta stated that it reached an agreement with Southwest Airlines and Boeing Capital to lease or sublease 88 Boeing 717s previously operated by AirTran Airways. This gave Delta access to a sizable fleet without having to purchase an entirely new aircraft type.

Delta had intended to use the 717s to replace smaller regional jets. In its announcement, the airline said the jets would "primarily replace small 50-seat regional jets on a capacity-neutral basis." Then-CEO Richard Anderson also said the 717s would provide "a significant improvement in economic efficiency relative to the aircraft they are replacing." The arrangement gave Delta a way to bring smaller aircraft into its mainline operation while improving the economics of some existing routes.

The Airbus A220-100 offered another opportunity. Delta placed its initial order for 75 aircraft in 2016, when the jet was still known as the Bombardier C Series. During the ensuing trade dispute between Boeing and Bombardier, Boeing alleged that Bombardier had offered the aircraft to Delta for approximately $19.6 million (£14.61m) each, well below the reported production cost. That figure originated from Boeing, rather than a publicly listed contract price, but it illustrates the highly competitive pricing at the center of the dispute.

The two aircraft also perform different jobs within Delta's wide-ranging network. The 717 is primarily used on shorter, high-frequency routes, while the A220-100 is better suited to longer domestic services. According to The Points Guy, the A220-100 frequently operates routes of around 900 miles (1,450 km), including markets popular with business travelers that were previously served by the CRJ700, CRJ900, and Embraer E175.

Further, Delta equipped the aircraft with spacious 18.6-inch (47.24 cm)-wide economy seats, providing a wider seating arrangement than many competing narrowbodies. Between the terms of purchase and the different roles the aircraft fill, Delta has been able to make a relatively small mainline fleet work across a range of domestic routes.

How Brazil's most popular puddle jumper keeps Americans in the air.

Delta's strategy could look different as the airline continues retiring its Boeing 717 fleet. The aircraft has played an outsized role in Delta's domestic network for more than a decade, particularly on shorter routes where its capacity makes it a practical replacement for smaller regional jets. With the 717 gradually exiting stage left, Delta will need to decide how best to maintain its presence in those markets. The airline is not necessarily throwing in the towel on smaller mainline aircraft, however. Its A220-100, A220-300, and Airbus A319 provide other options for routes previously served by the 717.

Age is also becoming a factor in the 717's future. Delta's 2025 annual filing listed 80 Boeing 717s in its fleet at the end of the year, with an average age of 24.3 years. In June 2026, Air Data News indicated that Delta planned to retire six planes earlier than expected as they approached major maintenance inspections. The 717 is no longer in production, and its Rolls-Royce BR715 engines are unique to the aircraft. Keeping an aging fleet in service under those circumstances can become increasingly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

Replacing the 717s may not necessarily be a straightforward one-for-one swap. Although the A220-100 is newer and has greater range, its capacity and operating characteristics are different. Delta could use a combination of A220 variants and A319s, putting larger aircraft on some routes while reducing frequencies in markets that cannot support the additional seats. View From The Wing summarized the possible changes: "Replacing 717s would probably mean some larger A220-300s, some reassignment of comparable A220-100s and Airbus A319s, and fewer frequencies in some markets."

Delta's use of smaller mainline aircraft is likely to change as the 717 fleet leaves service, but there is still a place for jets below the capacity of its larger narrowbodies. The A220 family and A319 give the airline further options for serving destinations that may not need a larger aircraft, although they cannot replicate the 717's role on every route. How Delta deploys those aircraft will determine whether it can maintain the same level of flexibility across its domestic network.

The retirement of six aging Boeing 717s by Delta, nearly four years earlier than expected, may mark the beginning of a measured transition strategy.

Delta Air Lines' use of smaller mainline aircraft demonstrates how fleet planning involves more than simply matching passenger demand with aircraft capacity. Pilot scope clauses, favorable acquisition agreements, and the ability to serve markets with smaller jets have all played into the airline's distinctive approach. The Boeing 717 and Airbus A220-100 have allowed Delta to maintain flexibility across routes that may not require larger narrowbody planes.

However, as the 717 gradually makes its exit from the fleet, Delta's strategy is likely to evolve. The A220 family and A319 will continue to provide smaller-capacity options, although replacing the 717 will not always be straightforward. Ultimately, Delta's ability to balance aircraft economics, labor agreements, and passenger demand will shape its future domestic fleet strategy.

#6108. Emirates Is Stripping Its Airbus A380s To 'Bare Metal' While Qantas Retires Its Superjumbos 4 Years Early

Wikimedia Commons, Markus Mainka | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

While much of the airline industry is moving away from the Airbus A380, Emirates is taking a very different approach, stripping its Superjumbos back to bare metal and investing billions in rebuilding their interiors. The strategy reflects the aircraft's continued value on high-demand international routes, particularly at airports where limited takeoff and landing slots make replacing its enormous passenger capacity difficult.

Meanwhile, Australia's Qantas is bringing forward the retirement of its A380 fleet, turning instead toward newer, more fuel-efficient twin-engine aircraft. The contrasting strategies highlight why the world's largest passenger aircraft remains valuable to some airlines while becoming increasingly difficult for others to justify.

The Airbus A380, widely known as the Superjumbo, is an incredibly important aircraft for Emirates and has been part of its fleet since August 1, 2008, when it received its first aircraft of the type, registered as A6-EDF. According to Mogaz International, this elderly A380 is 20.5 years old and had logged 45,892 flight hours across 7,539 flights by May 31, 2026.

However, the average age of Emirates' A380 fleet is approximately 11.6 years. Airbus states that its "A380-800 offers several payload capabilities ranging from 400 passengers in a very comfortable multiclass configuration, up to 853 passengers in an all economy class configuration." Actual seating arrangements vary from airline to airline, depending on their individual requirements.

For Emirates, the A380 is a key connector and revenue generator due to its ability to concentrate large numbers of passengers within a single fuselage on high-demand routes and deliver them to key destinations. This capability is particularly important when serving airports with restricted slot availability, such as London Heathrow Airport (LHR), Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS), and Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD). Without the aircraft's substantial passenger capacity, the airline would need to operate more flights to transport the same number of passengers, placing additional pressure on airports where takeoff and landing slots are already limited.

Regarding the highly lucrative nature of the Superjumbo, Aviation Week quoted Sir Tim Clark, President of Emirates, as saying, “Last year, the A380 was the most profitable asset in our fleet, and that was the most profitable year we’ve ever had,” he said. “It tells you how successful, how popular that airplane is.” According to Emirates' financial data released last May, the company recorded an eye-watering profit during its 2025–26 financial year, amounting to $6.6 billion.

Due to these factors, Emirates will not be retiring the iconic aircraft in favor of smaller, more fuel-efficient twin-engine aircraft, as Qantas is doing. Rather, Emirates reportedly plans to maintain its A380 fleet until 2041, as no other aircraft currently in production offers anywhere near comparable passenger capacity. To keep the vast majority of its massive fleet of 116 Superjumbos looking their best and maximize passenger comfort, Emirates embarked on an ambitious and extensive retrofit program, the likes of which the company had never undertaken before.

Nine new SFO connections expand Pacific reach and bolster year round East Coast feeds while adding seasonal Midwest and Florida service.

As noted in the previous section, the A380 is a massive moneymaker for Emirates. Keeping these aircraft looking and feeling their best for the passengers who travel aboard them is a major priority, particularly as the average age of the fleet is nearly 12 years.

In an effort to keep these aircraft in top shape, Emirates is roughly halfway through one of the most ambitious retrofit programs in commercial aviation, which, according to the company, is worth $5 billion (£3.75 billion). Once completed, the airline will have completely retrofitted the interiors of 219 aircraft, including 110 A380s and 109 Boeing 777s.

The project began in November 2022, with the first A380 undergoing its retrofit at the Emirates Engineering hangars in Dubai. Since then, Emirates has stated that 47 of its Superjumbos and 53 Boeing 777s have received a complete nose-to-tail refresh, with the company averaging work on 28 aircraft per year. Completing the first 100 aircraft was an incredible milestone in this ambitious program.

The detailed work has involved 400 engineers and technicians who have collectively invested 4.4 million man-hours in transforming these aircraft. Incredibly, each revamped A380 requires more than 4,000 new parts, while the 777 requires more than 2,500, according to Emirates. The completed A380s feature a Premium Economy section for the first time, with a 2-3-2 configuration, full leg and footrests, six-way adjustable headrests, side cocktail tables, and a 13.3-inch personal screen. Additionally, Emirates is installing Starlink WiFi across 232 aircraft.

Ahead of the A380's planned fleet retirement in 2041, Aviation Week reports that Emirates expects to begin receiving the Boeing 777-9 in 2027, although the aircraft will accommodate approximately 150 fewer passengers. However, this transition towards twin-engine aircraft is becoming a necessity, as A380 production has ended and the industry has increasingly shifted towards lighter, more fuel-efficient passenger aircraft.

The only way for engineers to expand the A340-300 without a cleansheet aircraft was to stretch it into the world's longest passenger jet at the time.

Qantas, an international airline based in Australia, operates seven aircraft types, and the A380 has been an important component of the company's ability to transport passengers to high-demand markets, such as Western Europe, Asia, and the US. While these aircraft have performed admirably, Qantas has officially stated that it will begin the process of retiring its 10 A380s as early as 2028. However, it remains unclear exactly how long it will take to completely phase them out, although they are expected to remain in service until at least FY2032.

The company made the decision to retire its fleet of Superjumbos due to two primary factors: fuel expenses and the arrival of new, long-haul-capable aircraft. Regarding the former, strong travel demand has not been enough to offset the impact of jet fuel prices, which have been affected by instability in the Middle East. AeroTime reports that "Qantas estimated that the overall impact of the fuel crisis could have been as high as AU$610 million (US$438 million), although claims to have managed to reduce this figure to AU$420 million (US$301 million) thanks to mitigation measures."

Aside from the expenses associated with operating older four-engine aircraft, Qantas will be receiving new-build aircraft with improved fuel efficiency. These new aircraft will be able to take over some of the A380s' routes and capacity, giving the company greater confidence in its decision to begin retiring the aircraft earlier than originally planned. Regarding the arrival of these new aircraft, at the end of August, Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson announced:

“Our fleet renewal continued at pace, with 17 new aircraft arriving during the year and up to 31 more to arrive in the year ahead, with the majority joining Qantas . . . With our first Project Sunrise A350-1000ULR to arrive in April, and more A350s and 787s on the way, it’s a new era for Qantas’ international fleet with these next generation aircraft set to transform the way our customers travel. This means we can commence the retirement of our A380 fleet from 2028."

Regarding long-distance travel, the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 787 Dreamliner will form the backbone of the company's international flight strategy. While neither aircraft can fully replace the sheer passenger capacity of the A380, both can still carry substantial numbers of passengers over long distances.

Committed to these aircraft, in 2023, Qantas placed a multi-billion-dollar firm order for 12 Airbus A350s and 12 Boeing 787s, with deliveries expected to begin in FY2027. The order also included "access to up to 500 million litres of sustainable aviation fuel; enhancing pathway to reach the Group’s 2030 emissions targets."

Airbus states that its A350-1000 has a maximum seating capacity of 480 passengers and can comfortably accommodate between 375 and 400 passengers in a standard three-class configuration. It also offers a 40% increase in space within the premium seating category. Regarding fuel consumption, the A350-1000's Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines provide a 25% reduction in fuel burn and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation aircraft. Qantas expects to begin receiving these aircraft by FY2028.

Regarding the Boeing purchases, Qantas will receive four 787-9s and eight 787-10s. According to Boeing, the former can accommodate between 250 and 325 passengers, while the latter can carry between 300 and 375. In line with Qantas' commitment to fuel efficiency, the new Boeing 787s will be powered by General Electric GEnx engines. These aircraft offer improved fuel efficiency, with the 787-9 delivering a 20% reduction in fuel consumption and the 787-10 offering a 25% improvement, alongside a 60% reduction in noise.

They're all from Dallas, Charlotte, and Chicago, with some intriguing additions. Find them here!

The contrasting strategies of Emirates and Qantas demonstrate that the Airbus A380 still has a place in commercial aviation, although its long-term viability depends heavily on an airline's operating model. Emirates continues to see substantial value in its capacity, investing billions to keep its Superjumbos flying for years to come.

Meanwhile, Qantas is transitioning toward more efficient twin-engine aircraft, reflecting an industry-wide shift. Although the A380's era is gradually coming to an end, Emirates shows that the Superjumbo still has plenty of life left.

#6106. Massie's push to impeach Hegseth splits constituents in his own backyard: 'Pure spite'

Northern Kentucky voters talked to Fox News Digital and gave differing opinions of their firebrand libertarian representative, who was defeated in the Republican primary and will leave office.

KENTON COUNTY, Ky. — Rep. Thomas Massie's push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war drew sharply different reactions from northern Kentucky residents interviewed by Fox News Digital.

The residents offered competing assessments of the outgoing Republican congressman and whether his latest confrontation with the Trump administration reflects principle or political payback.

Fox News Digital visited Covington, the population center of Massie’s district, along with Newport, Erlanger and other communities across the river from Cincinnati, to ask residents about their outgoing congressman and his efforts to impeach the Pentagon chief.

TRUMP DEFENDS PENTAGON CHIEF AS MASSIE TARGETS HIM: 'HEGSETH SHOULD BE PRAISED, NOT IMPEACHED'

Richard Hassebrock, a Covington resident who said he has not always agreed with Massie, welcomed the impeachment effort.

"I'm not always a huge fan of Thomas Massie, but on this point I am," Hassebrock told Fox News Digital.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon Nov. 10 in Arlington, Va. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging he violated the Constitution by waging war in Iran without congressional authorization, among other charges. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Craig Cuskey, who works in the Covington area but lives just outside the bounds of Massie’s district in Louisville, described the impeachment push as "pure spite" and "petty," saying his opinion of the congressman had deteriorated.

The contrasting reactions came after House Republicans voted to refer Massie's impeachment effort against Hegseth to committee, adding another confrontation to the Kentucky Republican's long-running disagreements with President Donald Trump and his party's leadership.

Democrats poised to take the gavel in January, however, signaled they will likely take up Massie’s mantle and seek the Pentagon chief’s impeachment.

Hassebrock said he was disappointed by Massie's electoral defeat and praised the congressman's independence.

"He stands up for himself. He stands up to what he believes in. He's got principles unlike 99% of the other congresspeople out there," he said.

Rilla, a Fort Wright resident who provided only her first name, offered a more complicated assessment.

"I think he's just trying to get back at Trump," she said, adding she had been proud of Massie for standing up to the president and was disappointed by his defeat.

7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

Rilla said she opposed the Iran war, particularly the prospect of military action without congressional involvement.

"I don't think anyone should just go in and declare war without Congress being a part of it," she said.

Phil Wiseman, an Independence resident, said he doubted the impeachment effort would accomplish much, even as he questioned the administration's military strategy.

"I don't see a definable outcome," Wiseman said. "And if you're going to fight a war, there needs to be a definable outcome."

Wiseman said he identifies as a "RINO," a term often used derisively by conservatives for "Republican in name only," and voted for an independent instead of supporting Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, the Trump-endorsed Republican who defeated Massie in Kentucky's primary earlier this year.

He said his family has discussed Hegseth, noting that his father was a 27-year military veteran and his son served in the Marine Corps.

"We all had the same discussion," he said. "Who is advising him? Because this [war] is very ill-thought-out and not well-planned."

Wiseman compared that aspect of the Iran conflict to how the U.S. previously became mired in Afghanistan.

"So, I seriously question the military advisors that are giving them this advice, or maybe they gave them contrary advice, and it was ignored," he said.

Anthony Tuemler of Covington supported impeachment and accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution through his conduct of the war.

Tuemler's assessment of Massie was similarly mixed. Although he said he was glad the congressman was leaving office, he credited Massie with speaking up when he believed it was necessary.

"I'm glad he's gone," Tuemler said of Massie. "But the only thing I'm distressed about or sorry about is, like, when it came time to say the right things, Massie was the one who did it."

Randall Thompson of Newport, dressed in a military uniform for Veterans Day as he walked with his children near Covington's Mainstrasse Village corridor, said he supports the defense secretary and pointed to their shared military experience in the Middle East.

"I support the troops and Pete Hegseth," Thompson said, adding off-camera that he was in the same area of Iraq as the former Fox News host when they were both deployed.

Cuskey also defended Hegseth, saying he had initially been skeptical of his nomination but had grown more impressed with his performance.

"I think, for his background, he's done a remarkable job," Cuskey said, arguing that Hegseth was carrying out directives from the commander in chief.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has voiced support for impeaching the Pentagon chief, while other Democrats have signaled plans to revisit his conduct when they take control of Congress in January.

Some lawmakers are also eyeing investigations and potential impeachment proceedings involving other senior Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan, setting the stage for a broader confrontation between congressional Democrats and the White House.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

#6105. Amex Business Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 300K Points Welcome Offer

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express is one of the most perks-rich business cards out there, and is useful if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 300,000 points are worth a staggering $5,100. As I see it, that’s basically the best welcome offer you’ll find on any card.

Let me emphasize that Amex uses a variety of factors when deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Platinum Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible Amex Business Platinum bonus through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there.

That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method. However, it can always be worth checking back every so often, because the promotions people are targeted for can change over time.

The Amex Business Platinum bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to nearly $6,700 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners. Also keep in mind that having this card lets you unlock the full value of Amex Pay With Points, potentially allowing you to get up to 1.54 cents of value per point toward the cost of airfare on a designated airline (this comes in the form of a 35% Pay with Points rebate, up to one million points per year). You could then use that redemption rate for all your linked Amex Membership Rewards cards.

Flight cancellations are on the rise in 2026. Since Jan. 1, U.S. carriers have canceled roughly 2% of all flights, according to FlightAware, putting this year on pace for the highest cancellation rate since 2022. And delays remain common: About one in four departures nationwide was delayed between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

While most flights leave on time, delays and cancellations remain a reality of air travel — whether due to bad weather, mechanical issues, scheduling problems or other unforeseen circumstances, including the recent nationwide ground stop.

In case you experience flight delays or cancellations, here are tips on how to decrease your chances of getting stuck and increase your odds of arriving at your destination as quickly as possible. Plus, check out our advice on how to potentially get reimbursed for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation, depending on the reason that caused the delay.

In this era of full flights and easily available information, don’t wait for the airline to tell you there is a problem. You can keep an eye on general flight trends across the country by using FlightAware, which gives you a good overview of how a day in the sky looks.

FlightAware’s “MiseryMap” focuses on delays. In the 24 hours before travel, you can manually check the status of your flight on your airline’s website. If possible, be sure to check the plane's origin. Even if the conditions are clear where you are, there’s a good chance your plane won’t get to you on time if it’s sitting in a snowstorm somewhere else.

It’s also a good idea to sign up for flight notifications from your airline. Here are details on how to opt in to that process with American Airlines and United Airlines.

You can also get flight status updates sent directly from FlightAware. TPG staffers are also fond of the Flighty app, which offers a reliable "Where's My Plane?" feature to track your plane starting 25 hours before your flight.

Be sure to download your airline’s app on your phone, too. Many airlines will show you where your incoming plane is currently. In fact, your airline’s app often has more up-to-date flight departure information than what’s on the departure and arrival boards at the airport.

This can be a tricky one. If your flight is still listed as “on time” in the app, leave for the airport according to the original schedule.

Even if your flight shows as delayed in the app, that status is subject to change. So, in most cases, it’s best to be at the airport ready to go at the originally scheduled time. We’ve certainly heard stories of flights being delayed only to depart sooner than expected, leaving some passengers behind.

Sometimes, you’ll receive confirmation well in advance, letting you know if your flight will be significantly delayed. Say you are at an airport that isn’t a hub for the airline you are flying (meaning there's less chance of spare planes and crew), and the plane that's supposed to operate your flight is nowhere close to arriving at the airport. In that case, it's likely that your posted delay will be a real delay. However, it’s still safer to be at the airport, just in case.

Bad weather can sometimes cause a temporary ground stop at the airport. As soon as the weather improves and the stop lifts, airlines will try to get their flights off the ground ASAP. So, it’s best to be close by should things change on short notice.

Related: 3 things to do if your flight is delayed

It’s important to know your rights as an airline passenger, which have been changed in recent years.

For instance, if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed and you choose not to travel, you’re entitled to a refund, no matter the reason for the disruption. According to current rules from the U.S. Department of Transportation, passengers on domestic flights that are significantly changed, including arriving three or more hours late, and international flights arriving six or more hours late are entitled to automatic refunds if they choose not to travel and don't accept alternative transportation or travel credits. Those refunds must be issued within seven days for credit card purchases and 20 days for cash payments.

However, if you get stranded overnight, you may also be able to recoup costs for extra meals, hotel nights and ground transportation, depending on the reason for the delay. A widespread FAA ground stop, for example, is unlikely to be a covered reason.

You’ll find these and other passenger rights guarantees on flightrights.gov, the DOT’s dashboard.

On that website, you’ll find a rundown of what airlines guarantee in the event of “controllable” delays and cancellations — disruptions within an airline’s control. Keep in mind that these controllable situations typically exclude weather-related problems.

When looking at the dashboard, you’ll quickly see that some airlines promise to do more than others regarding overnight hotel stays, ground transportation, credit vouchers and rebooking on partners. Give that list a look not only when you’re deciding which airline to book with but also in the event of a long, controllable delay or cancellation. This way, you’ll know what the airline has promised to do in those situations. You can file a complaint with the DOT if the airline doesn’t hold up its end of the bargain.

Monitor weather patterns a few days before your flight to see if any major systems are anticipated. It’s vital to check the forecast the night before and on the day of travel to see how any issues could affect your departure and arrival airports.

Again, be sure to opt in to receive updates on your flight’s status. If you know bad weather is coming later in the day, ask for an earlier flight if you can. Alternatively, leaving the night before the weather arrives is a good idea if you want to minimize the risk of delays.

Many airlines will issue travel advisories during (and ahead of) severe weather, such as blizzards, ice storms or even heavy thunderstorms. These advisories allow travelers to make changes even when flying on a restrictive ticket that typically can’t be altered — like some basic economy fares. In some cases, the airline may even proactively change your flight.

If you know bad weather is on the horizon, visit your airline’s website and look for an advisory notice or call the airline to discuss options. If an airline gets ahead of weather issues, you may be able to reschedule your flight by a few days in either direction with no fees. Additionally, you can try asking for a nonstop flight if the weather jeopardizes your connecting flight.

However, if the airline hasn’t issued its own advisory, you might need to pay out of pocket for any fare differences if you really want to be proactive in changing plans.

Standing in a long line at the airport or waiting on hold by phone is usually no longer the most efficient (or most enjoyable) way to rebook when a flight is canceled or delayed.

Most major airlines will allow you to rebook yourself using a mobile app. You may be able to rebook for a new time or even to a new nearby origin or destination city. For that reason, the airline app should probably be your first stop when you learn of a hiccup in your travel plans.

United will even let you standby for up to three flights if something happens to your originally scheduled flight, while maintaining your original seat.

That said, there are times when automated rebooking systems are not your best option. Sometimes, the only automated option is a red-eye flight or a flight several days later that will head to your destination. That’s especially true when many flights are full.

If you can’t locate what you need on the app, find an airline employee who can work the ticketing desk. Check their uniforms and name tags to ensure you get a ticket agent, versus a baggage handler or a similarly outsourced contractor who is less likely to be able to help.

If the U.S. call center has long hold times (which can happen during widespread issues), you can try dialing an international number for faster service. You can often find those numbers on the airline’s website. You might also find success reaching out to an airline on the social platform X or other social media channels when customer service lines are busy.

For example, when the first leg of an American Airlines flight from New York to Arkansas, scheduled just before Christmas, was delayed, TPG Managing Editor Madison Blancaflor missed her connection. She contacted American Airlines on X to help ensure she was rebooked on the earliest possible flight. She still had to endure a long layover in Charlotte, but it was better (and less stressful) than rushing to the customer service desk to try to rebook upon arrival.

Additionally, some airlines offer live online chat or text options that can be quicker than calling.

If there are no reasonable booking options left with your carrier, ask whether there are options available on another airline. If the delay is weather-related and you are on a basic economy ticket or are flying on a low-cost carrier, there might not be other airline options at your fingertips. Still, it’s worth asking — and, if possible, presenting options you have researched yourself.

Related: Don’t wait on hold: Here’s how to reach airline customer service quickly

If you have airline lounge access at a United Club, a Delta Sky Club or something similar, you can head there for help from experienced agents with potentially shorter lines. Use it as a spot to gather your thoughts, charge your phone and make level-headed decisions. The agents there might be able to help you change or track your flight, as there are usually agents with that knowledge and ability in the airline lounges.

In third-party lounges, such as an American Express Centurion Lounge, you won’t be able to get that type of airline-specific assistance, but you’ll probably be in a better spot to wait out the storm than in a crowded terminal.

Related: Best credit cards for airport lounge access

Sometimes, if you really need to get home, you may need to do the work and pay for a new flight yourself.

In some of our prior experiences, the airlines we originally booked with couldn't get us home within 24 hours of our flights being canceled. In cases like these, you may be able to book a nonstop flight with at least one last seat available on another carrier.

Keep in mind, though, that rebooking yourself is typically not covered by any insurance provider or carrier. Still, you should be able to get a refund for your original ticket, which will at least offset some of the pain of a new one. The extra work may be worth it to control your own destiny and avoid being stuck as options narrow.

Your credit card’s built-in trip delay or trip cancellation coverage can help with many unexpected expenses in the face of delays and cancellations, but a brand-new flight home isn’t likely to be one of them. Still, in some cases, it may be the only way home for a while, so you’ll have to weigh the pros and cons.

Fortunately, many airlines now allow you to cancel main cabin tickets and, at the very least, get airline trip credit; you can use this credit to book a future flight — even if you are being proactive to try and avoid possible delays and, ultimately, your originally scheduled flight does not experience a delay. (This does not necessarily apply to basic economy fares or low-cost carriers' flights.)

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

While thinking through what to do in case of a flight delay or cancellation, consider your options at airport hotels; they can fill up during major delays and cancellations. Sometimes, it is best to call it a day, get some rest and try again in the morning.

Airport hotels are generally pretty affordable on points, but cash rates can skyrocket when demand surges. Accommodations are typically covered by trip delay protection in the event of cancellations or very long delays via cards like the (see rates and fees) and .*

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Why my favorite use of Hyatt points is a Category 1 airport hotel

If you know in advance that your flight will be canceled or delayed, heading to the airport early could score you a same-day standby flight that gets you to your destination on time.

For example, one TPG staffer used this strategy to avoid getting stuck overnight when a hiccup with his flight from Austin to New York would have caused him to miss a connection in Dallas. He arrived at the airport a bit early and was placed on the standby list for an earlier flight connecting to a different city.

Getting on the standby list isn’t foolproof, especially if the earlier flight is almost full. This is a case where having elite status can help since you’ll have priority over non-elite travelers. Additionally, some airlines charge non-elite travelers a fee to be added to the standby list for an earlier flight.

Related: The best credit cards to reach elite status

The hard truth is that in the event of airline delays and cancellations caused by weather, the airline itself is not going to help you out with the extra expenses you incur due to the change in plans, since the weather is outside its control. Travel insurance may have your back if you purchased it, but beyond that, the credit card you booked your flight with may also be able to reimburse you for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation — even if it was caused by weather.

Many rewards credit cards confer valuable travel protections when you have a delayed or canceled flight (if you used one of them to book your flight). Below are just a few examples of cards that provide some built-in coverage:

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Best credit cards with travel insurance

To highlight how valuable this can be, a couple of years ago, one TPG staffer's flights home from Colorado during the busy winter holiday season were canceled due to a snowstorm.

She was faced with an unexpected $1,100-per-night hotel stay during peak season in a pricey ski town, based on what was still available at the last minute. Ultimately, her eligible Chase card covered not only the $1,100 unexpected hotel stay but also the unexpected car service and meals during the delay. Within 26 days of the unexpected cancellation and delay, she had a check for $1,401.74 in her hand, thanks to using the right credit card to book the flight.

Unfortunately, some situations are not covered by the built-in trip delay and trip cancellation protections that commonly come with some rewards credit cards, but it never hurts to save receipts and try.

Last but not least, we recommend being decisive when making travel decisions amid delays or cancellations.

The longer you wait to switch flights or book a hotel, the greater the chances you’ll be at the mercy of whatever dwindling options are left as hundreds (or thousands) of other passengers rebook their plans.

Most of the time, your flight will get you where you need to be, close to when you want to be there. Still, flight delays and cancellations are a reality of air travel. If your flight is delayed by an hour or two, there’s not usually much to do other than be patient. However, when facing a long delay or cancellation, it’s good to have a plan to reduce the odds of getting stuck.

Given the common theme of full flights these days, acting quickly, researching options and making a speedy decision will put you ahead of the pack.

#6103. ‘Somebody Hit Us’: UPS Boeing 767 Collides With Copa 737 In Miami After Taxiing Too Far

A UPS Airlines Boeing 767 freighter and a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport (MIA) on Saturday night. According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the wingtip of the Copa passenger jet struck the nose of the 767 as the cargo aircraft taxied for departure.

Air traffic control (ATC) had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the 737, and one of its pilots acknowledged the mistake over the radio moments after the collision, saying, "We went too far." The FAA has opened an investigation into the collision, which happened a day after a rare nationwide ground stop brought US air travel to a halt.

The collision occurred at approximately 9:15 PM local time at the intersection of two taxiways. Copa Airlines flight 427, operated by a Boeing 737-800, had just arrived from Tocumen International Airport (PTY) in Panama City, while UPS flight 358 was taxiing for departure en route to El Dorado International Airport (BOG) in Bogotá.

As the Copa jet taxied toward its gate, controllers instructed the UPS crew to give way and let the 737 pass before continuing toward the runway. However, the 767 continued too far and moved into the Copa aircraft's path. The 737's left wingtip then struck the nose of the freighter as it passed, bringing both aircraft to a stop on the taxiway.

Audio from ATC.com captured the radio exchange during the collision. After the Copa crew reported, "Somebody hit us," the controller reminded UPS 358 that it was "supposed to give way" to the 737. The following exchange occurred immediately after the taxiway collision:

"Controller: "UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?"

UPS 358: "Yeah, we went too far and then he... he clipped us with the wing."

After instructing the Copa crew to hold position and confirming that fire trucks were on their way, the controller heard from the 737's pilot, who reported, "It seems that we are missing the left wingtip." Authorities later treated two people at the scene for minor injuries, but neither required transport to hospital.

The FAA has confirmed that controllers had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, meaning the 767 was supposed to wait until the 737 had passed. In a statement, the agency said:

"The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 while the airplanes were taxiing."

UPS added in a statement that it was committed to working with authorities to determine what happened, adding that its crew was safe. The extent of the damage to either aircraft has not yet been officially confirmed, although images posted on social media reveal significant damage to the 767's nose.

The winglets depict the upward-curling of bird features to gain efficiency.

There is a suggestion that a runway change may have added to the UPS crew's workload shortly before the collision. During the radio exchange, one of the pilots told the controller that they were in the middle of a checklist for a runway change. This can require pilots to update the flight management computer, a task that can be demanding while an aircraft is already taxiing.

However, pilots are expected to maintain situational awareness and follow instructions during checks. The FAA's taxiing guidance recommends keeping cockpit workload to a minimum and ensuring at least one pilot remains focused outside the aircraft.

The Miami incident is not an isolated case, with several similar collisions involving commercial aircraft reported at major international airports over the past year. Only last month, a Delta Air Lines Airbus A350-900 struck the horizontal stabilizer of an Air Canada Boeing 777-200LR while taxiing at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). The Air Canada aircraft was being towed to its gate when the Delta jet's left wingtip became lodged in its tail.
