#6074. Delta 360: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

All of the “big three” carriers in the United States have invitation-only elite status. I’ve written about how American has Concierge Key and United has Global Services, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at Delta 360, which is Delta’s invitation-only elite status. I’d argue it’s the most mysterious, least talked about, and perhaps the rarest, of the three.

What is Delta 360 status, how do you earn it, what are the benefits, and how many members are there? I’ll share everything I know…

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite status. It’s my understanding that this is the most exclusive of the invitation-only elite tiers, in the sense that there are the fewest members. Despite that, the benefits are actually pretty weak, at least on paper. For that matter, Delta 360 isn’t even a formal elite tier, which is to say that you separately still have to qualify for status in the Delta SkyMiles Medallion program.

For what it’s worth, here’s how Delta describes Delta 360 status on its website:

Delta 360° is an annual, invitation-only membership for our most loyal SkyMiles Members. A Delta 360° Membership offers Delta’s most premium suite of benefits and services exclusive to our top SkyMiles Members. Entry into Delta 360° will be extended to a very small percentage of Diamond Medallion Members. Considerations include, but are not limited to: overall Delta flight activity, premium product purchases (Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta First) and spending on Delta SkyMiles American Express Cards.

As is the case with the invitation-only status of American and United, the requirements to earn Delta 360 status aren’t published. However, based on the data points I’ve seen, the criteria are even more confusing. With American and United, as a general rule, you need to spend well over $50,000 per year to have a shot at the status. In the case of Delta, you probably need to spend even more.

As Delta officially states, getting an invitation to Delta 360 is for the “most loyal SkyMiles members.” Generally speaking:

Some suggest that you’d have to spend $100,000 per year on Delta flights to be invited as a Delta 360 member at major hubs, while the number could be much lower if you’re not based at a hub.

Note that qualification for Delta 360 is annual (so it expires at the end of the elite year), and criteria could change year-to-year. So it’s possible you have the same activity in two years, and earn Delta 360 one year, but not the other. There’s also no way to ask for or request the status (at least not in a way that will achieve the intended result). Instead, you’ll be contacted if you’re eligible, and you’ll see your account updated to reflect that.

There’s one other way to earn Delta 360 status. As part of the SkyMiles lifetime elite status program, you can receive Delta 360 status for life if you rack up five million lifetime miles. This metric is based on the number of eligible miles flown on Delta.

Just for some context on all of this, Delta’s top published tier is Diamond Medallion, and that requires earning 28,000 Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs) in a program year. That would require $28,000 in spending on Delta tickets, or $280,000 to $560,000 in spending on select co-branded Delta credit cards.

Interestingly, Delta 360 isn’t a separate tier in the SkyMiles program. That’s to say that Delta 360 members still have to earn status in the SkyMiles Medallion program. Most Delta 360 members are also Diamond Medallion members, but in theory it’s possible to earn Delta 360 without being a Diamond Medallion member.

This is different than American AAdvantage and United MileagePlus, where Concierge Key and Global Services are separate tiers, above the published top tier levels.

What are the benefits of Delta 360 status?

Those are all the Delta 360 benefits that I’m aware of. There’s no upgrade priority for Delta 360 members beyond their standard Diamond Medallion status, so Delta 360 doesn’t factor into upgrade priority. Furthermore, any confirmed upgrades would be earned through the standard Choice Benefits program, as this is how you can earn Global Upgrade Certificates (GUCs) and Regional Upgrade Certificates (RUCs).

So the benefits of Delta 360 are weak, though I’d imagine that the “soft” treatment is very good — Delta has great service to begin with, and I imagine it’s even better for Delta’s best customers.

I also think it’s noteworthy how Delta is much quieter about this status than American and United. There’s just not as much public acknowledgement of invitation only status at Delta as at American and United (and that might be by design).

This is a real mystery, and all I can do is speculate. For context, I’ve speculated that there are 10,000-20,000 American Concierge Key members, and I’ve speculated that there are 15,000-25,000 United Global Services members.

This is purely a guess on my part, but I think the number of Delta 360 members is probably in the 5,000-10,000 range. That’s simply because the status seems to be more difficult to earn. Like I said, this is purely a guess on my part, and I could be wrong. If anyone has any data or info, I’d love to hear it.

It’s hard to say whether something like Delta 360 is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Delta 360 varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Delta One Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal, above and beyond what you’d otherwise get.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including American Concierge Key and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, I’d say Delta 360 probably offers the fewest official perks of the three tiers. The one exception is that Delta One Lounge access is an absolutely awesome benefit, given the quality of lounges (though the lack of free guests limits the usefulness for those not usually traveling alone).

Here are a couple of thoughts on the comparable status tiers at American and United:

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite tier. It’s the US airline status that’s probably hardest to earn. Historically the benefits have been weaker than comparable status with American and United, though with access to Delta One Lounges, that’s perhaps no longer the case. Delta 360 offers dedicated customer support, a Sky Club membership, Delta One Lounge access, good odds of tarmac transfers, and more.

To earn Delta 360, be prepared to spend a lot on Delta flights, especially if you’re based out of a Delta hub.

Are any OMAAT readers Delta 360 members? If so, what has your experience been like?

#6073. The 2-Hour Rest Rule Ultra-Long-Haul Airbus A350 Pilots Have Before Landing

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Ultra-long-haul flights are built around a rule written backward from the landing. Federal regulations governing augmented operations require that the pilot who will fly the aircraft during landing must have two consecutive hours of in-flight rest available during the second half of the flight duty period. The requirement does not simply demand that pilots rest. It specifies which pilot, and when, based on what they will be responsible for at the end of the flight.

Singapore Airlines operates Singapore to New York with four pilots across a duty period of roughly 20 hours, double the crew the Airbus A350 requires. The Points Guy describes two ways the flight is divided: an even 8/8 split and a 6/8/2 rotation that trims relief-crew sleep so the operating crew is back on the flight deck around three hours before landing. Separately, a different rule governs the shorter naps pilots take in the seat rather than the bunk, capping them at 40 minutes and requiring a 20-minute recovery period before the pilot resumes any duty. Both rules exist for the same reason.

Federal regulations governing augmented flight operations contain a provision written specifically around the landing. During the flight duty period, the pilot who will fly the aircraft during landing must have two consecutive hours of in-flight rest available during the second half of the duty period. The rule does not simply require that pilots rest. It requires that a particular pilot rests at a particular point in the flight, determined by which phase of the operation they will be responsible for.

The provision sits within a broader framework for augmented operations. An augmented flight crew includes more pilots than the aircraft's minimum certification requirement, which allows one pilot to be replaced by another for inflight rest. US regulations define an augmented flight crew in those terms, and Part 117 establishes separate duty limits for augmented operations than for standard ones. Throughout the flight, at least one qualified flight crew member must remain at the controls.

Rest requirements extend beyond the flight itself. Before a duty period begins, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) rules require at least ten consecutive hours of rest, including a minimum of eight uninterrupted hours of sleep opportunity. The two-hour inflight provision therefore applies to a crew that has already met a pre-flight rest standard, and it governs how that crew distributes the additional sleep available to them once the aircraft is airborne.

Singapore Airlines operates Singapore to New York with four pilots, comprising two captains and two first officers, across a duty period of roughly 20 hours. The pilots split into two pairs, each taking turns at the controls while the other rests.

How the split is structured is a planning decision, not a fixed formula. The Points Guy described two approaches used on a flight of around 17.5 hours. The first is an 8/8 split, which gives each crew pair roughly eight hours of rest and divides the flight evenly between them. The second is a 6/8/2 rotation, which breaks the flight into three segments and distributes the rest unevenly.

The second option deliberately trims the relief crew's sleep. Under the 6/8/2 structure, the operating crew returns to the flight deck roughly three hours before landing rather than shortly before the approach. That extra time lets them assess weather changes and operational updates before descending. The relief pilots give up some rest to make it possible. Whatever structure is chosen, the handover itself is formal. Swapping crews involves a briefing covering fuel, weather, and traffic, which means a pilot returning from rest is brought up to date on the flight's current state rather than simply resuming where they left off.

The A350's reputation as a 'passenger favorite' masks a more complex truth for flight crews, whose rest experiences can vary widely.

The A350's flight crew rest facility sits above the forward galley, accessed through a hatch in the ceiling that most passengers walk beneath without noticing. It contains two bunks and, depending on configuration, a reclining seat and an entertainment monitor, with independent temperature controls. Simple Flying previously explored how the facility is used only when three or more pilots are on duty, making it specific to augmented operations.

The classification matters more than the furnishings. The FAA defines three classes of rest facilities under 14 CFR Part 117, and the ranking runs opposite to what the numbering suggests. A Class 1 facility is a bunk or other surface that allows a flat sleeping position, located separately from both the flight deck and the passenger cabin, temperature-controlled, with crew control over lighting, and isolated from noise and disturbance. Class 2 is a cabin seat allowing a flat or near-flat position, separated from passengers by at least a curtain. Class 3 is a seat in the cabin or on the flight deck that reclines at least 40 degrees and provides leg and foot support.

That classification determines how long the aircraft can legally fly. FAA guidance states that each rest facility carries a classification defining the maximum flight duty period limits for augmented operations, with a Class 1 facility providing for the longest duty period and a Class 3 the shortest. The FAA also specifies physical requirements: Class 1 sleeping surfaces measure 78 by 30 inches, surrounded by 35 cubic feet of space, plus a communal area of 65 cubic feet for entering, exiting, and changing. The A350's two-bunk overhead compartment meets the Class 1 description.

Bunk rest is not the only way a pilot sleeps in flight. Controlled rest is a separate procedure in which a pilot naps in their seat on the flight deck while the other pilot remains at the controls, and it operates under entirely different rules. Aviatize drew a clear distinction, describing controlled rest as different from uncontrolled microsleeps, which are dangerous, and from bunk or class-rest breaks taken away from the controls by augmented crews on long-haul flights.

The procedure focuses on avoiding deep sleep rather than achieving it. Flight Safety Foundation guidance specifies that a controlled rest period should be no longer than 40 minutes to minimize the risk of sleep inertia, keeping the nap short enough that the pilot does not slip into slow-wave sleep. Afterward, a recovery period of at least 20 minutes is required, during which the resting pilot takes no part in flight duties or briefings while sleep inertia dissipates. A crew briefing follows the recovery period, and the guidance states that both the recovery and the briefing should be completed at least 30 minutes before the top of descent.

The rule does not apply uniformly across the industry. Aviatize notes that the FAA does not authorize in-seat cockpit naps for Part 121 operations, having considered and deliberately excluded controlled rest when the modern flight and duty rules were written. The FAA does permit in-flight rest for augmented crews who leave the controls, which is the bunk arrangement rather than the seat one. Under EASA and many other authorities, controlled rest is permitted under defined conditions. A pilot flying for a European carrier may therefore take a 40-minute nap in the seat with a mandatory 20-minute recovery afterward, while a pilot flying the same aircraft for a US operator may not.

Domingo Saez | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Sleep inertia is the transitory period of impaired performance and alertness that occurs immediately after waking. It is not drowsiness in the ordinary sense but a measurable degradation in the ability to perform tasks, and it can significantly affect a pilot's capacity to carry out normal duties after waking. That is why a period free of both duties and briefings must follow any period of actual sleep in the flight deck.

The severity scales with sleep depth. Short naps of around 10 minutes produce relatively mild inertia, while longer periods of sleep generally produce more severe inertia and add to the recovery time before a pilot is fully alert. That trade-off is the reason controlled rest is capped at 40 minutes. A longer nap delivers greater restorative benefit but leaves the pilot less usable immediately afterward, and in a seat on the flight deck with one pilot already resting, immediate usability matters.

Bunk rest sits at the other end of that curve. A pilot sleeping for six or eight hours in a Class 1 facility reaches deep sleep by design, which is the entire point of carrying additional crew and building a compartment above the forward galley. The inertia on waking is correspondingly greater. That is the logic underneath the two-hour provision and underneath Singapore Airlines' 6/8/2 rotation alike. Neither positions the rest immediately before the approach. The regulation requires two consecutive hours in the second half of the duty period, and the airline's own planning returns the operating crew to the flight deck roughly three hours before landing. Both leave a gap between waking and the most demanding phase of the flight, which is the same principle that the 20-minute controlled rest recovery applies at a much smaller scale.

#6072. United CEO 100% Sure A Merger With American Would Get Approved. I’m 99% Sure He’s Wrong.

I’ll admit that there’s probably collectively a little too much reporting on what United CEO Scott Kirby says. The issue is, he’s a really bright guy, and I’d argue he’s the most impactful leader in the US airline industry since Richard Anderson at Delta. At the same time, on some level that seems to have gotten to his head, and I just feel like he’s making claims that are completely indefensible, at least if you approach them with any level of objectivity.

In April 2026, news broke about how United CEO Scott Kirby reportedly approached the Trump administration about the concept of merging with American, and forming a “flag” carrier for the United States.

Days later, American management publicly rejected this concept, which caused Kirby to publicly make his case for a merger with American. Months later, it came out that Kirby had also approached Delta about the concept of a merger. Ever since, Kirby has continued to insist that this is a great idea, and that those who oppose it are just misunderstanding his vision.

The widespread belief (among other industry executives and the public) is that such a deal wouldn’t get approval, because it shouldn’t… it would be really bad for competition! However, View from the Wing flags Kirby’s latest comments on his merger dream, which I can’t help but find to be interesting:

“I think the biggest impediment is having a willing partner. I am more convinced today than I was when I wrote my note six months ago that it could get approval. It could get approval because it is good for customers. So many people look at that kind of a merger through what has been the traditional airline commodity lens, that air travel is a commodity, and it doesn’t matter which airline flies. But customers care about the service, the product, the technology, the reliability. It wouldn’t be easy. We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.”

So Kirby claims he’s 100% certain that a merger between two of the three biggest US carriers would get approved by regulators. No, he’s not 80% sure, or 90% sure, or 99% sure. He’s 100% sure. Now, in fairness to him, he acknowledges that some divestitures would be required, but I think he’s underestimating the scale of divestitures that would be required for anything like this to get approval.

Maybe this is a hot take, but I think American management should call United’s bluff. Come to a deal that’s good for American shareholders, and create an absolutely massive breakup fee in the event it doesn’t get approval. There would only be upside for American, and then Kirby can put his money where his mouth is.

We know that Kirby has an axe to grind with American, since he was fired there, and then went on to work at United (which probably ended up being the best thing that could happen to him, because he sure seized that opportunity). So I can’t help but feel like a large motivation for his merger dream is based on wanting to get revenge, and that’s maybe clouding reality for him a bit.

Fundamentally, I disagree with Kirby’s merger dream on two levels — he overstates United’s greatness, and he understates the competitive implications of a merger of this scale.

United has absolutely improved massively under Kirby’s leadership. But Kirby acts like United is Singapore Airlines, while Delta and American are Air Algerie and TAAG Angola Airlines, by comparison.

Is Kirby forgetting that United is still catching up with Delta, and in the number two spot in the US industry? He acts as if the only way to have a pleasant flight on a US carrier is to fly with United, which just seems extreme. He seems to believe that, though, since he has called United “the best airline in the history of aviation.”

For that matter, from a consumer perspective, does Kirby not realize that the positive changes at United are now forcing American to make positive changes? American is getting seat back TVs, Starlink Wi-Fi, improved lounges, etc. That strong competition helps consumers, and it doesn’t hurt them.

Obviously eliminating one of the “big three” carriers would have huge implications for competition, and pricing power for airlines (especially when airline executives keep talking about how they want fare increases to stick around even after fuel prices decrease).

Kirby’s emphasis has long been on how it’s not just about offering the best price, but also about offering the best overall experience and value. While there has definitely been some decommoditization of airfare (in other words, more people are brand loyal), that still represents the minority of consumers. United is a publicly traded company that’s there to maximize shareholder value, and you can bet the airline will charge the highest fares it possibly can — if they didn’t, Kirby should be fired, because he’s not doing his job.

Even if you were to claim that domestic competition would be preserved (it wouldn’t be, in my opinion), what about internationally? The way global aviation has evolved is that the “big three” US carriers have helped create “big three” joint ventures, where they all partner with different airlines across the Atlantic and Pacific, allowing them to coordinate fares, schedules, etc. Abandoning an entire set of joint ventures would horribly hurt the competitive landscape.

United CEO Scott Kirby has for months been talking about how great it would be if United and American could merge, and he talks about how positive it would be for consumers. The issue is that such a deal would be unlikely to get regulatory approval, given the competitive implications.

Kirby disagrees, and he’s 100% certain that such a deal would get approval. I couldn’t disagree with him more, because the competitive implications would be massive (and negative). I kind of wish American would call his bluff and agree to a merger with a huge breakup fee, so that Kirby can be forced to actually stand behind his claims.

What do you make of Kirby’s merger “guarantees?”

#6071. Trump keeps signaling an end to Iran war, but expert warns a crucial piece of his strategy is missing

During a speech at Arlington National Cemetery Wednesday, President Donald Trump thanked U.S. service members for their ongoing sacrifices and argued that the U.S. has been pitted against Iran since 1979, when the Islamic Revolution happened.

President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, abruptly shifting his diplomatic message just three days after expressing optimism about negotiations and directing Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues instead.

"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

Trump's latest declaration came just one day after he proclaimed victory over Iran during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, while acknowledging that the conflict had not yet formally ended.

"We won," Trump said Wednesday. "It’s just a question of when we end it. I want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."

TRUMP DEFENDS IRAN WAR DURING VETERANS DAY ADDRESS, SAYS HE IS MAKING THE WORLD 'SAFER'

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a ceremony at Memorial Amphitheater at Arlington National Cemetery to mark Veterans Day Nov. 11, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The president also thanked veterans "working to ensure the world’s No. 1 sponsor of state terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon."

An administration official defended Trump's strategy, arguing the United States has substantial leverage over Iran through its naval blockade and continued military pressure, even as questions remain about how the conflict will end.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The president has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect," a U.S. official told Fox News Digital.

"President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States and will make sure that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."

Trump's latest words follow months of predictions that an agreement could be reached soon, including comments earlier this week that Tehran "would love to make a deal."

Trump's declaration raises questions about the future of U.S.-Iran negotiations, including whether diplomatic efforts will continue through other administration officials as Washington maintains its military and economic pressure on Tehran.

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

An Iranian flag is displayed at Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant during an official ceremony on Nov. 10, 2019, to kick-start work on a second reactor at the facility.   (AFP via Getty Images)

Trump has suggested on at least a dozen occasions since February that Iran wanted to negotiate or that an agreement could be reached soon, according to a preliminary review of his public remarks.

Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said the administration's combination of economic coercion, military force and regional partnerships is sensible but warned that a crucial diplomatic component remains underdeveloped.

"What’s lacking is disciplined diplomacy to complement the economic squeeze and possible airstrikes," Hood told Fox News Digital. "Our Gulf partners are singing from different hymn sheets, and we need to draw European partners in more meaningfully."

Trump's optimistic assessments began before U.S. military operations against Iran commenced. On Feb. 13, he suggested Tehran could avoid an attack by accepting Washington's terms. After military operations began, he increasingly emphasized Iran's weakened capabilities and the prospect of ending the conflict.

IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES

President Donald Trump arrives to deliver remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., Nov. 2, 2026. (Umit Bektas/Reuters)

On March 20, Trump said the United States was "getting very close" to achieving its military objectives.

The administration agreed to a ceasefire in April and continued pursuing a diplomatic settlement, but subsequent military actions and disagreements over Iran's nuclear program and regional shipping have left the broader conflict unresolved.

Trump continued expressing confidence that Iran wanted an agreement, including in May, when he suggested Tehran was eager to negotiate because of the damage inflicted on its military.

During an unscheduled appearance in the White House briefing room Monday, Trump said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over," while warning that U.S. forces remained "locked and loaded" should circumstances change.

Hood said Trump's seemingly contradictory messages could be part of a deliberate negotiating strategy.

"The administration is pursuing a sensible hybrid strategy of economic coercion, selective use of force and reliance on capable regional allies," Hood said.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN IS 'NEGOTIATING ON FUMES,' BELIEVES REGIME THOUGHT THEY COULD OUTWAIT HIM

Senior military leaders listen as U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at Marine Corps Base Quantico Sept. 30, 2025, in Quantico, Va. (robynmac)

"Trump’s messaging seems designed to both signal his preference for a diplomatic solution while preserving the option of force."

Hood defended the president's willingness to maintain military pressure.

"Bluster, bluffing and brinkmanship are inherent in the public dimension of negotiations like this; Trump does it, Rubio does it and senior figures in Tehran do it," he said.

"Strategic patience is essential in this standoff, which has essentially been 40 years in the making."

But Hood also suggested that securing meaningful nuclear concessions or a more cooperative government in Tehran would require coordination with regional partners.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

#6070. How To Tell Different Airplanes Apart, From 737s To A380s: An AvGeek’s Guide

The miles & points world has all kinds of different enthusiasts — some people are only interested in miles & points in order to save money on travel, while others are interested in miles & points because they love airplanes. I know there are plenty of people who are very frequent flyers but can barely tell the difference between an Airbus A380 and Boeing 747.

In this post, I’d like to share how I easily identify planes in a split second. Of course there are lots of methods for doing this, but I’ll share my techniques (and maybe other hardcore avgeeks can chime in with their methods in the comments section).

To keep things simple, I’ll just stick to the most popular mainline, commercial aircraft, and I’ll be talking about each “family” of aircraft in a particular section. Let’s start with Boeing aircraft, and then we’ll cover Airbus aircraft.

The Boeing 737 is the most common commercial aircraft in service. To me, there are a couple most obvious signs that a plane is a 737, as opposed to an A220 or A320.

One method is to look at the cockpit windows. The 737 has six cockpit windows (which is standard), and the window at the far end on each side “slopes up” at the bottom, so the window doesn’t go as far down as on other jets. Furthermore, when you look at the tail of the 737, you’ll see that it connects with the rest of the plane with an extended slope, much more so than on the A220 or A320 (below you can see a 737 in the front and an A321 in the back).

What can make identifying the 737 challenging is that there are so many different variants. Let’s differentiate between the 737 NG (the older version of the jet), and the 737 MAX (the newer and more controversial version of the jet).

There are three most obvious ways to tell if you’re traveling on a 737 MAX. The 737 MAX has the zig-zag pattern at the back of the engines, which I’ll talk more about below, as you’ll also find this on 787s and 747-8s.

Furthermore, the 737 MAX has the split winglet, which is large going both up and down, and the edges remain flat and straight. While some 737 NGs have split scimitar winglets, the upper and lower edges of the winglet are sloped.

Lastly, the 737 MAX has perfectly round engines, while the 737 NG engines flatten out a bit at the bottom, or look more oval.

How can you tell the difference between the variants? In terms of fuselage design, there’s the 737-700, 737-800/737 MAX 8, and 737-900/737 MAX 9 (with the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10 entering service soon). The 737-700 is the smallest variant, and the easiest way to identify it is based on the single exit on each side over the wing.

The 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 have two exits over the wing on each side, in addition to the exits at the front and back of the aircraft. The only exception would be the 737 MAX 8200, which is operated by some ultra low cost carriers, where there’s an extra exit in the back, with nine windows behind it.

Then the 737-900 and 737 MAX 9 have two exits over the wing, plus they have an additional door plug (as opposed to an actual exit) between the wing and rear exit, which is why the window spacing is a little weird in the back.

While Boeing’s modern narrow body aircraft is the 737, there are still a fair number of 757s flying around. The 757 is sort of like a flying pencil, as it’s quite long and the fuselage is narrow.

Unlike most other narrow body planes, the 757 has 10 wheels, as it has two wheels in the front, and two sets of four wheels in the back, which differentiates it from the 737, A320, etc., as those planes typically only have six wheels. The 757 also has a “proper” exit door behind the forward section, plus two overwing exits.

There are two variants of the 757 — the 757-200 and 757-300. The way to tell them apart is easy. The 757-200 does not typically have an additional exit between the overwing exits and the rear door.

Meanwhile the 757-300 does have another full exit in the rear section, with roughly a dozen windows on each side between it and the rear door. The 757-300 looks so long that you’d think it would break in half (don’t worry, it won’t).

As far as I’m concerned, the Boeing 747 will always be the queen of the skies. While the Airbus A380 has overtaken it in terms of size and passenger comfort, it can’t compete with the 747’s curves. The 747 has a full lower deck and then a partial upper deck, making it easy to identify.

While the passenger version of the 747 is becoming increasingly rare nowadays, there are two types that are most common — the 747-400 and the 747-8 (and no, it’s not the 747-800).

How can you tell the difference between the two planes? For one, the 747-400 has traditional winglets that stick “up.” On top of that, the 747-400 has a smaller upper deck. Behind the upper deck exit row, there are only seven windows on each side.

As a point of comparison, the 747-8’s wingtips gradually go up, and the upper deck is bigger, with 15 windows on each side behind the upper deck exit row.

The rear of the 747-8’s engines are also similar to those of the 787, with a zig-zag pattern, as I’ll explain below.

From a distance, it’s not unreasonable to think that a 767 and 777 look alike. I even sometimes make that mistake. It’s especially tricky since there’s the 767-300 and 767-400, and they’re roughly proportional to the 777-200 and 777-300 in terms of their dimensions.

What makes identifying the 767 especially tough is that many airlines have “modified” them. Some airlines have winglets on the 767, while others don’t. Some airlines have two doors on each side of the 767-300, while others have three doors.

So let me make this simple — at the base of each wing, the 767 has two sets of two wheels. In other words, on each side there are four wheels, for a total of 10 wheels on the plane (including the two nose wheels). Meanwhile the 777 has three sets of two wheels at the base of each wing, for a total of six wheels on each side. I know this might sound minor, but I’ve actually found it to be a very easy way to tell the planes apart.

How can you tell the difference between the 767-300 and 767-400? The 767-300 has at most three sets of doors on each side (and sometimes just two), while the 767-400 has four sets of doors on each side.

For me there are four identifying characteristics of the 777 — two huge engines, no winglets, a total of 14 wheels (two in the front, and six in the back on each side, with three rows of wheels there), and a vertically flat and boxy tail cone below the tail (as opposed to a rounded one on most other jets).

But how do you tell the difference between a Boeing 777-200 and a Boeing 777-300?

A Boeing 777-200 has just four doors on each side of the aircraft (one in the very front, one in front of the wing, one behind the wing, and one in the very back).

Meanwhile the 777-300 has five doors on each side of the aircraft (one in the very front, one in front of the wing, one immediately above the wing, one behind the wing, and one in the very back).

The easiest way to identify the 787 is by the zig-zag “cut outs” in the back of the engine, known as chevrons (designed for noise reduction). Also, the wings have a unique shape. While there aren’t abrupt winglets, the wings “stretch” pretty high up.

If you’re staring right at the front of the plane, there’s another easy identifier. The 787 is the only wide body jet to have four cockpit windows, rather than six.

How do you tell the difference between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10? Personally I can eyeball it pretty easily, but it can be tough for some people to do, since all versions of the plane have four exits on each side, similar wings, the same number of wheels, etc.

The only real difference between the planes is the length — the 787-8 is 186 feet long, the 787-9 is 206 feet long, and the 787-10 is 224 feet long. That’s a pretty significant difference, as the longest version is over 20% longer than the shortest version.

I think a 787-8 is pretty easy to spot, because it looks quite small from the outside. Usually I look at the number of windows between the first and second set of doors. If there are 10 or fewer windows on each side (including ones that are “blacked out”), it’s a 787-8.

Meanwhile if there are more than 10 but fewer than 15 windows on each side between the first and second set of doors, it’s the 787-9.

If there are more than 15 windows between the first and second set of doors on each side, it’s the 787-10.

The Airbus A220 is one of the most pleasant narrow body aircraft to fly. This is a fairly small, sleek, and modern looking aircraft. I know this might sound silly, but to me, it looks like an Airbus A350 that shrunk.

There are a few easiest ways to tell this apart from other jets. For one, unlike the 737 and A320, the A220 has four cockpit windows, rather than six. You’ll also notice that the nose of the aircraft is straighter and longer, compared to the more rounded nose of the A320.

The plane also has distinctive winglets, at least among narrow body planes. The winglets exclusively go up, and are pretty straight. They’re not as curved or vertical as on the A320.

There are two variants of the A220 — the A220-100 and A220-300. If you ask me, the easiest way to tell them apart is by how many windows there are between the forward door and the emergency exit over the wing. The A220-100 has roughly 12 windows on each side in this area, while the A220-300 has roughly 17 windows on each side in this area. You can also usually just eyeball it — the A220-300 looks a lot more stretched.

Much like with the 737, there are lots of A320 variants. There’s the A320ceo (the older version of the jet) and the A320neo (the more modern version of the jet, with “neo” standing for “new engine option”). Then you also have several variants, including the A319, A320, and A321.

Let’s start with the difference between the A320ceo and A320neo, which largely comes down to the engines, as you might have guessed based on the “neo” name. Not only does the A320neo have bigger engines than the A320ceo, but the A320neo also has extensions at the rear of the engine at the top and bottom. In simple words, you’ll notice how the engine looks more “open” in the back, unlike on the A320ceo, where it looks like it “closes” more.

Now let’s talk about how to tell the variants apart. The A319 is smaller than the A320 and A321, and an easy identifier is that it typically has only one exit over the wing on each side.

Meanwhile the A320ceo and A320neo have two exits on each side over the wing, but no other exits between the forward and rear doors.

Lastly, the A321ceo and A321neo are the largest variants of the jet, and just generally look stretched. These planes have an extra set of exits, beyond the forward and rear doors, plus the two exits on each side over the wing. So you’ll either notice an extra door, or some weird window spacing toward the back of the plane. The A321LR and A321XLR are just variants of the A321neo, and from the outside, there’s not an obvious way to tell them apart.

The major challenge with identifying the A330 is that there are two very different types of these planes — there’s the A330-200/300, which is the original version of the plane, and then there’s the A330-800/900neo, which is the new version of the plane. To some people, the A330-900neo may look more like an A350-900 than an A330-300.

Let’s start with the A330-200/300. This plane is pretty “proportional” looking, and can easily be identified by the fact that it has two engines and the most “traditional” winglets out there. The winglets are an easy way to differentiate it from the other twin-engine wide bodies out there. Furthermore, the plane has four doors on each side.

The A330-800/900neo has a similar body style, except the winglets are different. While the A330-200/300 winglets are wide and point almost straight up, the A330-800/900neo winglets get narrower, and curve a bit more.

The A330neo and A350 have similar general designs, though there is a big difference in the wingtips, as you’ll see below when I cover the A350. If anyone has any other easy ways to spot the difference between the two planes, please let me know.

The A340 is a single deck plane with four engines, which makes it pretty easy to identify, since it’s the only non-double decker that has four engines. But how do you tell the difference between the A340-200/300 and A340-600? Okay, truth be told there aren’t a lot of these planes flying anymore, so there aren’t many situations where you’ll have to do that. With Lufthansa having just retired the A340-600, you’ll barely find the plane outside of Iran nowadays. But still…

The A340-200/300 has engines that looks disproportionately small (like, are these things gonna propel us through the sky at 500 miles per hour, or dry my hair?), and also has just four doors on each side of the aircraft.

Meanwhile the A340-600 is a gorgeous, beastly work of art. It’s so long, so skinny, and has appropriately sized-looking engines. There are also five doors on each side of the aircraft. Personally after the 747, I find the A340-600 to be the most beautiful plane. However, like I said, you won’t find it in the skies of most countries anymore.

The Airbus A350 has two main identifying characteristics — an extremely sleek design (especially near the nose, and with the Batman-looking cockpit windows), and very “steep” winglets (they’re not gradual, unlike the 787).

How do you tell the difference between the A350-900 and A350-1000? There are two main differences.

For one, the A350-900 has 10 wheels, while the A350-1000 has 14 wheels. The difference comes from the base of each wing having six wheels (three rows of two) rather than four wheels (two rows of two). That’s because the A350-1000 is the stretched version of the A350-900.

The easiest other way to tell the difference is based on the number of windows between doors one and two. The A350-900 has somewhere around 15 windows on each side between the first two sets of doors.

Meanwhile the A350-1000 has over 20 windows on each side between the first and second set of doors.

I don’t think anyone has trouble identifying this whale-jet, given that it has two full decks.

Understandably not everyone can spot the difference between airplanes, because, well, to most people it doesn’t actually matter. That being said, for us avgeeks it’s often a favorite pastime. Hopefully the above is a simple guide that can help people tell apart planes, should they be interested in learning a bit more.

While there are lots of other differences, I figure it makes sense to highlight some of the most “obvious” tricks, as opposed to studying each plane in great detail.

To fellow avgeeks, I’d be curious to hear how you easily tell planes apart!

@Ben The Boeing 737-900 and MAX9 are a bit more complex than indicated. The plain old 737-900 did not come with the extra emergency exit behind the wings. That was only introduced for the 737-900ER. The 737-9 can come with a door plug which is entirely sealed or with an actual emergency exit door. Airlines that do not need the full seating capacity can opt for the plug, rather than an exit. I’m on the road about half the year on assignment for TPG and on any given week, you might find me browsing the jade market in Taipei, window-shopping through Galerie Vivienne in Paris or strolling through the San Telmo market in Buenos Aires on the hunt for collectibles.

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen a souvenir, piece of art, sweet treat or other little curio and thought, “Wouldn’t this make a great gift for so and so?”

The only trouble is, I travel light, so there’s nary a nook or cranny in my carry-on to fit a gift, let alone several.

I do, however, make a mental inventory of potential gifts I see so that I can order them for friends and family later. Here are a few of my favorite recent finds that might be perfect for someone on your holiday gift list, all inspired by my travels.

Best for: Armchair travelers who like to keep cozy

There’s a lot I love about 1 Hotels — their sustainable ethos, the Bamford bath amenities, in-room filtered water taps, the smattering of hyperlocal, destination-specific activities on offer to guests, bustling public spaces with unique dining concepts and…the bathrobes. I’m not usually a bathrobe kind of guy, but I can’t resist donning one of these ultracomfortable numbers anytime I’m a guest at one of these properties. Simple and soft, with a gray jersey-knit lining and a loose hoodie, they’re perfect for lounging with a cappuccino while you try to stave off jet lag.

TPG tip: You might want to make this purchase at an actual 1 Hotel boutique so you can earn more points per dollar with a credit card that offers a travel or hotel category bonus.

Best for: The Japanophile you want to impress

Like an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object, my delight in purchasing travel souvenirs is only impeded by the limited space in my small city apartment. That’s why I love the little lacquerware boxes and trays from Zohiko, a boutique in Kyoto’s Nakagyo Ward that traces its history back to the 17th century. I especially love the finely filigreed Kirikane style, where patterns or shapes are cut out in gold or silver leaf and pressed into place. I purchased a glossy black box with gold inlay of cherry blossoms and autumn leaves on my last visit, and I keep it on my nightstand to hold my wedding ring and watch.

TPG tip: Make a trip to Japan out of it and browse the physical Zohiko boutique (you can also enjoy tax-free purchases if you’re visiting) while checking out some of Kyoto’s exciting new hotels.

Best for: Folks who appreciate colorful, culturally significant crafts

Inevitably, every time I’m traipsing around Bogotá, I find myself drawn to this gorgeous little boutique in the city’s upscale Chapinero neighborhood, which sources fair-trade handcrafted pieces of art and decor from small communities around the country, including woven baskets starting at just $18. I am personally drawn to carefully carved wooden Tamo bowls from the coastal Nariño region, decorated with brightly dyed strands of wheat or barley fiber, but you can find everything from woven baskets to hammocks, jewelry and even pieces of furniture.

TPG tip: While you can often haggle for handicrafts in Colombia, prices in this boutique are as marked, so save your negotiating skills for street vendors.

Best for: Helping a friend spruce up their interior decor game

Although long popular with backpackers and river cruisers, Luang Prabang still feels like an under-the-radar find in mountainous Laos, sitting on the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan Rivers. It’s also a hotbed of fair-trade arts and crafts. A standout atelier in town is Ock Pop Tok, an art school, store and restaurant that aims to revive, support and teach traditional Lao artistic techniques. Visitors can take classes in silk-weaving, batik-dyeing and embroidery, among other offerings. I am always tempted to buy out the textile section of the boutique, but I usually limit myself to a vibrant wall hanging or two.

TPG tip: Don’t just make a purchase; spend a few days as a student at Ock Pop Tok to pick up a new craft yourself.

Best for: Travelers who like their perfumes with a hint of historical luxury

Of course, I’d suggest visiting the original Florence flagship of this bath and beauty purveyor, which dates back to 1221. It feels a little like visiting Ollivanders Wand Shop from “Harry Potter,” with antique cases bursting with all-natural unguents and elixirs whose formulas were originally developed by Dominican friars. But if you can’t get there, there are also locations around the U.S., including those in West Hollywood, California, Soho in New York City and Bal Harbour, Florida. I tend to keep it simple and go for the pure sweet almond oil, but you could also go regal and buy a bottle of the perfumery’s citrusy Acqua della Regina, created for Catherine de' Medici as a gift for her husband, the future king of France, back in 1533.

TPG tip: It can sometimes be less expensive to purchase these products from the original store in Florence, so why not make a trip out of it?

Best for: The fashionable cowboys at your rodeo

I love an eye-catching accessory, and belts are my statement pieces of choice. So on my last visit to Buenos Aires, I stopped by Arandu Talabarteria’s tony boutique in Recoleta. The whole store is inspired by a romanticized version of gaucho life on the pampas. You can find sturdy leather boots, billowy bombacha pants, cozy ponchos and my favorite: woven belts with intricate threadwork and high-quality leather. They start at $45 and can range into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the level of detail and craftsmanship. Best of all, you can ship to the U.S., so you don’t have to cross the equator to stock up.

TPG tip: They also have dog collars for your faithful canine companion.

Best for: The high-flying #avgeek in your life

If you’ve followed me for the past few years, you know I’m pretty much obsessed with KLM’s tile Delft houses, the little replicas of actual historical buildings around the Netherlands that the airline hands out to long-haul business-class passengers. I’ve attended the unveiling of each year’s new house for several years now, and my own collection has grown into a veritable village. If you have an equally #avgeeky member of your gifting circle and are looking for the perfect present, then you might want to consider buying one of these beauties for them. Historian Mark Zegeling’s “Little Kingdom by the Sea” book set, which delves into the history of all 107 of the houses, is a great accompanying gift as well.

TPG tip: Be sure to use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees so you don’t get dinged with a 1-3% surcharge when buying your house.

Best for: Swanky sunseekers who want to make a splash

How do you tell me you summer on the French Riviera without telling me you summer on the French Riviera? You simply tote around a sunshiney yellow-and-white-striped beach bag from the iconic Carlton Cannes, the first luxury hotel to open in the city, way back in 1911. A lot has changed since then, but the simple design is meant to evoke the Côte d’Azur of yore, when you might have found Cary Grant and Grace Kelly sunbathing on the plage between scenes of “To Catch a Thief.”

TPG tip: Make your purchase in person and use an IHG One Rewards credit card to earn multiple points per dollar.

Best for: International imbibers with a sweet tooth

You might find it hard to remember your visit to Singapore, let alone pick up some souvenirs as gifts for friends, after you’ve had a few Singapore Slings at the Raffles Hotel’s iconic Long Bar. That’s why it might come in handy to pick up a keepsake Singapore Sling glass for your friends from the hotel’s online boutique. It’s like taking a sip of history with you. The nation’s signature drink was invented by Ngiam Tong Boon back in 1915 and is an intoxicating (and sweet!) mix of gin, grenadine, cherry liqueur, Benedictine, Curacao and both pineapple and lime juice. Even a sip can transport you back to a sultry Southeast Asian evening.

TPG tip: Pick a card that earns bonus rewards on everyday purchases, like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so you’re making the most of your spending.

Best for: Your friends’ (or your own) globe-trotting tots

We can’t forget about the kids! In my experience, there are few better or more engaging (or educational) ways to get the tykes in your life interested in travel than Little Passports, a subscription membership where each month, your child is mailed a new box focusing on individual countries, animals, crafts and even DIY science experiments, depending on their specific subscription and age.

TPG tip: Don’t forget to choose the subscription length you want from the start, otherwise, these charges might sneak up on you month after month if you don’t cancel.

Best for: Your favorite skincare aficionado

I first came across Officine Universelle Buly’s sweet-smelling body products during a stay at the Rosewood Hotel de Crillon in Paris last year, and I promptly swiped several tubes of shampoo, conditioner and body lotion from my suite to use at home. On my next visit to the City of Light, though, I stopped by the enchanting store in the 6th arrondissement to sniff through various scents and balms tinged with exotic notes like Madagascar amber and Maltese iris. They also have fabulous tortoiseshell hair clips and combs that you can have monogrammed for even the most discerningly coiffed companions in your life.

TPG tip: If you’re purchasing liquid products and not checking a bag, make sure they comply with carry-on limits.

Best for: Yourself! This is the ultimate self-care splurge

In recent years, more and more hotel chains have started selling the mattresses they use directly to customers. And while you might be a Westin Heavenly Bed fan, or perhaps a devotee of DoubleTree’s signature Sweet Dreams mattress, I personally recommend a Four Seasons mattress, which has the plushest pillowtop of any hotel bed I’ve experienced. After staying at dozens of Four Seasons over the years, I finally took the plunge and purchased one for myself about six years ago and I’ve never slept better. It’s definitely a splurge, but you can’t put a price tag on a great night’s sleep. So make this one a gift for yourself.

TPG tip: Given the price tag, wait until you have a new credit card with a minimum spending requirement to meet to earn its welcome offer so you can put your splurge to good use.

#6068. Which Credit Cards Give You Hotel Elite Status, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there, thanks to the strong perks that they offer. In this post, I’d like to specifically focus on credit cards that offer hotel elite status, and talk about under what circumstances they could be worth it.

I’ve already written about the best hotel credit cards offering free nights, either as an annual benefit or as a reward for reaching certain spending thresholds. In many cases, these anniversary free night certificates can more than justify the annual fees on cards, given that they can be redeemed at some great hotels.

Nowadays it’s possible to earn elite status with most major hotel group through credit cards, so let’s talk about the options there are, and under what circumstances this is actually worth it.

I’d like to take a look at all the ways that you can use US-issued credit cards to earn elite status with a hotel loyalty program. In some cases, you get status just for having a card, and in other cases, a certain amount of spending is required.

There are potentially all kinds of benefits to hotel elite status, ranging from free breakfast to late check-out to bonus points to suite upgrades. Obviously the higher your status, the better the perks.

Here are all the options, going in alphabetical order based on the name of the loyalty program. Note that I’m only including credit cards that are only open to new cardmembers.

Choice Privileges has two credit cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can earn you Choice Privileges Gold status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can earn you Choice Privileges Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 20 qualifying nights per calendar year):

There are no cards that offer Choice Privileges Diamond status.

Hilton Honors has several cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can help you earn Hilton Honors™ Silver status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights, four qualifying stays, or $2,500 in qualifying spending, per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn Hilton Honors™ Gold status (which ordinarily requires 25 qualifying nights, 15 qualifying stays, or $6,000 in qualifying spending, per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn Hilton Honors™ Diamond status (which ordinarily requires 50 qualifying nights, 25 qualifying stays, or $11,500 in qualifying spending, per calendar year):

There are no cards that offer Hilton Honors Diamond Reserve status.

IHG One Rewards has several cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can help you earn IHG One Rewards Silver status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn IHG One Rewards Gold status (which ordinarily requires 20 qualifying nights or 40,000 base points per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn IHG One Rewards Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 40 qualifying nights or 60,000 base points per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn IHG One Rewards Diamond status (which ordinarily requires 70 qualifying nights or 120,000 base points per calendar year):

Marriott Bonvoy has several cards that can help you earn elite status. One important thing to understand upfront is that some Marriott credit cards outright offer a certain elite tier, while other cards offer a certain number of elite nights toward elite status, and some cards offer a combination of the two. So the below reflects all of those factors.

Note that each Marriott Bonvoy member can earn at most 40 elite nights per year from credit cards, with 25 elite nights coming from a personal card, and 15 elite nights coming from a business card.

The following cards can help you earn Marriott Bonvoy® Silver Elite status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn Marriott Bonvoy® Gold Elite status (which ordinarily requires 25 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can help you earn Marriott Bonvoy® Platinum Elite status (which ordinarily requires 50 qualifying nights per calendar year):

There are no cards that offer Marriott Bonvoy® Titanium Elite Status or Marriott Bonvoy® Ambassador Elite status.

World of Hyatt has several cards that can help you earn elite status. This both comes in the form of outright receiving status, and also in the form of receiving elite nights that count toward status.

The following cards can help you earn World of Hyatt Discoverist status (which ordinarily requires 10 qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per calendar year):

The following cards can help you earn World of Hyatt Explorist status (which ordinarily requires 30 qualifying nights or 50,000 base points per year):

The following cards can help you earn World of Hyatt Globalist status (which ordinarily requires 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 base points per year):

Wyndham Rewards has a few cards that can help you earn elite status.

The following card can help you earn Wyndham Rewards Gold status (which ordinarily requires five qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can help you earn Wyndham Rewards Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 15 qualifying nights per calendar year):

The following card can help you earn Wyndham Rewards Platinum status (which ordinarily requires 40 qualifying nights per calendar year):

If you’re going to stay with a certain hotel group, it goes without saying that having some elite status is better than not having elite status. At the same time, I don’t want to overpromise, and suggest that being an elite member is going to get you the most amazing treatment on earth.

After all, if you get elite status just for having a credit card, you can assume that you’re not alone in pursuing this strategy. 😉 That being said, there are definitely some credit card elite status opportunities that are more lucrative than others.

My single favorite hotel credit card for elite status is the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card (learn more), as it offers Diamond status in the Hilton Honors program. This gets you 100% bonus points, room upgrades subject to availability, breakfast (or a food & beverage credit in the US), lounge access at select brands, etc.

As is common with the major hotel groups, the further from the United States you get, the better the elite treatment, and the better the shot of a good upgrade. Hilton Honors is my third preferred hotel group, and the Diamond status on the card does the trick for me. Given all the card’s other perks, I also find it really easy to justify.

My second favorite hotel credit card is the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more), as it offers Platinum status in the Marriott Bonvoy program. This gets you 50% bonus points, room upgrades subject to availability, the option of selecting breakfast as your welcome amenity at most brands, lounge access at most brands, guaranteed 4PM check-out at non-resorts, etc.

Don’t expect all that much when it comes to upgrades (at least in major markets), but the guaranteed perks, like late check-out, breakfast at most brands, etc., really do add up.

Beyond that, I think there should be a special mention for all the cards offering Hilton Gold status, given how easy it is to earn. Most crucially, it offers breakfast at properties outside the United States (and a food & beverage credit within the United States), so at least it offers something in the way of guaranteed benefits, compared to other comparable tiers.

It’s pretty remarkable that nowadays you can earn valuable status with Hilton, Marriott, and Wyndham, just for having a credit card (without a spending requirement), and with Hyatt and IHG you can earn valuable status with credit card spending.

On top of that, there are many mid-range credit cards that offer status just for having the card, which can be valuable as well. For example, it’s really easy to earn Hilton Gold elite status, and that gets you perks like free breakfast at most brands, bonus points, and more.

If you are going to spend money on your hotel credit card to earn status, just make sure you consider the opportunity cost of that spending.

Which credit cards do you find to be most valuable for earning elite hotel status?

#6067. Dozens Of Boeing 787s Face Checks Over Fuel Tanks That Could Ignite When Hit By Lightning

The Federal Aviation Administration has ordered inspections of certain Boeing 787 Dreamliners, warning that sealant defects could create a spark inside the tank during a lightning strike, potentially triggering a fuel tank explosion. The airworthiness directive will take effect next month and covers specific 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10 aircraft identified by Boeing. According to the FAA, 60 US-registered 787s fall under the order, with US airlines collectively operating over 170 Dreamliners. However, dozens of Dreamliners operated by foreign airlines and so the total number of affected aircraft worldwide could be higher.

#6065. United Global Services: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

All of the “big three” carriers in the United States have invitation-only elite status. I’ve written about how American has Concierge Key and Delta has 360 status, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at Global Services, which is United’s invitation-only elite status.

What is United Global Services status, how do you earn it, what are the benefits, and how many members are there? I’ll share everything I know…

Global Services is United Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. Aside from lifetime status (which I’ll cover below), there are no published ways to earn this exclusive tier. Most members have to qualify for Global Services status year after year.

In addition to offering the highest priority for just about everything at United, Global Services status also offers better “soft” treatment with the airline.

There’s only one published way to earn Global Services, and that’s through United’s Million Miler program. If you earn four million lifetime miles with United MileagePlus then you get lifetime Global Services status, and you can even share that with a companion in the same household.

Admittedly this is a very high threshold, so you’d have to be loyal to United for a long time to earn that (for example, you’d need to fly 100,000 miles per year for 40 years). I’d guess that only a small minority of Global Services members have earned status this way.

The much more common way to earn Global Services status is through an invitation, using unpublished criteria:

It’s worth emphasizing that Global Services is a lot more about the types of tickets you book than the number of miles you fly. You’re more likely to earn Global Services if you fly 150,000 miles per year exclusively on paid business class tickets, vs. 400,000 miles per year on a mix of tickets, even if the revenue amounts between the two scenarios are similar.

Note that if someone earns Global Services status and is also at least a one million miler, they can nominate a companion to also be Global Services for as long as they have status (this is different than four million miler status, where you and a companion get the status for life). However, starting in 2027, United is adding limits on sharing status with others.

Just to put the qualification requirements into perspective, below is a chart with the typical status requirements for 2027.

Earning status is ordinarily based on the concept of PQPs (Premier Qualifying Points), and you can earn one PQP per dollar spent on United, or up to one PQP per $15 spent on an eligible credit card. In other words, Premier 1K status requires $32,000 in spending on flights, or $480,000 in credit card spending.

One interesting thing is that unlike at American and Delta, credit card spending doesn’t seem to count toward invitation-only status at United. That could change over time, of course.

United Global Services members automatically receive all of the perks of Premier 1K status, which is United’s top published elite tier. This includes everything from Economy Plus seating, to complimentary space available upgrades to first class, and more. This also includes Star Alliance Gold status, which offers priority perks across Star Alliance carriers, including priority check-in, an additional baggage allowance, lounge access, priority boarding, and more.

Beyond that, perks for United Airlines Global Services members include the following:

I find it interesting that Global Services members don’t get access to United Polaris Lounges (unless their ticket otherwise offers access). Admittedly many Global Services members are probably traveling in business class on long haul flights anyway, but still, it’s a contrast to the policies for American Flagship Lounges and Delta One Lounges, and it’s not great for domestic travel.

Airline elite status can be a bit of a you-know-what measuring contest, and people are always curious about how many members there are in a particular elite tier. Since Global Services is primarily invitation-only, the airline is also tight-lipped about how many Global Services members there are. All we can do is speculate… and there’s a lot of speculation out there.

For example, when this question was asked on Quora, someone deduced that there were 20 million MileagePlus elite members, 40,000 Premier 1K members, and 2,000 Global Services members. All of those numbers seem way off to me. I’d guess there are way fewer elite members, way more Premier 1K members, and way more Global Services members.

This is purely speculation on my part, but I would guess that there are somewhere around 15,000-25,000 Global Services members. For context, I’ve speculated that there are somewhere around 15,000 American Concierge Key members (and we know for a fact that there were at least 11,300 members in 2019), so why do I think there are more United Global Services members?

If anyone has any theories or thoughts they’d like to share, I’d love to hear it (and if anyone has any inside info they want to share anonymously, that would be great too). It’s possible I’m totally off, but I’m just sharing my best educated guess.

It’s hard to say whether something like United Global Services is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like United Global Services varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

The better “soft” treatment, which I’d consider to be the prime benefit of the service, will be much more noticeable if you’re someone who travels domestically every week (given how likely you are to encounter irregular operations), rather than someone who just takes a handful of long haul flights each year.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

One thing worth mentioning is that if you really value the perks of Global Services but don’t have the status, there’s United Signature Service, provided by Global Airport Concierge, which gives you similar protection and airport service. I can’t imagine it’ll have widespread appeal, but it’s worth being aware of.

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including American Concierge Key and Delta 360. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, I’d say United Global Services is strong when it comes to recognition, but is lacking when it comes to lounge access, given that the status doesn’t offer any access to premium international lounges at United (unlike comparable status at American and Delta).

Here are a couple of thoughts on the comparable status tiers at American and Delta:

If you think United is tight-lipped about Global Services status, then wait until you hear about Chairman’s Circle. This is an extra-special invitation-only status that is typically given to people who have contracts that include at least $5 million in annual spending on United. Only one person at the company gets it.

At least that’s how it used to be, and the details here are very limited. I’d guess the number of members there is in the dozens…

Global Services is United Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. You can earn it either by being very loyal to United over the course of your life, controlling major travel contracts and having a lot of influence, or by spending a lot on United (think $50,000+, though probably even a lot more, nowadays).

Global Services comes with top priority for everything at United, and on top of that you can expect that the “soft” treatment will be much better as well.

To United Global Services members, what has your experience been with the status? And anyone want to guess how many members there are?

#6064. Copa 737 & UPS 767 Collide On Miami Airport Taxiway: Pilot Blames Checklist Distraction

Last night, a Copa Boeing 737 and a UPS Boeing 767 collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport (MIA). South Florida is known for its horrendous drivers, and I guess that trend is making its way to the taxiways at airports as well.

This accident happened shortly after 9PM on Saturday, November 14, 2026. It involves a Copa Boeing 737-800 that had just arrived from Panama City (PTY) as flight CM427, and a UPS Boeing 767-300 that was getting ready to depart to Bogota (BOG) as flight 5X358.

The UPS 767 had been advised to give way to the Copa 737 on the taxiway, but the pilots failed to do that. As a result, the wing of the Copa 737 hit the nose of the UPS 767. While a full investigation will of course be performed, the air traffic control audio gives us a good sense of what happened:

Copa pilot: “427, somebody hit us.”ATC: “427, roger. UPS, you’re supposed to give way to the 73 there.”UPS pilot: “Roger, we running checklist, runway change.”ATC: “UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?”UPS pilot: “Yeah, we went too far, and then he clipped us with the wing.”

So as you can see, the UPS pilots were at fault here, and the excuse seems to be that they were distracted because they were going through checklists because of a runway change.

Fortunately there were no major injuries, but two people on the Copa flight did complain of minor back pain. The damage to the planes is extensive, though, including to the nose of the UPS 767 and the left wing of the Copa 737.

Taxiway contact at MIA last night.Copa 737 left wingtip into the nose of a UPS 767. UPS was instructed to give way, crew acknowledged they went too far. Two treated for minor injuries on scene. pic.twitter.com/sB0kJamQ3J

That UPS B767 looks pissed after clipping the winglet of that Copa Airlines B737! https://t.co/9vu34jsVkk pic.twitter.com/e0l5ergWei

Can I just respectfully make a point here, without being sarcastic? If the accident were reversed here, and the female, foreign pilot had been at fault for this, we would immediately see people screaming “DEI.” Meanwhile when someone sounds like your average American dude, we just consider it to be an honest mistake.

The concept of “DEI” in the aviation world is not about hiring unqualified people, but it’s about expanding the potential pool of people who could qualify for a job, so that the best people can be hired.

Why do I even bring this up now? Well, remember the recent Amazon Air crash at Miami Airport? When the air traffic control audio came out, people heard a foreign accent from the pilot. People immediately started yelling “DEI,” talking about H1-B visas, etc.

However, that was the pilot communicating, and the pilot actually flying was a white, older, ex-military dude. And he was flying completely recklessly, and failed to listen to the first officer’s warnings. I know it’s hard when reality doesn’t match people’s narratives, but that’s why I feel like it’s important to call these things out.

A major corporation, Amazon, subcontracts with other foreign carriers to operate their aircraft. What I’m saying is a few of those subcontractors hire lesser qualified crews and maintenance, resulting in what happened in Miami. And, I’m sure DEI plays a role. In my estimation,… https://t.co/GhFeJHMuMK

Presumably this is coincidental, but I think it’s interesting to note that on November 5, 2026, there was a very close call on a taxiway at Miami Airport, not that far from where this happened.

A Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 was departing to Frankfurt (FRA) as LH463, and an American Boeing 787-8 had just arrived from Philadelphia (PHL) as AA1155. The American 787 was advised to “give way to Lufthansa off the right,” which… they then failed to do.

As you’d expect, the Lufthansa pilots took the situation very seriously. The Lufthansa pilot said “we had to make a full stop at a full taxi speed, American is turning in our way.” The air traffic controller responded by saying “they’ve made every wrong turn possible” (in reference to the American plane — which I don’t actually think is true here). The Lufthansa pilot said they’d file a report, because that “was very close to an accident in the making.”

I love how German the Lufthansa pilot is in how he handles this, and how he finishes by saying “you need to make sure stuff like that doesn’t happen too often.” Lol, you don’t say…

A Copa Boeing 737 and a UPS Boeing 767 had an accident on a taxiway at Miami Airport. The UPS 767 was supposed to give way to the Copa 737, but failed to do so, as the pilots claimed they were distracted by their checklists.

This accident took out a chunk of the wing of the Copa 737, and did quite a bit of damage to the nose of the UPS 767 as well. Earlier this month, a very close call between a Lufthansa 747 and American 787 also got quite a bit of attention, but fortunately this had a better outcome.

What do you make of this Miami Airport accident?
