Any time I get overwhelmed these days, the first thought I have is: I need to go touch grass. And I really mean it — the great outdoors is exactly where I go to unwind, relax, challenge myself and have a good think. In fact, for many of us at TPG, it's a big part of the reason we love to travel.

This holiday season, you might find yourself shopping for someone who plans their entire winter travel schedule around where to ski the best powder on the planet, or maybe for someone whose traveling around the world bagging peak after peak. Maybe you're close with a national park enthusiast, or you need a really good stocking stuffer for a dedicated marathon runner. Or maybe someone in your life loves nothing more than cozying up at the perfect camping spot for a long weekend.

No matter what type of outdoor adventure their passion might be, this gift guide (though non-exhaustive; I had to cut myself off at some point!) compiles some of my absolute favorite, go-to items for those who simply love to spend time outside. Have a scroll, and let us know in the comments what your dream outdoor gift would be.

It goes without saying that anyone who skis or snowboards throughout the winter season can benefit from a pass. My personal favorite in recent years has been the Ikon pass, which has taken me to mountains like Mammoth, Steamboat Springs and Killington. But the opportunity to get your turns in certainly doesn't stop at the U.S.; the Ikon pass famously gets passholders access to all four major ski resorts in Niseko, Japan, known for having some of the best (if not the best) powder in the world.

TPG tip: With a purchase as hefty as this one, you'll want to ensure you use a card that will maximize rewards. I'd recommend a card that earns an elevated, flat rate across all purchases — like the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Best for: The sustainability-minded gourmand

While I've taken Pataognia Provisions tinned fish on the trail before, I have to admit I eat it at home all the time, too. Anyone with an affinity for tinned fish — and for sustainably sourced seafood — will love this variety pack that gives you a taste of everything from lemon herb mussels to sardines in coconut curry.

TPG tip: American Express often has valuable Patagonia deals for cardholders, so check your Amex offers during the holiday season to see if you'll get a statement credit for spending a certain amount at Patagonia.

Shop Patagonia Provisions Tinned Fish Variety Pack

Not all hiking socks are created equal, and after many a mile spent scrambling up the granite of the White Mountains, I've found that Darn Tough are true to their name in every sense. I'm partial to the micro crew cushion sock — they provide just enough cushion without taking up too much space in my boot, they're breathable and they hold up well on multi-day trips. But pick any Darn Tough style and it's pretty tough to go wrong.

TPG tip: Darn Tough is often eligible for Capital One Shopping Rewards via several online retailers like Cabela's and Shoebacca. If you're a cardholder, make sure you're shopping with the Capital One portal Chrome extension to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Cozy is the primary concept with Outerknown's Blanket Shirt (available for men and women in a wide array of colors and patterns). The first time I put one of these on about a decade ago, I knew it would become a staple in my everyday wardrobe, but especially for shoulder season camping trips and cabin getaways, when evenings and early mornings are cold and crisp.

TPG tip: Outerknown is available at Nordstrom, so Nordstrom cardholders and Nordy Club members can consider cashing in their valuable awards for this item — or even earn cash back on top of your Nordy Club rewards by starting your online Nordstrom purchases via Rakuten.

Anyone who goes out into the backcountry regularly knows that having a plan for hydration is a necessity — and having a dependable, safe way to filter water is simply nonnegotiable. Sawyer makes some of the most popular and reliable water filtration systems for those hitting the trail — I recently used my Sawyer Squeeze on a four day backpacking and was blown away by how simple and functional it is. It removes 99.99999% of bacteria — that's a lot of nines. Whether its used while camping, hiking, backpacking, hunting, fishing or just packed for an outdoor-centric travel excursion, this is a valuable tool for any outdoor enthusiast to carry with them.

TPG tip: You can buy a Sawyer water filtration system on Amazon to get Amazon Prime benefits like free two-day shipping. Just make sure to use a card that's great for Amazon purchases.

If you know someone who loves to backpack — or maybe they're a first timer and you're helping them round out their backpacking setup — the MSR Pocket Rocket is the camp stove I come back to again and again (and I think many, if not most, backpackers would say the same). It's famously lightweight and foldable, boils water very quickly, has a sturdy base for excellent pot support  and is super easy to use and set up (this is coming from someone who lit a camp stove on fire once — I've never had that issue with this one).

#6062. Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress

Incoming House Minority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., joins ‘The Ingraham Angle’ to discuss the GOP’s legislative priorities, efforts to support American manufacturing and whether Democrats will work with Republicans to advance their agenda.

EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans are heading into the next Congress ready to brawl.

Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who will rise from the No. 3 most powerful House Republican to No. 2 next year, told Fox News Digital the GOP will hold the new Democrat majority "accountable" for the far-left faction's ideas over the next two years, even if it cannot control what bills get a vote.

Emmer, who has served as House majority whip the past four years, was elected Tuesday to serve as minority whip alongside incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. The speaker of the House position turns over to Democrats and will likely be won by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.

And despite Jeffries being poised to take control of what legislation gets to the House floor, Emmer signaled House Republicans would find ways to push their agenda as well.

JIM JORDAN BECOMES NEW HOUSE GOP LEADER AFTER CLOSED-DOOR VOTE, DEFEATING STEVE SCALISE

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer speaks during a news conference after the House GOP elected new leadership on Capitol Hill Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"What's their answer to dealing with costs and wages? We're going to investigate Trump," Emmer said in reference to Democrats. "That's not going to solve the problems that they created. So, that's going to be the job of the whip, is to make sure that we have a coordinated process — committee hearings, floor votes — to expose and define exactly who these people really are."

PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES

Emmer, in his first print interview since winning the House minority whip job, would not go into detail about how Republicans would utilize floor votes, however.

"There's a toolbox with a bunch of different tools, and you're going to have to build that strategy as you go from week to week," he said.

The Minnesota Republican also signaled there would be little appetite for bipartisanship over the next two years, a sentiment he suggested would come from the other side of the aisle.

"Well, look, they're not going to work with us. That's pretty clear, and I don't even know if they're going to be able to work with each other," Emmer said.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE

Congressman Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., address a news conference during the congressional delegation's visit to Denmark in Copenhagen April 25, 2025 (Emil Nicolai Helms/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)

"I see nowhere where they're going to work with Republicans. And Republicans who think they are should think again, because they will tell you nice things, and then they will just go do what they do."

Other House Republicans are already coming up with ideas on how to put Democrats on the spot on the House floor in the new Congress.

"We'll file amendments," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "And I think that'll be where having good debaters and communicators would be important."

Holding amendment votes is commonplace before large pieces of legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which Congress has enacted annually for decades to update and reauthorize critical national security policies.

Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., suggested an emphasis on a parliamentary procedure called the "motion to recommit," which allows the minority party to get a vote on altering or even killing a bill in its tracks.

"I expect we'll use that smartly," LaLota said. "But, as well, a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will be wise to work these problems backwards, to know that anything he puts on the floor that he wants to become law or budget needs President Trump's signature and probably 60 votes in the Senate."

Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., said "there's been a lot of conversation about going on offense."

"We want to make sure that they know when they come to the floor, they're gonna dread it, I hope," Harris said.

DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY

But there's another mechanism for forcing a House vote that's been used more and more often in recent years, often by their fellow Republicans.

Privileged resolutions allow lawmakers on either side to get a vote on a given bill within two days of its introduction. It generally begins with a procedural vote on whether to "table" the bill or refer it to committee to stop it before a vote on the measure itself.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., most recently invoked it to force the House to consider impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. But that was defeated when the rest of the House GOP banded together to refer the bill to committee.

The GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital, however, signaled little appetite for using it.

U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan speaks during a news conference after House Republicans elected new leadership for the upcoming session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"I think either party would be wise to build consensus around things that help actually deliver for the American people," LaLota said. "The privileged resolutions have been abused in my time here, and there's a better way to do business."

And Emmer said his main goal for the next two years would be winning back the House majority in 2028, which he insisted was a realistic goal.

He said at least 38 seats flipped by Democrats would be "ready to return to Republican hands" and could see some old faces return.

Asked whether he wanted to see some of those losing GOP incumbents run for their seats again, Emmer said, "I absolutely hope so. I've talked to several already."

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

#6060. Yikes: FAA Union Claims Nationwide Ground Stop Was Totally Avoidable

On Friday, we saw a nationwide ground stop that lasted for around four hours, making it the longest ground stop that we’ve seen in the country in over 25 years, since 9/11. This is of course a major screw-up, and it’ll likely take some time before an investigation fully reveals what the root cause of this was.

So far, the response from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has been downright pitiful, and that’s the polite way of putting it. Along those lines, the union representing workers at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is suggesting that this might’ve been completely avoidable, because unlike in the past, no risk assessment was performed prior to the mistake that caused this mess.

On Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of the shutdown. The whole thing felt to me like an SNL skit, because Duffy and Mullin couldn’t even keep their narratives straight, and the whole message was so tone deaf.

Rather than thanking the public for their patience, Duffy went on a rant demanding $50 billion from Congress, suggesting it’s their fault that they haven’t given Trump money for the past year. On Friday night, Duffy suggested the following was the reason that our skies shut down:

“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old air traffic control systems for the telecommunication issues behind the FAA nationwide ground stop on Friday."Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data," he said. "They started to give us inconsistency in the data… pic.twitter.com/5iX8mqL7RP

So he suggested that this was because of switches being overloaded due to how outdated the system is, which of course raised lots of questions about what made Friday different than any other day, in terms of the system being overloaded. Not surprisingly, he didn’t have a good answer, because he was just talking out of his you-know-what.

Very good set of questions from Luke Radel for Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. pic.twitter.com/f6tlfDtbJG

Less than 24 hours later, Duffy switched his tune, explaining the situation as follows:

In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from old copper wire and they were bringing it over to fiber. That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They are our legacy provider, they’ve been working for the FAA for over 20 years.”

“What we are working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said FAA contractor L3Harris was working at a remote location to switch telecommunication lines from cooper to fiber, which led to the longest nationwide shutdown of flights since the September 11, 2001, attacks https://t.co/6m0coVd6mo pic.twitter.com/5zdZoINAcA

So on Friday, the problem was that the switches got overloaded due to how old the system was, and Duffy used that to essentially make the press conference a $50 billion demand to modernize air traffic control (which I’m all in favor of, for the record, if done correctly, but this doesn’t seem to be the time or place for this). Then on Saturday, it was a mess up by a contractor.

Does anyone remember when press briefings during a period of crisis were about sharing facts, and not just making random stuff up, and sharing theories that suit narratives? Those were the days…

This is way beyond my area of expertise, but I’m sure I’m not alone in wondering how one contractor can make a mistake that just shuts down our entire aviation ecosystem? Shouldn’t there be a little more oversight so that such a major mistake can’t happen?”

This is where it gets interesting. PASS (“Professional Aviation Safety Specialists”) is the union representing 11,000 workers at the FAA. According to the union, historically projects like this would’ve been overseen by FAA employees with a risk assessment and more coordination, but that hasn’t been happening anymore. Here’s the statement:

The issue was isolated to two contractor owned and maintained routers that were being updated mid-day. Historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment. PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop yesterday.

PASS fully supports the administration’s efforts to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. It must be recognized by the FAA that modernization will move more quickly with fewer disruptions if PASS is fully engaged.The employees represented by the union are on the front lines and they have the skills and expertise to make the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) a reality. These employees should receive training on new equipment and could ensure more robust installation and optimization—if the workforce were properly staffed.

So a big question is when did FAA technicians stop being involved in these kinds of projects, in terms of coordination and risk assessment?

We don’t know to what extent this is related, but it of course has to be pointed out that in early 2025, Elon Musk’s DOGE (“Department of Government Efficiency”) laid off approximately 400 FAA employees. There wasn’t much transparency about who was laid off, though reports suggested that it included those tasked with aircraft safety inspections, and repairing air traffic control facilities.

One would hope that it will be investigated whether there’s any link here between the lack of oversight of projects like this, and the job cuts at the FAA.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has done an abhorrent job handling the nationwide air traffic control shutdown, in my opinion.

On Friday night, he took the time to come up with a random, convenient theory as to what happened, to suit his narrative. He demanded $50 billion from Congress (which Republicans have had control of for the past two years), and expressed no sympathy for the public that has been impacted by all of this. Then less than 24 hours later, he blamed contractors, saying they messed up some wire upgrades.

Understandably, we’re all wondering how the heck an upgrade to wiring in one place could shut down our entire air traffic system. The union representing FAA employees is suggesting that historically these projects would be overseen by FAA employees, and would also include a risk assessment, but they insist no FAA employees were involved here.

Duffy is right about one thing — there was definitely some incompetence here…

What do you make of these updates about the FAA ground stop?

This was just one of multiple major technology upgrades gone bad last week so it cuts across all of corporate America. yes, money needs to be spent to upgrade systems and conversion will be a piecemeal exercise because the system has to keep operating. The men and women that provide ATC services do an incredible job w/ what they are given - but they have an adversarial relationship w/ their employer just like every union. the real takeaway is how each airline is doing in returning to service to normal. DL and UA might get back to close to normal today. AA was already doing worse and tstorms are expected to hit N. Texas later today. WN was making progress before a bomb threat last night. B6 is their usual operational nightmare. Lower fuel prices are helping take the financial sting out of this meltdown but passengers are facing yet another operational meltdown that could have been managed better - both by the government and airlines.

Who in their right minds does a big upgrade mid-day Friday? The incompetence of this administration is beyond words.

There is definitely something rotten in Denmark. A lifetime ago I worked for a government agency. We would perform upgrades like these on Tuesday mornings at 2am, intentionally. That way if something happened the effect would be minor because traffic was low at that time. Additionally, if we had to call in extra workers Tuesday is the perfect day of the week for that. Friday afternoon is just a stupid time to do critical updates. If something goes wrong the effect is greater and try calling in extra workers on Friday afternoon. This doesn’t seem to have been coordinated properly. Besides how can one bad switch in one region cause a nationwide outage? That doesn’t make any sense.

This exposes just how dishonest Friday night's press conference was. Turns out gutting FAA oversight and letting a private vendor push an uncoordinated mid-day upgrade without a risk assessment ends badly—who knew?? The real fix isn't handing $50 billion to Duffy's cronies; it's staffing, training, and actually listening to the frontline FAA technicians who keep our skies safe.

#6059. World Of Hyatt Credit Card Review: Why It’s My Go-To Hotel Card

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is Hyatt’s co-branded Chase personal credit card. The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers strong benefits that can easily offset that, including an anniversary free night award, elite nights toward status, and more. It can even be worth spending money on the card, in order to unlock an additional free night and/or elite status.

This post is my in-depth World of Hyatt Card review. What makes Hyatt’s personal credit card so brilliant is that it’s worth having regardless of whether you want to keep it just for the ongoing perks, or whether you want to spend money on it.

Before I get into my World of Hyatt Credit Card review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:

Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the World of Hyatt Credit Card:

When we apply for credit cards, some of the most important factors are the welcome bonus, the eligibility rules for getting the card, and the annual fee. How does the World of Hyatt Credit Card do on those fronts? Let’s take a look.

At the moment, the World of Hyatt Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can earn four free night awards after spending $5,000 within the first three months. Each free night award is valid at a Category 1-4 World of Hyatt property.

World of Hyatt Category 4 properties retail for up to 25,000 points per night, so the absolute maximum value of this offer is 100,000 points. However, I of course wouldn’t value it that highly. That’s because these free night awards expire 12 months after they’re issued, and you also can’t top off these awards to redeem at more expensive properties. So actually maxing out the value of these isn’t easy.

One thing I should mention is that while I don’t love the lack of flexibility of this welcome offer, it’s significantly better than the standard bonus, which tends to be lackluster. Obviously Chase and Hyatt know that this is a card people will get for the long term value, rather than just for the bonus.

For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each.

When you pull up the World of Hyatt Credit Card application, you’ll see the following terms:

This product is available to you if you do not have this card and have not received a new cardmember bonus for this card in the past 24 months.

This is good news, as eligibility is considered independently of any other Chase credit card, and it’s also considered independently of the World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more).

It’s also worth remembering the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you sometimes won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (certain business cards are excluded). However, that no longer seems to be consistently enforced.

Fortunately nowadays Chase uses a pop-up feature during the application process, which should let you know if you’re not eligible for the bonus on a card (this appears after submitting your application), before there’s a hard pull on your credit.

There’s not a consistent rule as to what credit score you need to be approved for the World of Hyatt Credit Card. In general, I’d recommend having a credit score in the “good” to “excellent” range.

Personally, I’d hope to have a credit score of at least 700. That being said, people with scores lower than that have been approved, and conversely, people with scores higher than that have been rejected. There are lots of factors that go into approval. Chase will consider your income, your credit history, how much credit Chase has already extended you, etc.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee. You can add additional cardmembers to your account at no extra cost. This annual fee is well worth it even if you don’t spend money on the card, since you get an anniversary free night award that can be redeemed at hotels costing $250+ per night.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That’s especially true when staying with Hyatt abroad, as well as for dining and commuting outside the US.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers pretty good points earning opportunities. While this isn’t the card that I use for all of my spending, I strategically spend money on the card, and it works great for me. How good are the points earning rates? Here are the very basics, and then I’ll discuss it in more detail below:

Let me emphasize that points earning is only part of the value proposition of spending on the card. It’s also about being able to earn elite status, which I’ll cover in more detail a bit later.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 4x points for spending at Hyatt hotels and resorts, including Mr & Mrs Smith properties. That’s a solid return on hotel spending, though admittedly it doesn’t beat the return you get on the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more), which also offers 4x points on hotel purchases, and points can be moved to World of Hyatt.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 5.6% return on Hyatt spending.

Keep in mind that this is all in addition to the standard points earning at properties. World of Hyatt members ordinarily earn 5x points per dollar spent, plus elite bonuses of 10-30%. So the 4x points stacks on top of that.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points for restaurant spending globally. That’s obviously a widely useful return, though in fairness, it’s also hard to get too excited about 2x points in this category, given the number of cards that offer 3-5x points on dining spending.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on restaurant spending.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points on airline tickets purchased globally directly from airlines. While it’s nice to have this as a bonus category, again, it’s hard to get too excited about 2x points, given the number of cards that offer 3-5x points on airfare spending.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on airfare spending.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points on fitness clubs and gym memberships. For anyone wondering, this also includes group fitness businesses, like Barry’s Bootcamp, SoulCycle, etc. It’s nice to have this as a bonus category, since it’s pretty rare to see a bonus for these kinds of purchases. However, with other cards offering 2x points on everyday spending, it’s not all that exciting.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on fitness spending.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers 2x points on local transit and commuting, which includes ride share services such as Lyft and Uber.

Based on my valuation of Hyatt points, that’s like a 2.8% return on local transit and commuting spending.

The World of Hyatt Card offers 1x points per dollar spent on everyday spending. Generally speaking, there are better cards for everyday spending, though as I’ll explain below, some of the spending bonuses could make it worth shifting spending onto this card.

The area where the World of Hyatt Credit Card really excels is when it comes to the benefits it offers. In my opinion, these benefits more than justify the annual fee, regardless of whether you’re spending nothing on the card, or are spending a significant amount. Specifically, the benefits largely center around earning free nights award and elite status, so let’s cover those details.

Just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a Category 1-4 free night award on your account anniversary every year. This will be issued shortly after your anniversary and is valid for 12 months.

Categories 1-4 cover a majority of Hyatt’s properties, and those hotels can retail for up to 25,000 points per night. I’ve consistently been able to redeem these at hotels costing $250+ per night, so that (way) more than justifies the annual fee.

One downside worth flagging is that you unfortunately can’t top off these awards with additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. That’s quite the contrast to the free night awards issued by IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy.

Beyond the anniversary free night award just for being a cardmember, the World of Hyatt Card offers a second free night award if you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. This could be a major incentive to spend money on the card, as it makes $15,000 in spending quite a good sweet spot.

You receive World of Hyatt’s entry-level Discoverist status for as long as you have the World of Hyatt Card. The status will post for the primary cardmember shortly after you are approved. Perks of Discoverist status include the following:

Don’t get too excited here, but some status is better than no status! Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights or 25,000 base points (which correlates to $5,000 in spending).

The World of Hyatt Card gives you five elite qualifying nights toward status annually just for being a cardmember. You will receive these within eight weeks of being approved for the card (though usually much faster), and in subsequent years they will post within eight weeks of January 1.

This will be useful if you’re hoping to earn World of Hyatt Explorist status, World of Hyatt Globalist status, and/or World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards. For context, World of Hyatt Explorist status requires 30 elite nights, while World of Hyatt Globalist status requires 60 elite nights.

In addition to the five elite nights you get just for having the World of Hyatt Card, you earn a further two elite qualifying nights for every $5,000 you spend on the card. This means that in theory, you could spend your way all the way to Explorist or Globalist status, if you wanted to.

Reaching the $5,000 threshold has nothing to do with the calendar or cardmember year — the counter simply resets every time you spend $5,000, and then you start earning toward your next two elite nights. So if you spend $4,000 in one year and $1,000 in the next year, you’d get two elite nights in the second year.

The World of Hyatt Card offers auto rental collision damage waiver coverage. Decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card. Coverage is provided for theft and collision damage for most cars in the United States and abroad. Do note that in the US, the coverage is secondary to your personal insurance, though.

The World of Hyatt Card offers a variety of protection when traveling, including the following:

I’d consider World of Hyatt points to be among the most valuable hotel points currencies out there, though admittedly they’ve been devalued a bit over time.

The best value for redeeming World of Hyatt points is using the free night award chart. The great thing is that you earn elite nights for your stay even if you’re redeeming points or using a free night award. Below is World of Hyatt’s award chart.

There’s value to be had at all levels of the chart. As a general rule of thumb, I try to redeem at properties where I’m getting more than two cents of value per point. That’s because personally I value World of Hyatt points at ~1.4 cents each. It’s also worth being aware of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa Awards, which let you redeem points toward on-property spending.

Let me answer this very simply. If you’re eligible for the World of Hyatt Credit Card and have any interest in staying at Hyatt properties then yes, the World of Hyatt Credit Card is absolutely worth it. This is a card I personally have, and that I wholeheartedly recommend.

As I see it, the World of Hyatt Card is good for:

Meanwhile the World of Hyatt Card is probably not good for:

Personally, my approach is to put $15,000 of spending on the World of Hyatt Card every calendar year, and I think that’s a real sweet spot. By spending $15,000 on the card in a year you receive:

Even taking the value of the elite nights out of the equation, if you spend $15,000 on the card in categories on which you otherwise wouldn’t earn bonus points, you’re earning a Category 1-4 certificate that could be redeemed at a hotel potentially costing up to 25,000 points. That’s potentially like earning over two World of Hyatt points per dollar spent, which is a great return on everyday spending.

The World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more) could be a good option for any small business looking to earn Hyatt points or status. Here’s how the two cards compare:

Personally I think the personal card is generally more rewarding, though the business version of the card earns you elite nights at an accelerated rate. See my comparison of the two cards.

World of Hyatt Globalist status requires 60 elite nights per year, so how does the math work on spending your way to Globalist status with the World of Hyatt Credit Card? If you were to earn Globalist status from scratch exclusively with this credit card, you’d need to spend $140,000:

Personally I’d never spend all the way to Globalist status, but rather I’d use a hybrid approach, and would earn Globalist status partly through credit card spending and partly through actual stays. After all, if you’re not actually staying a significant number of nights, what’s the point of earning the status?

It’s also worth emphasizing that if your goal is to just spend your way toward elite status, the World of Hyatt Business Card would be the best option, since you’d earn the status after $120,000 in spending (with no head start).

Globalist status is my favorite top-tier hotel status, and it comes with all kinds of awesome perks. Many of the benefits are tied to the Milestone Rewards program, but just to give you a sense of what you could receive if you earned 60 elite nights in a calendar year:

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is an exceptional hotel credit card. It’s a card I have, and a card I spend at least $15,000 on per year.

The card is worth having even if you don’t plan on putting spending on it — you get an anniversary free night award you can use at a hotel that costs significantly more than the annual fee, you get complimentary Discoverist status, and you get five elite nights toward a higher status tier.

Beyond that, it can be worth putting spending on the card, thanks to the unique bonus categories (4x points on Hyatt stays and 2x points on fitness and gyms), as well as the additional elite nights and second free night award.

#6058. Bitter Christmas: A Bah Humbug to Moviemaking

Almodóvar’s loss of creativity and camp is cause for alarm.

Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas explores his own recent creative crisis. Using a prismatic structure, Almodóvar tells three stories that reflect one another with diminishing returns. These interwoven tales never blend due to the blockage suffered by gay male Spanish filmmaker Raul (Leonardo Sbaraglia, styled with a storm of gray-white hair to resemble Almodóvar himself). Viewers must do a meta reading about the nature and purpose of filmmaking and artistic expression.

Almodóvar makes the mistake of introducing Raul’s imaginary stories before revealing their real-life source. As Bitter Christmas becomes more and more convoluted and uninvolving, it undeniably reflects a peculiar Millennial crisis: the internalized post-Covid repression that has paralyzed many filmmakers. Once the most exciting filmmaker of the late 1980s, Almodóvar now suffers the same malaise that has also befallen comparable colleagues Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. You don’t have to be a cinephile to realize that most contemporary filmmakers are bereft of fresh ideas and genuine inspiration.

Before getting to that core Raul/Almodóvar narrative, Bitter Christmas first presents stories in which a female filmmaker Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) imagines the drama of a woman, Patrizia (Victoria Luengo), who feels her same maladies and longs to escape an unhappy marriage, and then another woman, Natalia (Milena Smit), who is deep in mourning. This narrative contraption is the worst example of a gay male’s feminine empathy that Almodóvar has ever contrived. Unlike Law of Desire and Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, this film lacks the camp buoyancy that made Almodóvar a comic hybrid of Jean Cocteau and Luis Buñuel, putting him at the vanguard of the world’s evolving sexual sophistication.

Now foregrounding his identification with female experience, Almodóvar seems to cater to political correctness rather than flout it. That a once-major pop artist can no longer make irresistible movies but instead succumbs to patronizing political trends is a cause for alarm more significant than any particular misbegotten film.

In one subplot, Raul is told, “You can lie in your life but not in your fiction,” referring to how he mistreats his partner Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) while also exploiting his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) as fodder for his newest script.

This contorted set-up suggests that Almodóvar feels pressure to join the global progressivism that a former bad boy of the Spanish underground is now obliged to endorse. That’s why the ultra-bourgeois Bitter Christmas lacks comedy and eroticism. Raul’s sex life is transferred to the shallow, quasi-porn of Elsa’s relationship with boytoy Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a firefighter and part-time stripper (probably an homage to the superior João Pedro Rodrigues satire Will-O’-the-Wisp.

Almodóvar has lost audacity. Sadness pervades the movie. Its title comes from “Amarga Navidad” (“Bitter Christmas”), a ranchera (folk torch song) performed by Chavela Vargas. But this is the least impassioned film Almodóvar has made; its emotions are distanced by artifice — in imagination, storytelling, and performance. The projection of Raul/Almodóvar’s true feelings into fakery distances real life so much that the melodrama is drab. It’s not fabulous or funny (despite ornamental design and another urgent Alberto Iglesias score), but arid like Lanzarote, the black-sand volcanic island where make-believe characters Elsa and Victoria retreat into a dull version of Ingmar Bergman’s Persona — another go at Almodóvar’s insipid The Room Next Door. None of these meta-antics result in moral summation like Fellini’s masterpieces La Dolce Vita and Otto e mezzo.

Although Almodóvar avoids obvious political pronouncement like those that ruined Killers of the Flower Moon, West Side Story, and Disclosure Day, the twisted autobiographical aspects of Bitter Christmas still indicate that he suffers a similar personal liberal panic. (Unlike Spielberg and Scorsese, Almodóvar has made foolish partisan comments on American politics.) Almodóvar can’t escape the private anxiety that Scorsese and Spielberg experience along with the rest of us. Almodóvar’s inability to disentangle primal emotional need from political confusion is evident on screen in Bitter Christmas and ultimately unsatisfying.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

I've never flown with Hawaiian Airlines, yet the Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard® is the latest addition to my wallet. With Hawaiian and Alaska Airlines sharing the same loyalty program, Atmos Rewards, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard is an attractive option for anyone who regularly flies with either airline.

This card offers common airline-associated perks, but like many cobranded airline cards, it will likely prove hard to justify if you aren't flying at least a couple of times each year with Alaska or Hawaiian. That said, if you're able to properly take advantage of its perks, it can offer a lot to boost your travels. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

The information for the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The $99-per-year Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard comes with some of the benefits you'd expect out of a mid-tier airline card, including:

You won't find lounge access or statement credits on this card, but that simplicity may be welcome for those tired of needing a spreadsheet to help them justify a card's annual fee.

Living in the Pacific Northwest, I often fly Alaska Airlines domestically. As someone who unsuccessfully tried to get the earlier this year, I'm happy that my Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard offers perks on both Hawaiian and Alaska. They may not be as comprehensive as those offered by the Summit, but this card is substantially cheaper.

Receiving two free checked bags isn't too common for a mid-tier card, so I appreciate this perk. But it's important to note that free checked bags with this card are subject to a few restrictions:

If you're traveling with a companion, you could check their bag as your own bag to navigate around this card only allowing the primary cardholder free checked bags.

I face a $45 checked bag fee for my first bag and a $55 fee for my second when flying Alaska within the continental U.S. and Alaska. Even as someone who usually only checks one bag, I just need to do so on one round-trip with Alaska to almost entirely cover this card's annual fee.

Aside from that, using the full $100 annual companion discount on a trip you’d otherwise book can offset the $99 annual fee. New cardholders also receive a one-time 50%-off companion discount. Both discounts can be used on eligible round-trip Main Cabin travel between Hawaii and North America on either airline.

I wish the Hawaiian Airlines card had priority boarding, since overhead bin space can be hard to come by and I'm not a fan of gate-checking my bag. Still, it isn't a deal-breaker for me given this card's annual fee is easy to at least break even on.

This card has no foreign transaction fees and offers standard travel protections like trip cancellation/interruption and travel accident insurance.

The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard earns Atmos Rewards points, which is the loyalty currency both Hawaiian Airlines and Alaska Airlines use. It earns:

Through Dec. 31, you'll earn 50% bonus points on every dollar spent if you're a resident of Hawaii (up to 5,000 points).

With this card, you'll also earn 1 Atmos Rewards status point per $3 spent, with no cap. You won't get an elite status boost at the start of the qualification year, but this card can help you close the gap to elite status if you're close.

The best way to use your Atmos Rewards points is for flights on Hawaiian and Alaska or with partner airlines, such as American Airlines. Alaska Airlines in particular offers a lot of value for your points, especially on short-haul domestic flights.

Recently, I redeemed 5,000 Atmos Rewards points (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees) for a flight between Portland International Airport (PDX) and Spokane International Airport (GEG). Given the cash price was $184, I received over 3.5 cents per point in value (after taking taxes and fees into consideration). That's more than double TPG's November 2026 valuation of Atmos Rewards points at 1.6 cents per point.

It's this combined loyalty program that allows me to justify holding this card despite never setting foot on a Hawaiian flight and having no current plans to do so. It's hard to earn Atmos Rewards points, since they currently only partner with Bilt as a transfer partner. Without an Alaska Airlines-associated card, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard is my best bet for earning points I can use with this program.

As an alternative to redeeming your points for flights, you can also use them for Alaska Vacations packages and Alaska Airlines-curated experiences.

As I mentioned previously, the Hawaiian Airlines card lacks priority boarding and a comprehensive elite status boost at the start of the year. In ways like this, it's clear this card hasn't received a refresh recently, unlike many other popular airline cards.

That means this card may fall short of expectations if you're anticipating a card with well-rounded airline perks. The inability to use this card's free checked bag perk with companions is a non-issue if you're only traveling with one person and two bags, but it becomes a larger limitation if you're traveling with many bags or a group.

If you fly at least a couple of times each year with Hawaiian or Alaska and don't have a cobranded Atmos Rewards card, I believe this card is more than likely worth it. Despite lacking several perks we've come to expect from airline cards these days, it's still quite easy to get outsize value from the $99 annual fee.

Currently, new Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard cardholders can earn up to 70,000 bonus points:

According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth up to $1,120. In an era when many welcome offers ask for thousands in spending, it's refreshing to see a valuable one that only requires $2,000 in total spending.

Even if you're on a limited budget, this should be an attainable welcome offer. I recommend applying now, given how much this bonus is worth and how easy it is to earn.

Just remember that Barclays can be inquiry-sensitive. If you've opened six or more cards in the past 24 months, you may have a hard time getting approved.

If this card isn't a good fit for you, consider one of these alternatives:

For additional options, check out our picks for the best airline cards.

I'm happy I chose to add the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard to my wallet. Between two free checked bags and the annual $100 companion discount, I expect I'll be able to easily get outsize value against the $99 annual fee each year.

While this card offers significant value to the right traveler, if you don't fly with either Alaska or Hawaiian at least a couple of times each year, you will likely struggle to find a lot of value in this card. If you're an Alaska Airlines loyalist and you qualify for a Bank of America card, I'd suggest the instead.

That said, if you fly at least occasionally with Hawaiian or Alaska, or you want to earn Atmos Rewards points to use with partner airlines, I recommend giving this card serious consideration.

#6056. How the Electoral College Dies

Blue-state activists are about to be perfectly positioned to execute an end run around the constitutional system.

In the wake of the 2026 midterms, we are on the cusp of a total transformation of the U.S. election system. After decades of Republican dominance in state legislatures, Democrats now control enough state governments to push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past its 270-vote activation threshold and dismantle the Electoral College from below.

But it seems like the right has barely realized the importance of the fight that’s about to begin.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

Sunday was shaping up to be another rough day at airports across the country.

Airlines were working to get operations back on track after Friday's rare nationwide ground stop. But travelers faced a third straight day of widespread flight cancellations.

By 8 a.m. EST Sunday, another 1,400 flights had been canceled, according to data from FlightAware.

1,600 additional flights had already encountered delays.

It's the continued fallout from Friday afternoon's outage at the Federal Aviation Administration, which saw most takeoffs halted across the U.S. for several hours.

The disruption left planes, crewmembers, passengers and their baggage out of place — and fueled what one major U.S. carrier has called one of the most significant disruptions it's ever seen.

Travelers stranded Friday at New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA). ADAM GRAY/GETTY IMAGES

Flight cancellations appeared to slow — some — entering Sunday, compared to the past two days.

But operations had not fully returned to normal, especially on some carriers.

As of 8 a.m. EST Sunday, per FlightAware:

"We expect disruption throughout the weekend as we work to reset the airline," American's chief customer officer Heather Garboden said in a letter to customers Saturday evening, calling the disruption "among the most significant operational impacts American has experienced."

Delta urged passengers with flexible plans to consider postponing their travel until Monday.

Carriers extended travel waivers that allowed passengers more flexibility to re-book their travel.

FAA administrator Bryan Bedford had said the disruptions were expected to begin easing by Sunday evening.

"Based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday," Bedford said at a news conference Saturday.

As of Sunday morning, fewer than 30 flights for Monday had been canceled.

The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop late Friday afternoon after discovering a communications outage affecting air traffic control.

It happened as crews were working to upgrade critical FAA equipment, apparently overloading the system amid a switch from copper wiring to fiber at one of the agency's facilities.

“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a Saturday press conference. "Our contractor didn’t meet the moment, or the equipment didn’t meet the moment and caused the outages.”

The disruption marked only the second time since 9/11 that a ground stop affecting the entire nation had been issued.

If your flight is affected by this weekend's disruptions, stay glued to your airline app — you may be able to search for a new flight and rebook yourself without waiting on hold or in line at the airport.

Don't see a good flight option for days? Keep checking back: with a lot of passengers shifting plans across the country, it's still possible seats will open up.

Passengers whose flights are canceled or significantly delayed are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel or accept a rebooked flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption.

Under U.S. Department of Transportation rules, a significant delay generally means arriving at your final destination at least three hours late on a domestic itinerary or six hours late on an international itinerary. For passengers who decide to not travel on those flights, airlines must provide refunds to the original form of payment, not just travel credits.

In large-scale travel disruptions like this, rental cars and hotel rooms at or near airports can book up quickly, so it can make sense to act fast if you want to secure a backup option.

If you have airline miles you can use to book a flight for this weekend, that can also be a good self-insurance policy in case the disruption isn't resolved quickly. Just make sure you understand the cancellation and refund rules before booking a backup ticket.

Because this disruption was due to issues outside airlines' control, carriers are unlikely to reimburse stranded passengers for hotel, ground transportation and meal costs.

Some rewards credit cards do offer built-in trip delay or cancellation protection if you used them to book your original airline tickets.

However, it's not guaranteed that those benefits will cover FAA groundings of this nature. Still, save your receipts for any unexpected expenses in case you're eligible for reimbursement.

#6054. United CEO Scott Kirby Says “100%” Chance Merger With American Airlines Would Get Approved

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says he’s “100%” convinced a merger with American Airlines could get approved. He says he’s even more confident than he was this spring, when news of the talks came out, and he sees getting American to agree as the biggest obstacle. But ‘get approved’ doesn’t mean what he seems to suggest. A friendly Justice Department signing off would still leave any such combination with state attorneys general, foreign governments and two competing sets of international airline partnerships to deal with. Speaking at Yahoo Finance Invest, Kirby said: “It wouldn’t be easy.” “We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.” His argument is that bringing United’s service, technology and operational performance to more passengers would make them better off. He thinks critics misunderstand the deal because they treat airline seats as interchangeable. Contra Kirby, better service is actually a core part of DOJ merger guidelines recognizing quality, innovation and choice. Plus, United service isn’t that good! And while their operations are better than they used to be, they aren’t industry-leading. They’re consistently modestly better than American’s but the difference is hardly vast. Kirby Hasn’t Given Up On The Airline That Fired Him When I covered Kirby’s merger pitch in April, the appeal to United was obvious: American would give them a much bigger New York presence, more strength in Los Angeles, a southeastern hub and a powerful Latin America network. Kirby later said he’d build a Miami hub if he could get 40 or 50 gates. He also wants more at New York JFK than United’s planned return will provide. American rejected merger discussions, arguing that combining the airlines would hurt consumers and competition. Any antitrust case – even at the state level – would just quote American’s own release. As I covered October 31, Kirby described conversations he thought were continuing until American blindsided him with that press release. In any case, American can make investments without being bought. They’ve already made real progress over the past 21 months towards improving their product almost across-the-board. The Justice Department Doesn’t Get The Only Vote I laid out the problems beyond Washington back in April. Getting the administration to support a deal isn’t even close to enough. States can bring their own case. A federal settlement doesn’t bind state attorneys general who aren’t parties to it. Private plaintiffs can sue, too. The Clayton Act allows injunctions against threatened antitrust harm. Closing doesn’t automatically end the risk. The merger notification statute preserves later challenges. Letting the federal waiting period expire isn’t permanent antitrust immunity. He’d Have To Untangle Two Competing Global Networks American and US Airways needed European Commission clearance for their merger. The London–Philadelphia remedy included slots for a competing daily flight. Two U.S. companies combining doesn’t make the transaction solely an American matter. United and American also have joint ventures that let them coordinate prices, schedules and revenue with different foreign airlines. Among those arrangements: Market United’s Partners American’s Partners Atlantic   Lufthansa Group and Air Canada   British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus and Finnair Japan   All Nippon Airways   Japan Airlines South Pacific   Air New Zealand   Qantas A combined airline couldn’t assume it could keep these competing arrangements unchanged. Moving American’s flying into United’s partnerships would change the competition analysis. Ending American’s existing deals would also change the connecting traffic and economics Kirby is buying. The Transportation Department’s alliance approvals are another process, separate from Justice Department merger review. And foreign oversight is already an issue: Britain. American’s existing Atlantic partnership already faces slot remedies for London–Boston, London–Chicago and London–Miami, plus protections for London–Dallas passengers. In February, the British competition authority announced approved slot agreements for Delta on Boston and Virgin Atlantic on Miami. Buying American could create new hurdles for either transatlantic joint venture the combined carrier participated in. The European Union would have its own merger review, too. Japan. United and American have separate immunized partnerships with Japan’s two major network airlines. The merger would also raise questions about their scarce Tokyo Haneda access. Japan might not approve a combined American and United in either partnership. Keeping both carriers’ Haneda slots aren’t necessarily in the DOT’s view of the public interest. Australia and New Zealand. Australia renewed the American–Qantas alliance authorization on October 14. New Zealand renewed it in March, and separately authorizes United’s cooperation with Air New Zealand. Combining the American partners in those competing relationships would give both governments new questions to consider regardless of which airline they decided they wanted to keep a partnership with. Canada. United and Air Canada announced an expanded transborder agreement last month and submitted it to Transport Canada for approval. Combining that operation with American’s Canada seems almost impossible on its own. What Would United Have To Give Up? Chicago is the biggest domestic problem. United and American operate competing hubs at O’Hare. New York, Los Angeles and Washington raise challenges as well. United has Newark while American considers the combined LaGuardia and JFK a hub; both airlines have hubs at LAX, and United has a hub at Washington Dulles while American is the dominant carrier at Washington National. And surely American’s debt is a poison pill? It ended September with $29.6 billion in debt and finance leases (without operating leases and pension obligations). The “100% approved” isn’t at all credible, unless he means only at the federal level and because he’s had assurances from the President (who could change his mind!). Ending American’s existing deals would also change the connecting traffic and economics Kirby is buying. The Transportation Department’s alliance approvals are another process, separate from Justice Department merger review. And foreign oversight is already an issue:

Japan. United and American have separate immunized partnerships with Japan’s two major network airlines. The merger would also raise questions about their scarce Tokyo Haneda access. Japan might not approve a combined American and United in either partnership. Keeping both carriers’ Haneda slots aren’t necessarily in the DOT’s view of the public interest.

Australia and New Zealand. Australia renewed the American–Qantas alliance authorization on October 14. New Zealand renewed it in March, and separately authorizes United’s cooperation with Air New Zealand. Combining the American partners in those competing relationships would give both governments new questions to consider regardless of which airline they decided they wanted to keep a partnership with.

Canada. United and Air Canada announced an expanded transborder agreement last month and submitted it to Transport Canada for approval. Combining that operation with American’s Canada seems almost impossible on its own.

Chicago is the biggest domestic problem. United and American operate competing hubs at O’Hare. New York, Los Angeles and Washington raise challenges as well. United has Newark while American considers the combined LaGuardia and JFK a hub; both airlines have hubs at LAX, and United has a hub at Washington Dulles while American is the dominant carrier at Washington National. And surely American’s debt is a poison pill? It ended September with $29.6 billion in debt and finance leases (without operating leases and pension obligations). The “100% approved” isn’t at all credible, unless he means only at the federal level and because he’s had assurances from the President (who could change his mind!). #6052. Why Airlines Schedule Flights To Take Longer Than They Used To—Even Though It Costs Them More

Former Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost says his flight to Washington’s National Airport still takes about 50 minutes, but the published schedule has grown to an hour and 42 minutes. He thinks he’s figured out why: airlines get to look more on-time by giving themselves longer to arrive. He’s right that the schedule determines whether a flight counts as on time. But airlines pay for those extra minutes, and they generally have good reasons to avoid adding more than they need. My flight to DCA takes about 50 minutes. It used to be listed as an hour & change. The *posted* flight duration keeps getting longer, now 1hr 42 min. Still takes 50 minutes. I can only conclude that these posted durations are used in determining on-time statistics. — Dave Yost (@DaveYostOH) November 12, 2026 The Schedule Includes Time On The Ground Airlines publish block time: the time scheduled from leaving the departure gate to reaching the arrival gate. That includes taxiing, waiting for a runway, flying, and getting to a gate at the other end. And National airport is a particularly odd place to dismiss congestion. In a January update, the Federal Aviation Administration explained that it had reduced the airport’s hourly arrival rate from 36 to 26 after the January 2025 collision, before increasing it to 30. The airport could handle more – if the air traffic control system hadn’t had such challenges. More demand concentrated into busy periods, limited runway and gate capacity, controller shortages and equipment problems all affect how long the trip takes. The problem also isn’t just the average. It’s how much travel time varies. An airline needs a schedule that works when there’s a normal amount of congestion, not just when the plane gets straight to the runway and encounters no delay at the other end. If that variability grows, the schedule can need more time even when the flight takes 50 minutes in the air. I made this point when covering claims about increased schedule padding in 2023. Airport and air traffic control bottlenecks make trip time less predictable. Airlines build that uncertainty into their schedules. Airlines Pay For Those Extra Minutes I’ve been pushing back on the simple ‘they’re juking the stats’ explanation since at least 2015. Making flights look longer is an expensive way to improve a scorecard. Crew costs. Scheduled time can determine pay even when a flight arrives early. American Airlines flight attendants, for instance, receive flight time pay based on the greater of scheduled or actual block time for each flight. Less productive airplanes. Add time across the day’s flying and there’s less room for another revenue flight. The airline can wind up needing more airplanes and crews to operate the same service. Less attractive itineraries. Longer trips can lose bookings to faster connections, competing airlines, or driving. Airlines want to sell you a convenient schedule. Back in 2015, I cited Southwest Airlines’ estimate that adding just a couple of minutes of block time across its schedule would cost the equivalent of 8 to 10 airplanes’ daily flying. You can’t just push flights later in the day, because airlines need to schedule flights when people want to fly. And airlines help create some of their own congestion through banked schedules at hubs. Packing flights into connecting waves makes more itineraries possible, but it also puts more demand on gates, runways and employees at the same time. Longer Schedules Can Improve More Than The Statistics The government counts an arrival as on time when the plane reaches the gate less than 15 minutes after its scheduled arrival. But if an airline keeps missing its arrival times by small margins, increasing block time can be a sensible first step toward fixing reliability. It’s acknowledging how long operating the flight actually takes, including the delays that occur often enough to plan for. American announced longer block times alongside a redesign of their Dallas operation, moving from 9 large connecting waves to 13 smaller ones in April. I explained why that investment could pay for itself through fewer missed connections, delayed bags and disrupted aircraft and crews. In April, American’s Dallas hub chief reported that missed connections were down 50%. At United Airlines’ 2019 media day, an executive explained that 25% of their flights were expected to arrive 10 minutes early. That gave them room to hold some departures for connecting passengers and still arrive on time through their ConnectionSaver program. United had started improving its reliability with longer block times. Arriving Early Can Create A Gate Problem Of course, extra time in the schedule doesn’t create extra gates. Get in early and the gate assigned to your flight may still have another airplane on it. An empty gate may belong to another airline, be unsuitable for your aircraft, or lack the employees needed to bring you in and operate the jetbridge. I covered Doug Parker explaining this problem in 2018: American used essentially all its hub gate capacity at peak times, and a few airplanes failing to leave could leave arriving flights with nowhere to go. So you can land early, sit waiting, and reach the terminal around the originally scheduled time. The government’s arrival clock keeps running until gate arrival. Regardless, it’s not all a conspiracy to juke the stats. Often it’s just a realistic expectation for how long the airline thinks on average it’ll take to travel, though sometimes they beat those expectations. The real solution isn’t just tightening schedules, it’s improving throughput – more capacity in air travel control and at airports. #6051. Combat Took on America’s Socialism Fever

The National Review newsletter captured a time in which revolutionary violence tried to join the mainstream.

Young men raise their fists and chant slogans during the “Days of Rage” demonstrations organized by the Weatherman to protest the Chicago Seven trial and “to bring the war home” in Chicago, Ill., in 1969.

Socialism looks in 2026 a lot like bell bottoms: tried on, worn out, and out of fashion.

Decades ago, Germany, Russia, Cambodia, Ethiopia, and points beyond tried socialism to disastrous results. Many American leftists, as judged by the election returns, believe in an American exceptionalism of sorts, too. They think that socialism in the United States will be different. We won’t need a world war, societal collapse, or the obligatory charitable single and accompanying global benefit show to save us from its consequences. Socialism, for its true believers, amounts to salvation and not that from which people living under it require deliverance.

Daniel J. Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S. Meyer, is an American Spectator senior editor, visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution, and YouTuber @RightWingWilderness.

#6050. GOP newcomer who toppled Cory Mills sets sights on fraud, inflation as he heads to Capitol Hill

Reps. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio; Max Miller, R-Ohio; and Joe Wilson, R-S.C., reflect on GOP losses in the midterm elections and the Democratic flip in Ohio and South Carolina. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

EXCLUSIVE: Florida Republican Congressman-elect Ryan Elijah told Fox News Digital he is heading to Washington with an "appetite" to crack down on fraud and protect consumers and tackle inflation, while calling for bipartisan cooperation in the incoming Congress.

Elijah, a former Central Florida sports broadcaster, made his remarks amid heightened scrutiny of fraud involving taxpayer-funded federal programs across the country.

"I'm going to lean into consumer protection — that's something I fought for my whole life — and lean into fraud," Elijah told Fox News Digital.

"There is so much more Washington could do against fraud. I hope there is a bipartisan appetite on both sides to not only protect consumers but also target some of this fraud that is wasting so much of our tax dollars."

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

Former local TV news anchor Ryan Elijah unseated Rep. Cory Mills in a high-stakes Florida GOP primary race. (Mike McClain/Ryan Elijah for Congress)

The incoming Republican, who beat embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., in the Republican primary in August, expressed optimism that lawmakers from both parties could find common ground on addressing fraud and rising costs, arguing that voters sent a clear message during Tuesday's midterm elections.

Elijah said voters "made it loud and clear to both parties" that they "want change, they want inflation to come down and they want life to become a little easier. So, I think both parties need to look at that."

Elijah also emphasized that members of Congress represent "100% of the people in their district, not just 50%," arguing that bipartisan solutions are necessary to restore public trust and accountability in Washington.

Beyond fighting fraud, Elijah pledged to restore a spirit of public service to Congress, criticizing lawmakers who use their positions to enrich themselves.

"What you do see is the people that enhance themselves, and people don't want to see that. None of that should be taking place," Elijah said while discussing congressional insider trading.

A view of the east side of the U.S. Capitol Building Aug. 25, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Members of Congress should not sit on a committee and be able to trade stocks, and that is something that I would support if it moves forward in the next Congress," he continued. "We all have to be on the same playing field, the person back home and the person on Capitol Hill."

Elijah outlined his preferred committee assignments, telling Fox News Digital he would like to serve on the House Energy and Commerce Committee or the House Financial Services Committee, where he could focus on consumer protection and financial oversight.

He also expressed interest in serving on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, describing it as "a great way to bring projects back to my district."

Elijah said his district has "so much growth ahead of us," arguing that a seat on the committee could help address its infrastructure needs.

The incoming lawmaker addressed the challenges Republicans face after losing control of Congress in the midterm elections, urging his party to remain united.

Republican House candidate Ryan Elijah, left, attends a UFL event. (Ryan Elijah campaign)

Elijah said Republicans must "hold the line" on the "progress we've made so far" while working to advance their priorities in a divided Washington.

Elijah is expected to be sworn into the 120th Congress in January.

Get the latest updates on the Trump administration and Congress, exclusive interviews and more Fox News politics content.

#6049. American Airlines Reverses Its Original New York Strategy—Wants Local Customers Back In Major Cities

American Airlines says focusing on local customers has produced “material margin improvement” at LaGuardia. They’re doing better in New York by focusing on the needs of New Yorkers. Meanwhile, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said at at Thursday’s Skift Aviation Forum that he sees Chicago’s biggest opportunity in winning corporate traffic, and he’s working on Los Angeles schedules that better serve the people who live there too. That’s a full rejection of the New York strategy American laid out in 2014, immediately after the US Airways merger. They wanted to bring passengers to New York, rather than offer a schedule for New Yorkers. That was dumb. They thought they couldn’t compete in New York, and they walked away from the credit card spending of New Yorkers. American Chose Not To Be The Airline For New Yorkers The original post-merger strategy was building schedules around people coming to New York for business and then going home. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening works for an out of town visitor. A New Yorker making a day trip wants the reverse. American dropped LaGuardia service to Cleveland, Minneapolis and Atlanta while adding cities like Roanoke and Wilmington, North Carolina. They were using scarce New York slots to strengthen their appeal to customers they believed were underserved elsewhere in the country, instead of building a schedule to take people who lived in New York to the places they needed to go. It was an extension of the old US Airways playbook of avoiding direct competition. By 2018, Robert Isom was pitching a boutique business airline for New York, built around London, premium transcons and a limited collection of other routes. That was already a change from the original inbound strategy. It still missed that the person buying a business class ticket to London also takes their family on vacation. And by not providing either a better product or a more well-rounded schedule, they were setting themselves up to be a ‘spill carrier’ taking business only when offering a lower price that competitors wouldn’t meet. The JetBlue partnership demonstrated what a broader network could do. In October 2021, I reported American’s fastest growing markets for AAdvantage signups were its JetBlue and Alaska partnership cities. Doug Parker Explained The Credit Card Math Problem In March, I wrote about former American CEO Doug Parker’s explanation of how airlines allocate credit card revenue to routes. He described assigning the money to flights where customers redeem their miles. That accounts for the seats being used. It doesn’t tell you which flights caused the customer to get the card and put spending on it in the first place. A New Yorker might use their miles for Hawaii. But they chose American because it worked for their trips to Chicago, London and Miami. If American stops being useful for those trips, the customer may switch airlines and cards. Crediting the Hawaii flight doesn’t capture what the New York schedule was doing for the business. That was my criticism of American’s retreat seven and eight years ago: cutting a flight can improve its route accounting while making the company worse off by losing the customer’s other business. You can’t count the card revenue twice, but you need to count what disappears when the customer leaves. Chicago And Los Angeles Need The Same Rethink This is also why the O’Hare fight matters beyond departure counts and Scott Kirby’s desire to beat American. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months. As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects. Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier: I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30. American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation. American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens. So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will! The Alaska Partnership Fits This, Too American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results.
