As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects.

Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier:

I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world

In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30.

American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation.

American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens.

So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will!

American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business.

But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card.

American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks.

That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results.

I’m not surprised to hear AA talking about wanting to be more competitive in New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles. They’ve been running a promo, seemingly targeted at travelers who have flown American for business, offering bonus miles for segments to/from/through NYC/ORD/LAX.

AA is finally starting to learn the lesson that George Costanza learned. Every instinct that they have had for the past 10 years has been wrong. So, just do the opposite.

You really do have to wonder how much longer Devon May can survive. He’s been on the wrong side of every product decision at AA and been the key voice against product improvement.

But it’s also a very AA phenomenon — keeping bad leaders who have never shown a shred of strategic thinking.

Speaking from the position of a +40 year ~4 million-mile Platinum Pro A/Advantage customer, when American began abandoning New York for both transcontinental and international flights, I began abandoning American and it will take a lot to bring me and many other top tier former loyal NYC area customers back. Unfortunately, the airline has been mismanaged and mistreated loyal customers since Bob Crandell left in 1998 and both shareholders and loyal customers have suffered. It’s time for a major overall of both senior management and the Board and a new attitude/approach from American’s current poor customer service team.

Day by day Nat and Heather are fixing the Vasu, Parker and Isom effups.

They can reshuffle the existing fleet to serve both segments…early morning locals departing the hub and early morning visitors to the hub.

This is good to see and it is reflected in the schedules (for example, JFK-ORD is now 4 x daily) and the resumption of JFK-SEA with 2 x daily (which will be complemented by the AS flying). AA has some holes to fill in its NY portfolio. It should fly from JFK to SAT for example, and continue to pick up markets that B6 is walking away from. Eventually, American will have the majority of the B6 portfolio to themselves and that will unlock their ability to be a competitive force in the NYC market. AA must still continue to refine and improve its offering and maintain and grow the pivot to premium. The money is in the NYC, Chicago, and LA markets, not in the sunbelt.

@Gary–This article is an excellent analysis. I agree that flight times are important to local passengers. When I visit NYC or Chicago, I like to depart such that I arrive in the mid to late afternoon. That allows me to check into a hotel upon arrival and have the evening to get a good meal, go to a show, erc. I like to come home on a late afternoon flight ti maximize my time on the trip. (That kind of scheduling appeals to leisure travelers as well as business travelers.). If I lived in NY or Chicago, I would like similar schedules if flying west.

@Joe–I agree that whenever possible, an airline should try to schedule in a way that works for both ends of the city pair.

@Peter – exactly right! Best post of the day.

I would add AA needs to add back a few non stop flights from NY and BOS to South Florida and Orlando. This is the key to winning the NY/ BOS domestic market.

Seems like Parker and Kerr (the US Airways CFO who served at AA until 2023, promoting May) were the ones who are most responsible for where we are now – finance ran the show. Vasu, and even Isom inherited a lot of the implications of their thinking.

And let’s not forget Kirby before he learned new ways at United – decisions in the early 2010s set up the fleet and network we have today

Southwest has a miniscule presence in New York. Delta has a miniscule presence in Chicago. Yet both are much more profitable than American. How can that be?

@DesertGhost – Delta has #1 at JFK/LGA and #1 at LAX. They themselves say the reason for AUS expansion is card revenue. Southwest is huge in California. Huge in Florida. And has lower costs. And their profits aren’t that much higher than American’s.

AA should also try to add SAN, maybe CPH and ZRH from JFK. Also should build more of a focus city at Boston Logan. There is card revenue there!

Is it possible AA could get from ~11% of JFK market share to 15-20%?

this is precisely why Scott Kirby is paranoid.

AA is coming back and UA can no longer count on revenue that AA has been bleeding for years.

DL’s focus on “stealing from” AA was largely pre-covid and at LAX during covid. DL is comfortable w/ its domestic size now and is not focused on market share and is reaping the profits accordingly even while continuing to take share from B6 in the NE.

AA is the largest domestic airline because of their size in a whole lot of small and medium sized cities.

AA steal carries a lot of low fare traffic it should not be carrying but it cannot get rid of it until it replaces it with higher quality revenue in coastal cities.

Gary – you did the math wrong on LAX gates. American has five “permanent” priority use gates at TBIT and five temporary gates due to T5 construction. When construction ends it will still have those five gates. That’s where the 30 comes from. But what AA ultimately wants is 35.

The situation with the five TBIT gates it permanently holds is that it has priority first use of four of them, and the fifth is triggered by minimum usage of the first four. It also does need to share these with BA, QF and JAL.

Two words describe why this 3M miler Southern Californian no longer flies AA out of LAX,for work or vacation. “Eagles Nest”.

The place is a dump, the crowded buses are insufferable, and T4 is a construction nightmare. UA was smart dumping that remote terminal many years ago.

How the hell does Isom still have a job? How the hell does Dougie sleep at night?

#6048. The Republican Party Must Be Bigger Than Any One Person

The GOP’s future depends on putting principles first.

President Ronald Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas

In 1967, Ronald Reagan offered a reminder about the Republican Party that is as relevant today as it was nearly 60 years ago: “Unity does not require unanimity of thought.” Reagan understood something fundamental about political leadership: A party is not a personality cult. It is a coalition of Americans united by shared principles, even when they disagree about policy specifics.

In the aftermath of the midterm elections, Republicans have serious questions to confront. The results demand reflection and an examination of what we believe and what kind of political institution we intend to be. I believe in the Constitution, limited government, individual liberty, fiscal responsibility, and personal accountability. Those convictions have not changed because of political pressure, nor are they dependent on who occupies the White House.

President Ronald Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas

Brad Raffensperger is the secretary of state for Georgia.

#6047. United Raises Credit Card Bonuses To 100,000 Miles—Cardholders Earn More On Flights And Pay Less For Awards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

United and Chase have raised initial bonuses on all four personal credit cards, with offers now reaching 100,000 miles. That’s worth considering because United has made its credit card much harder to skip: eligible primary cardholders earn more miles for flying, then pay fewer miles to book United awards. Even elite status doesn’t eliminate the disadvantage of going without one.

I’ve written about United cutting mileage-earning for customers without a card while giving cardholders more. If you’re active with the airline and MileagePlus, you need to look at the cost of a card against the miles you’re giving up without it. And with the annual fee cards, you don’t have to put all your spending on one to get the better flight earning and award pricing.

Here’s the current lineup. Each offer has a spending component plus another 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user (an employee card on the business products) within three months of account opening. Card    Initial Bonus    Purchases In First 3 Months    Annual Fee United GatewaySM Card (See rates and fees) 40,000 after $1,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user50,000 total $1,000 $0 UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) 70,000 after $3,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user80,000 total $3,000 $0 first year, then $150 United QuestSM Card (See rates and fees) 80,000 after $4,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user90,000 total $4,000 $350 United ClubSM Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $695 UnitedSM Business Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $150 There are also elite status incentives: Quest: 500 Premier qualifying points after your first purchase. Business: 2,000 Premier qualifying points after the same $5,000 in purchases within three months that earns the mileage bonus. The extra 10,000 miles for adding a user are awarded once per account, and that user must remain on the account when the bonus is fulfilled. What You’re Giving Up Without A Qualifying Card For United tickets purchased on or after April 2, 2026, here’s what the airline awards for flying. The cardholder column applies to the primary holder of an eligible annual fee card. The United GatewaySM Card requires spending to qualify. MileagePlus Status    Without A Qualifying Card    With A Qualifying Card General member 3 miles per dollar 6 miles per dollar Premier Silver 5 miles per dollar 8 miles per dollar Premier Gold 6 miles per dollar 9 miles per dollar Premier Platinum 7 miles per dollar 10 miles per dollar Premier 1K 9 miles per dollar 12 miles per dollar These rates apply to base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges and exclude taxes. Basic Economy and other base-option fares have different earning rules. This is mileage earned from flying, separate from whatever the card you use to buy the tickets earns. A general member earns twice as many flight miles with a qualifying card. A 1K doesn’t double their earning, but still picks up three more miles per eligible dollar. Spend $5,000 on eligible fares and that’s 15,000 additional miles at either status level. Then there’s the redemption side. United gives eligible primary cardholders: At least 10% off United and United Express award prices without Premier status. At least 15% off with Premier status. Access to additional Polaris business class Saver award inventory. More seats at the lower price can matter more than the percentage discount. At the minimum discounts, an award with a base price of 100,000 miles becomes 90,000 miles for a cardholder without status, or 85,000 for a cardholder with status. The discounts don’t cover partner-operated flights, Money + Miles bookings, or taxes and fees. You need to book through the primary cardholder’s MileagePlus account. Adding someone as an authorized user doesn’t give their MileagePlus account these benefits. The award pricing benefit can take up to five weeks after card issuance to become available. The No Annual Fee Card Has A $10,000 Spend Requirement To Unlock Benefits United GatewaySM Card‘s offer is 50,000 miles with just $1,000 in purchases and an added authorized user. That’s a record bonus and a low spending requirement. Chase is right to call it the card’s best offer ever. However, Gateway requires $10,000 in purchases in a calendar year to unlock the higher flight earning and cardmember award pricing. Once earned, the award pricing benefit lasts for the rest of that calendar year and the following one. I actually think that UnitedSM Explorer Card (which has a $0 annual fee the first year) and the UnitedSM Business Card are both better options. Which Offer Makes The Most Sense? UnitedSM Explorer Card is the base personal card. You get up to 80,000 miles and the better MileagePlus earning and award prices without a first year annual fee. It also comes with Group 2 boarding, two United Club one-time passes each year, and a free first checked bag for the primary cardholder and one companion on the same reservation. The bag benefit generally requires buying the tickets with the card. Club passes are subject to admission restrictions and capacity. The UnitedSM Business Card is especially attractive if you qualify. It matches the 100,000-mile maximum on the Club cards, adds 2,000 qualifying points, and costs $150 a year. It offers a $125 United travel credit after five United flight purchases of at least $100 each in a calendar year. And you get 5,000 anniversary miles when you also hold a personal Chase United card. United QuestSM Card has strong benefits if you’ll use them. The $350 annual fee buys $200 in United TravelBank cash after opening and at each anniversary, plus a 10,000-mile award flight discount starting at the first anniversary. It also provides 1,000 qualifying points annually starting the calendar year after opening. If the $200 credit replaces airfare you’d otherwise buy, you’re left evaluating $150 of the fee against the remaining benefits and that’s the annual fee of Explorer. The United ClubSM Card is for people who will use the lounges. It has a $695 annual fee and includes United Club membership. #6046. Iran Is Still a Menace

A member of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at a military training center for citizens in Tehran, Iran, November 2, 2026.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters

The American public may not be interested in the Iran war, but it is still interested in us.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his home to a military base after credible Iranian threats against his life. Bessent helps oversee the crippling financial sanctions imposed on Iran, making him a particular target for the regime.

In the past several years, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Adviser John Bolton, and President Trump himself have also been the targets of Iranian assassination plots.

With the Iran war playing a prominent role in the GOP’s stunning defeat in last week’s elections, there is renewed pressure — both from incoming Democrats and critics on the right — to put an end to the conflict.

On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that JD Vance had become lead negotiator with Iran, to the point of even contemplating direct talks with a top Iranian security official. The same article related that Trump had started to second-guess the wisdom of the June memorandum of understanding that Vance negotiated and that Trump gladly signed, wondering whether it allowed time for Iran to regroup and earn more oil revenue.

On Thursday morning, Trump, who has been vacillating between threatening to bomb Iran and touting imminent peace almost by the day, poured cold water on the idea of any renewed negotiations. The president took to Truth Social to say that he was asking Vance to focus on corruption in Democrat-run cities. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Bombast aside, a status quo in which the U.S. maintains a naval blockade against Iran and escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz may be the least bad of the remaining options. While maintaining that pressure, the U.S. should also look for ways to actively support the Iranian opposition, something President Trump implicitly promised in January with his “help is on its way” comments. But we obviously cannot bank on the Iranian regime falling or moderating any time soon. It is hard to see what can be accomplished strategically through another weeks-long air campaign, but the immediate diplomatic prospects are dim, as well.

Presumably, any deal that Iran would agree to in the aftermath of what it considers its victory in the midterms would be a bad one for the U.S., likely a repeat of Barack Obama’s disastrous Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, if not worse. Under that agreement, Iran enjoyed hundreds of billions of dollars in sanctions relief, preserved its ability to enrich uranium, and maintained its ballistic missile program. The scandal of the Iran deal was that even if it worked exactly as intended, it would have still allowed Iran to continue to develop a more powerful conventional military, to sponsor terrorism, and to exert a malign influence within the region and around the world. All the while, restrictions on its nuclear program were set to expire over time, putting the regime on a long-term glide path to weaponization. If any eventual agreements are to be reached with Iran, they must meet two tests: First, do no harm, and second, trade nothing for any promises of future conduct by the Iranians.

Iran’s plots against one of the most important U.S. cabinet officials, as well as Americans throughout the Middle East, underline the malignity of an Iranian regime that has been in a conflict with the United States for a half century. In short, it is still very interested in the war, and in doing us harm.

#6045. Southwest Pilot Calls Out Nationwide Flight Shutdown As A Government Control Plot

A pilot, reportedly with Southwest Airlines, says he flew from Cancún to Phoenix without any communications problems. He’s concluded that Friday’s nationwide flight shutdown was a government operation to control people. He calls the whole thing “a big farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam. The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh. Standing in a parking garage in uniform, he lists the facilities he spoke with and says they all worked fine. Then he offers his theory: So whatever’s going on, I think it’s designed to create fear and disruption and chaos, because that’s how the government gets control of things, controls people. Watch the pilot’s video He never explains how this advances the government’s goal, what additional control it gains, or why it wants that control. Which power are stranded passengers supposed to surrender? The government already decides whether planes can take off. Keeping people at the airport for hours accomplishes what, exactly? And how does costing airlines hundreds of millions of dollars in a day advance its goals? He says “I don’t know what’s going on,” but instead of then keeping quiet he decides to tell the world it’s a government operation. His fight went fine, but that doesn’t mean everything was actually fine. Some communications worked, others didn’t. Radar information could become unreliable even while a pilot could hear a controller. A pilot hears the frequencies he’s assigned at the times he’s using them. That doesn’t say much. The decision to let aircraft already airborne continue while stopping departures isn’t a contradiction. Limiting the number of flights controllers had to work given the conditions they faced made sense. Every landing reduced the workload. Every new departure would have added another aircraft needing instructions, separation and handoffs between controllers. Remaining capacity could be reserved for aircraft already flying. Working frequencies and contingency procedures could help bring those flights in without supporting a normal stream of new departures. The FAA’s ground stop rules cover facilities that are only partially unable to provide service. You don’t wait until every radio goes silent before reducing traffic. In fact, depending on when he flew, the ground stop may have helped make his trip uneventful. Fewer planes competing for the remaining capacity would make his experience easier. He may be pointing to the benefit of the restriction as evidence it wasn’t needed in the first place. Friday’s nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and was lifted around 8:15 p.m. It lasted over four hours. By early Saturday morning, there were more than 12,500 cancellations across Friday and Saturday. He said the newer internet protocol switches hadn’t experienced these problems. The L3Harris-operated FAA telecommunications network carries voice and surveillance information between facilities. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. Standing beside him at the briefing, Mullin said the apparent problem involved Duffy and the FAA installing patches, equipment and technology that overwhelmed the older system. The new tech was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy’s defense was that the new equipment hadn’t failed. Watch Markwayne Mullin explain the apparent cause beside Sean Duffy When I reviewed the administration’s modernization plan, I warned that compressing decades of hardware replacements, software integrations and transitions into 36 months brought risks of service disruption. He wants more taxpayer money rather than user fees to prop up an agency that’s failed to modernize with the billions given to it before, without explaining why only money – and not fixing project management, budgeting and leadership at the agency – is all that’s needed. According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, legacy telecommunications switches and routers became overloaded, producing inconsistent radar information and communications at en route centers and airport approach facilities. He said the newer internet protocol switches hadn’t experienced these problems.

The L3Harris-operated FAA telecommunications network carries voice and surveillance information between facilities. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. Standing beside him at the briefing, Mullin said the apparent problem involved Duffy and the FAA installing patches, equipment and technology that overwhelmed the older system. The new tech was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy’s defense was that the new equipment hadn’t failed.

Watch Markwayne Mullin explain the apparent cause beside Sean Duffy

When I reviewed the administration’s modernization plan, I warned that compressing decades of hardware replacements, software integrations and transitions into 36 months brought risks of service disruption.

Duffy used the briefing to press Congress for $50 billion. He wants more taxpayer money rather than user fees to prop up an agency that’s failed to modernize with the billions given to it before, without explaining why only money – and not fixing project management, budgeting and leadership at the agency – is all that’s needed.

There is an element of truth. Project 2025 has a section that discusses dismantling the FAA and privatizing the system. And in general, yes, fascist regimes do sow chaos and distrust in existing systems as a form of control over the population.

Back in 1984 Charles Perrow wrote a book called, “Normal Accidents”. His contention is that as systems get more complicated thy are more likely to have points where failures magnify through the tightly coupling of various parts. Eventually these can cascade into a catastrophic collapse of the entire system. These situations may be reduced, and to some extent mitigated with good designs and training, but by the very nature of complexity will still occur in totally unexpected ways. In fact, building in redundancies can sometimes be counter-productive as it makes systems even more complicated and prone to failure.

We may have reached this point in air traffic control, made worse by old equipment and a sluggish bureaucracy that reacts rather than is proactive in avoiding accidents. You don’t need a vast plot (though I admit that I wondered if this was the start of a coup) to have a total system failure. One thing does seem likely, and that is more such events will occur, and without intelligent action they will be more frequent.

#6044. Saudi Hotel Builders Keep Going as Attacks Scare Off Foreign Visitors

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Caption: A render of Four Seasons Resort and Residences Amaala at Triple Bay

Saudi hotel developers are still building through Houthi attacks, and a record pipeline shows it. But their bet rests on domestic and religious travel. The international guests that Vision 2030 needs are the ones the attacks are scaring off.

A month after a Houthi missile killed 13 people at Riyadh’s main airport, Saudi Arabia’s hotel pipeline is at a record. Developers and operators say they know of no projects canceled because of the attacks. What the attacks have damaged is harder to rebuild: the kingdom’s image as a safe place to visit.

The attacks have closed airports, canceled the kingdom’s biggest events and pushed up the cost of insuring against conflict. Investors are still signing deals, betting that domestic and religious travel will carry the market until the fighting stops. How long that takes is an open question.

Saudi Arabia’s hotel pipeline has kept growing. The kingdom has a record 401 projects in development, up 15% from a year ago, according to Lodging Econometrics. Those projects will collectively add 109,320 rooms, a 16% increase. That is 52% of the Middle East’s total project count, and 58% of its rooms.

A month after a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people, Saudi Arabia's hotel pipeline is at a record 401 projects and 109,320 rooms, up 15% and 16% respectively from a year ago, according to Lodging Econometrics. Developers and operators told Skift they know of no projects canceled because of the attacks, though IHG CEO Elie Maalouf said some would probably be delayed. The damage is showing up elsewhere: 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between October 8 and late October, according to Cirium data; the Saudi Grand Prix, the Future Investment Initiative, and the Red Sea International Film Festival were scrapped, postponed, or moved; and the U.S. Embassy now requires government employees to get special authorization to use any Saudi airport. This year's openings are concentrated on the Red Sea coast — Four Seasons, Rosewood, Six Senses, Equinox, Nammos, and Raffles — the properties most dependent on the international guests the attacks are deterring. Investors are leaning on a domestic base that accounted for 93.3 million tourists in 2025, or 76.1% of the total, plus religious travel for Hajj and Umrah. Growth had already stalled before October, with 61.2 million tourists in the first half of 2026, up about 1% year over year, against a Vision 2030 target of 150 million a year.

#6043. The Week: Jensen Huang, Honeytrapped

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks with the media ahead of a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., December 3, 2025.

• China has gained an edge in one of the world’s most dangerous technologies: the honeypot.

• Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of the tech giant Nvidia, as news of extramarital affairs with multiple subordinates and a spy scandal engulfed the company. The “other woman” in the honeytrap has been identified in numerous reports as a Chinese national and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company in the business of renting out computing power that relies on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities). U.S. intelligence has accused Megaspeed of smuggling contraband chips to China and identified the Nvidia CEO’s paramour as a Chinese spy, information that was passed on to senior officials in Washington. The FBI and Congress are taking a closer look. Nvidia’s advanced chips are absolutely critical for cutting-edge AI models, so handling this scandal will be complicated. We are ahead of China in the AI “arms race” to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

#6042. The Hotel Restaurant Is Becoming the Main Event Again

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: The Baldi Bar in the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills.  Jakob Layman

Hotel restaurants are becoming destinations again. The smartest owners are giving chefs and operators the freedom to create places with their own character and following, rather than trying to serve every guest at every hour.

When César Ritz and Auguste Escoffier took over the Savoy hotel in London around 1890, they made its dining room the place to be seen. High-society women rarely ate in public then, but Ritz set out to make it irresistible. He fussed over lampshades until the light turned a flattering apricot, hired an orchestra for weekend nights, and insisted on evening dress.

On the food front, Escoffier supplied the reasons to come back, creating Peach Melba for Nellie Melba and getting frogs' legs past the Prince of Wales by calling them nymphs' thighs.

New money soon rubbed elbows with dukes, actors and the occasional prince. For eight years, the dining room was the reason the hotel stood out. Success went to their heads. The Savoy fired them in 1898 over missing wine and supplier kickbacks, with its owner, Richard D'Oyly Carte, complaining that they had "forgot they were servants."

Three months later they opened the Hôtel Ritz in Paris, and the man's name

Hotel restaurants are being rebuilt as destinations with their own identity rather than all-purpose outlets serving every guest need. The article traces the idea to César Ritz and Auguste Escoffier at the Savoy in the 1890s, when the dining room was the reason the hotel stood out, and argues that hotel kitchens later became Swiss Army knife utilities covering early breakfast, business lunch, late dinner, and midnight room service — a menu written to offend nobody. The current shift separates the headline restaurant from daily guest feeding: Baldi at the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills serves neither breakfast nor lunch, NUNA at the Four Seasons Miami focuses on dinner while Edge handles breakfast and lunch, and Kwame Onwuachi's Dōgon at the Salamander in Washington operates five evenings a week. Owners are also choosing operators with existing local followings over celebrity-chef prestige alone — the Waldorf replaced Jean-Georges's first West Coast restaurant with a local restaurant dynasty. The payoff, per the article, is social gravity: repeat local visits, cultural relevance, and business value that has little to do with occupancy upstairs. The cost is giving restaurateurs freedom to operate on their own terms.

#6041. Airlines Are Giving Passengers ‘Hoe Bags’—But You May Be Owed More When Your Luggage Goes Missing

A Southwest Airlines passenger says her luggage went missing on a flight to Detroit, and the airline handed her what she calls a “hoe bag”: a plastic bag containing a toothbrush, razor, mouthwash and deodorant. “This is a care package for hoes.” Comedian Delo Brown, who posts as @keepitonthedelo, says Southwest lost her luggage “last week.” She expected a voucher or some sort of credit. Instead, she got toiletries to use while they looked for her belongings. “Take this hoe bag and be happy.” Watch Delo Brown’s Southwest Airlines toiletry kit unboxing. Then she starts pulling out the contents. There’s a brush, facial pads and cotton swabs, a toothbrush, a razor, wipes, mouthwash and a tiny deodorant. The razor gets a particularly enthusiastic explanation of what it might be used for. By the end, she’s sold: “This is the best hoe bag I have ever received in my life. This is a caring hoe bag. This is a care package for hoes. I love this. Thank you, Southwest, for my hoe bag.” A “hoe bag” means a bag with the overnight essentials you’d bring when you might wind up spending the night at somebody else’s place. Toothbrush, deodorant, something to clean up with, perhaps fresh underwear. A couple of the better comments: “I used to leave those in the top drawer of nightstand on the other side of my bed.” “Got your hoe bag but still missing a WHOLE BAG.” Other commenters think the plain plastic bag and generic toiletries look more like a hospital admission kit or something handed out in jail. Several compare it to the $148 Skims advent calendar that drew complaints over its inexpensive accessories. These are meant to get you through a night without your checked bag, whether your luggage didn’t arrive or a disrupted trip leaves it somewhere you can’t get to. You’d get the at the baggage service office. And you’ll find them at other airlines, too. In a 2009 comparison of airline overnight kits, Wired actually picked Southwest as best overall. Its kit came in a reusable bag with pockets and a hanging hook, and included Speed Stick, Colgate, Scope, Pert Plus and TRESemmé. That was a much more elaborate kit than the plastic bag in this video. Passengers still need their bags back. Expenses in the meantime may be covered by the credit card they used to purchase the ticket, and airlines have to reimburse reasonable, documented expenses caused by delayed baggage. That can include necessary toiletries and replacement clothing. Hotels can help, too. Ask the front desk before buying a toothbrush, toothpaste, razor, shaving cream or comb. Many have complimentary basics, while deodorant, mouthwash, makeup wipes and other items depend on the property. A hotel’s lobby shop often isn’t the only option. I wrote about “Hyatt Has It” when it launched in 2013. What I liked was that Hyatt would actually tell guests what was available and invite them to ask. At participating full service hotels, they’d deliver the items, knock and leave the bag on the doorknob. Hyatt still advertises the program, including requests through the World of Hyatt app. Holiday Inn’s “Forget Something?” service can offer complimentary toothbrushes, toothpaste, shaving cream, razors and combs. Of course, some hotels would rather sell you the basics. I covered a stranded Marriott Ambassador member who said the Detroit Metro Airport Marriott wanted $12 for deodorant and another $12 for mouthwash. Their shuttle would take him anywhere within a mile, but the drugstore was 1.1 miles away. He moved to a Hyatt Place and got the toiletries for free. Comedian Delo Brown, who posts as @keepitonthedelo, says Southwest lost her luggage “last week.” She expected a voucher or some sort of credit. Instead, she got toiletries to use while they looked for her belongings. “Take this hoe bag and be happy.”

Watch Delo Brown’s Southwest Airlines toiletry kit unboxing.

Then she starts pulling out the contents. There’s a brush, facial pads and cotton swabs, a toothbrush, a razor, wipes, mouthwash and a tiny deodorant. The razor gets a particularly enthusiastic explanation of what it might be used for. By the end, she’s sold:

“This is the best hoe bag I have ever received in my life. This is a caring hoe bag. This is a care package for hoes. I love this. Thank you, Southwest, for my hoe bag.”

A “hoe bag” means a bag with the overnight essentials you’d bring when you might wind up spending the night at somebody else’s place. Toothbrush, deodorant, something to clean up with, perhaps fresh underwear. A couple of the better comments:

“I used to leave those in the top drawer of nightstand on the other side of my bed.” “Got your hoe bag but still missing a WHOLE BAG.”

Other commenters think the plain plastic bag and generic toiletries look more like a hospital admission kit or something handed out in jail. Several compare it to the $148 Skims advent calendar that drew complaints over its inexpensive accessories.

These are meant to get you through a night without your checked bag, whether your luggage didn’t arrive or a disrupted trip leaves it somewhere you can’t get to. You’d get the at the baggage service office. And you’ll find them at other airlines, too.

In a 2009 comparison of airline overnight kits, Wired actually picked Southwest as best overall. Its kit came in a reusable bag with pockets and a hanging hook, and included Speed Stick, Colgate, Scope, Pert Plus and TRESemmé. That was a much more elaborate kit than the plastic bag in this video.

Passengers still need their bags back. Expenses in the meantime may be covered by the credit card they used to purchase the ticket, and airlines have to reimburse reasonable, documented expenses caused by delayed baggage. That can include necessary toiletries and replacement clothing.

Hotels can help, too. Ask the front desk before buying a toothbrush, toothpaste, razor, shaving cream or comb. Many have complimentary basics, while deodorant, mouthwash, makeup wipes and other items depend on the property. A hotel’s lobby shop often isn’t the only option.

I wrote about “Hyatt Has It” when it launched in 2013. What I liked was that Hyatt would actually tell guests what was available and invite them to ask. At participating full service hotels, they’d deliver the items, knock and leave the bag on the doorknob. Hyatt still advertises the program, including requests through the World of Hyatt app.

Holiday Inn’s “Forget Something?” service can offer complimentary toothbrushes, toothpaste, shaving cream, razors and combs.

Of course, some hotels would rather sell you the basics. I covered a stranded Marriott Ambassador member who said the Detroit Metro Airport Marriott wanted $12 for deodorant and another $12 for mouthwash. Their shuttle would take him anywhere within a mile, but the drugstore was 1.1 miles away. He moved to a Hyatt Place and got the toiletries for free.

#6040. One industry increased DC lobbying 337% under Trump; here’s what’s driving the push

Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada could raise costs for businesses and consumers in key battleground states before voters head to the polls.

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his trade agenda, and businesses are spending more on D.C. bureaucrats to help navigate those rules.

Rachel Greszler, who authored a new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF), said companies are paying lobbyists to seek exemptions from tariffs instead of using that money to expand their businesses, hire workers or raise wages.

A new report from former Vice President Mike Pence's group found that lobbying disclosures mention tariffs rising 239% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2024.

The total spending reported on those filings jumped 337%, though it may include lobbying on issues beyond tariffs.

A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR

Businesses are increasingly turning to Washington lobbyists to navigate President Donald Trump’s shifting trade policies, with tariff-related lobbying disclosures surging 239% in the third quarter. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

"Affordability is top of mind for many Americans," Greszler told Fox News Digital, arguing that changing tariffs are raising costs, threatening jobs and squeezing paychecks.

Businesses are responding by stepping up their lobbying efforts. Fourteen organizations spent more than $1 million on lobbying in the third quarter, up from two in the same quarter of 2024. Another 105 spent more than $100,000, compared with 26 two years earlier.

Tariffs may also be affecting prices consumers pay.

TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS; NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK

Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers estimated they added 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods they studied, including imported and U.S.-made products.

Greszler warned that small businesses unable to afford lobbyists to seek tariff exclusions could be forced to scale back or close.

Trump has defended tariffs as a central part of his trade agenda, arguing they will strengthen U.S. manufacturing and bring jobs and investment back to the country. The White House has also said foreign exporters will ultimately bear the cost.

A separate analysis from Advancing American Freedom estimated tariffs resulted in about 75,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in their first year and up to 1 million fewer jobs nationwide than would have been expected under pre-tariff trends.

The group said manufacturing was among the hardest-hit sectors despite being a central target of the administration’s effort to bring factory work back.

Trade has been a central focus of the Trump administration, which has used tariffs to reshape U.S. trade relationships and encourage more manufacturing at home. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The group also said U.S. trade with Canada fell by $50 billion, or 6.5%, before the latest round of Section 338 tariffs took effect. During that period, imports from other countries rose instead of U.S. manufacturing expanding.

As the administration continues to reshape trade policy, businesses will have to decide whether to keep spending on lobbyists and tariff planning or delay investments, hiring and expansion until the rules become clearer.

#6039. How Proactive AI Is Changing the Airline Customer Experience

Erik Zahnlecker, Industry Lead, Travel, Sierra

Moderated by Alison McCarthy, Content Director, Skift Studio

Passengers remember a well-handled disruption far more than an on-time flight, Sierra’s Erik Zahnlecker said, and AI agents can now give every traveler an immediate response. The same agents can use what they learn from passenger interactions to build relationships between trips and drive bookings, upgrades, and ancillary revenue that traditional marketing can’t match.

#6038. LAST CHANCE: Chase’s New $350 IHG Card Offers 200,000 Points—Plus $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Last chance: This offer will end at 9 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, November 19, 2026.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (See rates and fees)

Chase’s new $350 annual fee IHG credit card can return $400 in flight credits before your first renewal, on top of a 200,000-point initial bonus. It also gives you enough elite nights to choose a confirmable suite upgrade without first earning those nights through hotel stays.

I covered the changes to Chase’s IHG card portfolio earlier, but the new IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card deserves a good look. I’ve generally thought of IHG cards as something to get for the bonus and keep for the benefits. This one gives me a reason to consider putting some spending on it, too.

And Chase confirmed to me that its elite nights stack with those from other IHG cards. For someone who already has both the Premier and Business cards, adding Premier Select means 50 annual elite nights total starting with the existing cards’ January 2027 deposits which is enough to choose hotel lounge membership without stays or spending.

The launch offer lets you earn 200,000 IHG points after $5,000 in purchases within three months of account opening. At my half-cent valuation, the 200,000-point bonus is worth $1,000. Having another IHG personal or business card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The published restriction applies to current holders of this particular card, and previous holders who received its new cardmember bonus offer within the past 24 months. Chase told me that 5/24 applies. How To Get $400 In Flight Credits Before Your First Renewal The card offers a $200 airline statement credit per calendar year through December 31, 2027. It takes a single purchase of at least $250 in flight tickets booked directly with an airline. Open the card this fall, make a qualifying purchase in 2026, and make another in 2027 before your first anniversary. That’s $400 back against airfare you’d otherwise buy, compared with a $350 first-year fee. The spending has to land in the appropriate calendar year, so I wouldn’t leave the December purchase until the last minute. That’s a particularly good first year deal. For ongoing value, one $200 airline credit leaves $150 of annual fee to justify. The currently published benefit ends in 2027, so we’ll see if it continues after that. But $150 should not be hard. The Free Night And Hotel Dining Benefits Additional key benefits include: A free night after each account anniversary, capped at 60,000 points. You can add your own points for a more expensive redemption. A 90,000-point night would take the certificate plus 30,000 points. The stay must be completed within 12 months of issuance. This starts at your first anniversary. Up to $300 a year in IHG Food & Beverage Rewards. You get one $75 voucher each quarter. It expires at the end of the quarter, must be applied to eligible charges on your room folio during a participating stay, and any unused balance disappears when you redeem it (e.g. use just $45 and you lose the other $30). Every fourth night free on qualifying points stays. This applies to consecutive standard room award nights at the same hotel. Certificates don’t substitute for the points nights needed to trigger it. Automatic Platinum status. That brings benefits including upgrades subject to availability, but it doesn’t include Diamond’s breakfast welcome amenity choice. Up to $50 in United TravelBank cash. Register to receive $25 in each half of the year. The first-half deposit expires July 15 and the second-half deposit expires January 15 of the following year. I wouldn’t value the dining vouchers at $300 unless I already expected eligible hotel dining in every quarter. And while a 60,000 point certificate can replace $300 worth of points at my valuation, it’s less flexible than 60,000 points in an account since you have to use it for one night before it expires. There are smaller benefits as well like an application fee credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or NEXUS; no foreign transaction fees; and a 30% points-purchase discount that doesn’t stack with other purchase promotions. There’s also a year of DoorDash DashPass and three months of Instacart+, with enrollment by December 31, 2027, plus monthly $10 non-restaurant DoorDash and $10 Instacart offers through that date while the relevant membership is active. A Suite Upgrade Choice Without 20 Hotel Nights The card comes with 20 elite night credits on opening and annually thereafter. Chase allows six to eight weeks for the initial credits, with subsequent annual deposits due by February 1. They count toward both elite status and Milestone Rewards. At the 20-night milestone you can choose 5,000 points, two $20 Food & Beverage Rewards, or one confirmable suite upgrade. I’d take the upgrade. That upgrade can cover an eligible stay of up to five nights, including a points stay. You call IHG between 14 days and 24 hours before arrival to confirm an available entry-level suite. It isn’t a promise that every hotel will have a suite for your dates, and the rules exclude free night certificates and certain brands and rates. The award expires 12 months after selection. At 40 nights you get two milestone choices, which can include both annual hotel lounge membership and another confirmable suite upgrade. The lounge membership covers the member and one guest on eligible stays at hotels with a participating lounge. It lasts through the end of the year you earn the milestone and the following calendar year. Elite Nights Stack Across Cards Chase confirmed to me: Cardmembers who hold multiple IHG One Rewards Credit Cards will receive the applicable Elite Night Credits each card provides. For existing cardmembers, annual ENCs will first be deposited in January 2027. New accounts opened on or after October 1, 2026, will receive their applicable ENCs upon card opening. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. For existing cardholders adding Premier Select, the January 2027 deposits mean: Premier Select plus either Premier or Business: 35 annual elite nights. That leaves just five qualifying hotel nights to reach the 40-night lounge-membership choice. Premier Select plus both Premier and Business: 50 annual elite nights. That gets you the 40-night choices, including lounge membership and a suite upgrade, plus the 50-night reward choice, without hotel stays or card spending. The timing is different for new accounts: cards opened on or after October 1 qualify for their opening credits now. Existing accounts receive their first annual deposits in January. And the spending counters stay separate—$3,000 on one card and $2,000 on another won’t combine into a $5,000 block that earns two nights. $15,000 In Spending Is More Interesting Than It First Looks The card earns 12 points per dollar at participating IHG hotels, 6 on dining and other travel, and 3 on other purchases. At half a cent per point, those are returns of 6%, 3% and 1.5%. Chase’s advertised “up to 28X” at IHG includes base hotel program earnings and the Platinum bonus not just the rewards for credit card spend. But there are spending rewards that change the calculation. You earn two elite nights per $5,000 in purchases, plus five additional nights and 20,000 bonus points at $15,000 in calendar-year spending. Here’s what the card alone produces, assuming the nights credit in the same calendar year. The spending thresholds are cumulative so actual qualifying hotel nights would add to these totals. Calendar-Year Spending   Total Card Elite Nights   Additional Spending Benefits Earned $0   20   20-night milestone choice $15,000   31: 20 + 6 + 5   20,000 bonus points; also reaches the 30-night milestone $25,000   35: 20 + 10 + 5   Diamond status through the following calendar year $40,000   41: 20 + 16 + 5   Additional free night capped at 60,000 points, with points top-up allowed; also reaches the 40-night milestone On $15,000 of purchases earning 3 points per dollar, you’d receive 45,000 points plus the 20,000-point spending bonus. That’s 65,000 points worth $325 at my valuation, compared with $300 from a 2% cash back card, before assigning anything to the eleven additional elite nights or the 30-night milestone choice. That’s better than just a basic return of just 3 points per dollar which I view as about 1.5%. At $40,000, you’d have 140,000 points from those same unbonused purchases and the spending bonus, worth $700 versus $800 in cash back. You’d also have Diamond status, the additional free night, and enough nights to select lounge membership and another suite upgrade. Elite Nights Stack Across Cards Chase confirmed to me: Cardmembers who hold multiple IHG One Rewards Credit Cards will receive the applicable Elite Night Credits each card provides. For existing cardmembers, annual ENCs will first be deposited in January 2027. New accounts opened on or after October 1, 2026, will receive their applicable ENCs upon card opening. In addition, cardmembers can earn 2 ENCs for every $5,000 spent on each eligible card, with spending tracked separately by card account. That corrects the non-stacking language many folks originally noted on the application page. For existing cardholders adding Premier Select, the January 2027 deposits mean: Premier Select plus either Premier or Business: 35 annual elite nights. That leaves just five qualifying hotel nights to reach the 40-night lounge-membership choice. Premier Select plus both Premier and Business: 50 annual elite nights. That gets you the 40-night choices, including lounge membership and a suite upgrade, plus the 50-night reward choice, without hotel stays or card spending. The timing is different for new accounts: cards opened on or after October 1 qualify for their opening credits now. Existing accounts receive their first annual deposits in January. And the spending counters stay separate—$3,000 on one card and $2,000 on another won’t combine into a $5,000 block that earns two nights. $15,000 In Spending Is More Interesting Than It First Looks The card earns 12 points per dollar at participating IHG hotels, 6 on dining and other travel, and 3 on other purchases. At half a cent per point, those are returns of 6%, 3% and 1.5%. Chase’s advertised “up to 28X” at IHG includes base hotel program earnings and the Platinum bonus not just the rewards for credit card spend. But there are spending rewards that change the calculation. You earn two elite nights per $5,000 in purchases, plus five additional nights and 20,000 bonus points at $15,000 in calendar-year spending. Here’s what the card alone produces, assuming the nights credit in the same calendar year. The spending thresholds are cumulative so actual qualifying hotel nights would add to these totals. Calendar-Year Spending   Total Card Elite Nights   Additional Spending Benefits Earned $0   20   20-night milestone choice $15,000   31: 20 + 6 + 5   20,000 bonus points; also reaches the 30-night milestone $25,000   35: 20 + 10 + 5   Diamond status through the following calendar year $40,000   41: 20 + 16 + 5   Additional free night capped at 60,000 points, with points top-up allowed; also reaches the 40-night milestone On $15,000 of purchases earning 3 points per dollar, you’d receive 45,000 points plus the 20,000-point spending bonus. That’s 65,000 points worth $325 at my valuation, compared with $300 from a 2% cash back card, before assigning anything to the eleven additional elite nights or the 30-night milestone choice. That’s better than just a basic return of just 3 points per dollar which I view as about 1.5%. At $40,000, you’d have 140,000 points from those same unbonused purchases and the spending bonus, worth $700 versus $800 in cash back. You’d also have Diamond status, the additional free night, and enough nights to select lounge membership and another suite upgrade. #6037. New Webinar: Turning Travel Disruptions Into Guest Loyalty

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Travel is sold in pieces. Guests experience it as one trip. When a flight delay knocks out the connection, the first hotel night, and the plans after it, guests expect someone to help put it back together. That’s travel’s accountability gap.

Disruption has become the real test of loyalty, and a chance for hotels to build it beyond points. Matt Miller of Marriott International and Lindsay Tuhey of Allianz Partners join Skift to break down how hotels can support guests across the whole trip and keep ownership of the relationship.

Tags: allianz partners, disruption, loyalty, marriott international, partner content, Skift Studio, Skift Studio Showcase: Hospitality, webinar

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Skift is hosting a webinar with Matt Miller of Marriott International and Lindsay Tuhey of Allianz Partners on what the session calls travel's accountability gap: travel is sold in pieces, but guests experience it as one trip, and when a flight delay knocks out a connection, the first hotel night, and the plans after it, guests expect someone to help put it back together. The session frames disruption as the real test of loyalty, and as a chance for hotels to build loyalty beyond points. The agenda covers where to focus 2027 loyalty investment as flexible cancellation, points, and status lose their pull; what guests need when a trip goes wrong, from medical help abroad to coverage for everyone in the room; whether travel protection belongs in the hotel booking path; which guest moments are too high-stakes to automate; and how to structure a protection partnership so the guest relationship stays with the hotel brand.

#6034. Bilt Will Stop Awarding You 4% Bilt Cash Earning At Card Renewal—Unless You Change This App Setting

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Bilt Rewards is changing how rewards are earned on their credit cards. Today, cardmembers have a choice:

Earn 4% back in Bilt Cash, in addition to points. That Bilt Cash can be redeemed for points-earning on housing payments, faster points-earning (accelerators) and redemptions on hotel stays or with partners like Blade, Lyft, Walgreens, etc.

Skip Bilt Cash and earn ‘up to 1.25x on housing payments’ based on your month’s spending. Bilt is moving everyone over to the second option, however existing cardmembers and those who apply, are approved and accept their card through December 31 can opt in to preserving #1. It’s possible to do better with earning up to 1.25x on housing payments, but for most people doing significant spend on the card (where they’re earning more Bilt Cash than their housing payment would consume) they’ll come out ahead earning Bilt Cash. And of course you can always choose to move over to the new model later if you prefer! You need to proactively choose continuing to earn Bilt Cash, to avoid moving over. Once you actually move over (starting at your card renewal date) it cannot be reversed. I’ve already protected my Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) with the legacy earning structure. This is the card I use for most of my spending. Here’s where you go in the app to do it. Go to your wallet and select your Bilt card. Then either go to your current choice for Bonus Rewards (e.g. “Flexible Bilt Cash”) underneath Your card rewards or go to Manage card and select bonus rewards which is the last option at the bottom. Select ‘your rewards are updating’ which is the top option on the screen. The default, which is already selected, is the new rewards model. Swipe right… Select ‘flexible Bilt Cash’ and hit save. You have until your card renewal date to make this choice, but if you preserve the old earning model you can always make the (irreversible) switch later. I’ve already made my choice. #6032. Your Passport May Have ‘POO’ Stamped In It—And The U.S. Government Put It There [Roundup]

News and notes from around the interweb: Thousands of Passports Have Been Stamped With ‘Poo’ and You Might Not Have Realized: Here’s How to Check CBP decided it didn’t want to use PDX as its port-of-entry code, and for whatever reason, obvious choices like POR, PTL, and POL were rejected. Instead, the U.S. government decided the most appropriate port-of-entry code for Portland was POO. And that’s why there are thousands of passports with the word POO stamped on them. If you’ve ever flown into Portland, OR, from abroad, take a look at your passport to see if you also have the stamp.

#6031. The Censors Come for Michel Houellebecq

French author Michel Houellebecq speaks at an event in Parma, Italy, August 3, 2021.

As is so often the case, Vahaken Mouradian is on the case. His disquisition on the French novelist Michel Houellebecq’s torment at the hands of censorial French authorities is as enlightening as it is righteous in its revulsion.

Blessedly, Mouradian and National Review are not alone in taking France to task over its harassment of the prolific author. The New York Post is on it. #6030. Tripadvisor Reverses Merger of Experiences Teams, Cuts Cruise Critic Staff 60%: Scoop

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Tripadvisor's Matt Goldberg was interviewed by Skift Research's Seth Borko at Skift Global Forum on September 19, 2024. Skift

There's often a lot of hype about the strategic benefits in a restructuring. Tripadvisor admitted its November 2025 restructuring didn't work.

Tripadvisor has unwound a 2025 restructuring that combined its “things to do” and Viator experiences teams under one roof. The two businesses are back to separate teams, similar to how they were organized before the November 2025 changes, according to a source familiar with Tripadvisor’s operations.

Under the new structure, Tripadvisor’s things to do business will have its own team. That business mainly generates leads for Viator, the company’s main experiences brand and the focus of its investment. Viator’s experiences operations will have a separate team.

In a November 4 internal email to employees, sent after an all-hands meeting at which outgoing CEO Matt Goldberg announced a company-wide restructuring, Tripadvisor President Kristen Dalton wrote: “Experiences will be singularly focused on the Viator and Bokun brands with a focus on growth.” Bokun is Tripadvisor’s back-end reservations technology business for experiences operators, not a con

Tags: experiences, layoffs, metasearch, online travel newsletter, restructuring, skift scoop, tripadvisor, viator

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

Tripadvisor has reversed the November 2025 restructuring that merged its "things to do" and Viator experiences teams, returning to two separate organizations with, as President Kristen Dalton wrote to employees, "far less overlap between them and fewer shared services." The company told investors the combination "has not proven out as we expected": over the past 12 months, experiences booked through Viator and partner channels grew in the low teens while the Tripadvisor channel declined by high single digits, and third-quarter experiences revenue fell 3% year over year to $284.4 million. Tripadvisor said November 5 it would cut 425 employee and contractor roles in its legacy Hotels & Other segment — about 60% of roles dedicated to hotel metasearch, display and sponsored ads, flights, cruise, and car rentals — with about 150 moving to Viator and a net reduction of roughly 275 positions, or around 17% of the workforce according to the Boston Globe. Cruise Critic, which sources said is profitable, is shrinking by 60% to around 20 employees, with all but one editorial staffer gone. The restructuring is expected to save about $40 million a year against $15 million to $20 million in charges, and it lands amid a leadership overhaul: CEO Matt Goldberg steps down in February, CFO Michael Noonan leaves December 31, and Dalton becomes interim CFO on January 1. Activist investor Starboard Value disclosed a 9% stake in July 2025 and gained four of 10 board seats in March; Tripadvisor has said no option is off the table for monetizing Viator.

#6029. American Airlines Canceled My Family’s Tickets—Then Didn’t Answer My Reply To Regulators

American Airlines has let the deadline its final reply in my Department of Transportation complaint pass without offering any last defense. The airline had canceled award tickets I’d booked for my family nearly three weeks after issuing them. These were ‘mistake fare’ tickets – the airline had been pricing multi-city awards at a discount (just the cost of the first segment) for several weeks, and the Department of Transportation lets them cancel mistake fares under terms consistent with their contract of carriage. I’ve always believed that it’s reasonable to cancel a mistake promptly. I’ve written about that for over a decade. I’ll book a fare because if an airline is letting people fly, say, to Paris for $60 I’d like to be one of those people. But if they promptly cancel, I figure it’s no harm, no foul. The Department of Transportation has rules that an airline has to make a customer whole for any reasonable nonrefundable expenses incurred in reliance on the fare. I intentionally do not make any of those – I wait to see whether the trip will be honored first. (This is another reason why any cancellation needs to happen promptly.) American set rules precisely around this – they give themselves 72 hours after discovering the mistake. They set it this way intentionally favorable to themselves – it’s not 72 hours from booking, but from whenever they discover the issue which could come later. American broke its own rules, taking about two weeks to cancel the tickets after they discovered the error. My hunch is a middle manager thought they could handle things themselves without really escalating the issue and bungled it. American writes the rules. I believe they should at least have to follow their own rules. Consumers get 24 hours after booking to cancel a ticket they purchase such as when they make a mistake (with a bunch of caveats), American gives itself much more generous terms, they should at least follow those terms. American Airlines Files Its Defense I complained to the Department of Transportation that American was violating its Contract of Carriage. In their response to my complaint, American’s position was the redemption pricing was a mistake, AAdvantage terms let them cancel mistakes, and consumers shouldn’t be allowed a windfall. American says that their AAdvantage Terms are “the beginning and the end of this case.” Plus, consumers don’t have any rights. Legally, they can sue an airline only for breach of its own terms – the Supreme Court has said for anything else, go to the Department of Transportation. American’s position it consumers can’t go to the Department of Transportation (they have ‘no private right of action’). American’s Position Is Legally Shaky I responded to American’s arguments that the terms American wrote incorporate American’s Conditions of Carriage and International Tariff and specifically say those agreements take priority in a conflict. So they have to follow the rules they set out in those documents. They give themselves the right to cancel mistakes, but give themselves a deadline to do so. They didn’t want a short deadline after booking, so they gave themselves 72 hours after whenever they discover the error. That’s a standard favorable to them. But they still took about two weeks after they admit discovery to cancel. American quotes its general right to correct mistakes in its reply, while ignoring any discussion of the deadline it wrote for itself – never explaining why that deadline doesn’t apply. They claim there’s fundamentally nothing unfair or deceptive about correcting a “windfall.” I accepted American’s right to cancel promptly in my complaint. The practice I challenged is leaving issued tickets in place after their own cancellation period expired, then cancelling after the deadline they set passed. The Department has treated misleading contractual protections as an unfair and deceptive practice in the past. In Gurevich v. Alitalia, it found the airline misled passengers by publishing protections in its conditions of carriage and invoking inconsistent tariff provisions to deny them. Here, the Conditions and Tariff both promise the same cancellation deadline, yet American claims an unrestricted right to cancel under the AAdvantage Terms which they say give them a right inconsistent with the Contract of Carriage and Tariff (but they don’t, since the AAdvantage terms say that when there’s a conflict, those other agreements trump). American Says Consumers Don’t Even Get To Complain To The DOT American claims I lack a private right of action against them. They can unilaterally act against a passenger, and the passenger doesn’t get to do anything about it. That’s actually irrelevant here because I’m not suing them. I’m not taking action against them, I’m asking the Department of Transportation to investigate. British Airways tried a similar move and the Department rejected this defense in Edelman v. British Airways, explaining that the Secretary’s authority to investigate made defenses about an individual consumer’s standing and rights irrelevant. Why American May Not Have Bothered To Respond It seems to me that American’s lawyers made bad arguments here, probably because they really did break the rules they set so they don’t actually have good arguments. But American will still probably win, because it’s up to the Department of Transportation to choose whether to do anything about it or not. My hunch is that the American already knows that they aren’t going to. The Department of Transportation set a deadline of November 13 for American Airlines to respond with a reply to my response. American did not even offer one. When there’s a formal rulemaking, communications with the Department have to go through the docket or at least get logged in the docket. The same goes for an actual enforcement action. Neither one is the case here at this point. Ex parte communications aren’t prohibited prior to the commencement of an enforcement action. 14 C.F.R. § 300.2(c)(3) allows “Communications made in the course of an investigation to determine whether formal enforcement action should be begun.” So American’s lawyers can discuss the allegations and argue against commencing enforcement outside the docket. After enforcement proceedings begin there’s a requirement for communications with decision-making staff to occur on the record (with any ex parte communications recorded, with notice given to the parties), but not before commencement. So it’s possible that American Airlines has had offline conversations with the department about this issue and they believe they’ve convinced DOT not to pursue an enforcement action – no need for an on the record response. I don’t have evidence this is the case, but it’s exactly the scenario I was expecting if they didn’t respond by the deadline. DOT will ultimately need to either pursue an enforcement action, or explain why they aren’t doing so. But in practice there’s really no timeframe in which that has to happen. DOT can choose to sit on this for years. Honestly, though, I expected American’s lawyers to just try to muddy the issue, and say something like: Sure the Contract of Carriage sets a 72-hour expectation but doesn’t limit the right to cancel, those are separate. We did not meet the 72-hour deadline, but there’s no consequence for that failure. The Department’s 2015 policy on regulatory discretion for mistake fares did not specifically require action within 72 hours, DOT policy is to allow mistakes to be cancelled. I do not think this is at all true or close to what American’s own policies say. And it doesn’t require multiple biglaw partners to come up with it. The fact that they do not even bother to say this tells me they are confident of how DOT will (not) act. They can ignore their Contract of Carriage with impunity if the vibes are right and DOT sympathizes with them. Just last month, the Department of Transportation said “Under @SecDuffy , DOT will always stand up for passengers by holding airlines accountable” – we will see whether that’s true.
